topic: Endoscopic Pituitary / Anterior Skull Base Approach
text: **Pediatric endonasal corridor limits**: Three anatomic factors constrain endonasal skull base surgery in children: piriform aperture size (a real limit only under about age 2, overcome with a sublabial/translabial extension), sphenoid pneumatization, and intercarotid distance. Sphenoid pneumatization starts after age 2. By 6-7 years the anterior sphenoid wall is aerated in all children and the planum in 88%, but only 77% of the anterior sellar wall and 32% of the sellar floor; the clivus aerates after age 10. The cavernous intercarotid distance is narrower until about 6-7 years and adultlike by 9-10. None of these is a contraindication; they mean more drilling and heavier reliance on navigation. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1924, 1931)

topic: Endoscopic Pituitary / Anterior Skull Base Approach
text: **Pediatric reconstruction options**: The nasoseptal flap (posterior septal artery) can reconstruct anterior, sellar and clival defects in children, but it is small relative to the skull base before about age 14. Middle turbinate and palatal flaps are usually impractical in children. Backups are the pericranial flap (supraorbital/supratrochlear) for anterior defects, the inferior turbinate flap or temporoparietal fascia flap for central defects, and temporoparietal fascia or temporalis muscle for lateral defects. Dural defects are closed with an inlay fascial graft plus a vascularized onlay flap. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1922, 1930, 1940)

topic: Endoscopic Pituitary / Anterior Skull Base Approach
text: **Pediatric pituitary adenoma**: Pituitary adenomas are rare in children (about 3% of supratentorial masses) and are usually functioning: prolactinoma is most common, then ACTH- and GH-secreting tumors. Nonfunctioning, TSH and gonadotroph adenomas make up only 3-6%. Children often present with endocrine signs (growth failure, short stature, delayed puberty) rather than visual loss. Surgery is indicated for every type except prolactinoma, which is treated medically, and radiation is avoided in children. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1924, 1933)

topic: Endoscopic Pituitary / Anterior Skull Base Approach
text: **Rathke cleft cyst management**: A small nonenhancing nodule inside the cyst is considered pathognomonic for Rathke cleft cyst, which otherwise can be hard to tell from a cystic adenoma or craniopharyngioma. Incidental cysts are observed. Symptomatic (headache) or enlarging cysts are fenestrated and drained into the sphenoid through an endoscopic transsellar or infrasellar route. The lining is not stripped, because removal adds CSF leak and gland injury risk without benefit. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1933)

topic: Endoscopic Pituitary / Anterior Skull Base Approach
text: **Pediatric craniopharyngioma strategy**: Craniopharyngioma is the most common benign pediatric sellar/parasellar tumor (up to half of pediatric sellar tumors), usually adamantinomatous. Gross total resection gives the lowest recurrence (mean about 17%), and recurrences cluster 3.5-5 years after treatment. With hypothalamic invasion, subtotal resection plus radiation may be preferred, because aggressive removal risks hyperphagia and obesity, memory and behavior problems, and temperature dysregulation. Tumors are classed by position relative to the stalk (pre-, trans-, or retroinfundibular), which sets endonasal difficulty; pituitary transposition for retroinfundibular tumors risks hypopituitarism. Cystic recurrences can be aspirated or treated with intracystic bleomycin or beta-emitting isotopes, and these cases carry a high postoperative CSF leak risk. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1933-1934, 1939)

topic: Endoscopic Pituitary / Anterior Skull Base Approach
text: **Postoperative diabetes insipidus criteria**: After sellar surgery, urine output above 2-3 mL/kg over 2 hours suggests DI. It is confirmed by serum sodium above 150 mEq/L with dilute urine (specific gravity under 1.005, osmolality 50-150 mOsm/kg). Mild DI is managed with fluid and electrolyte replacement. Desmopressin is given for persistent DI, severe dehydration or sodium disturbance, or troublesome polyuria and thirst. Postoperative DI is usually self-limited. Patients at risk of cortisol deficiency get perioperative stress steroids. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1938)

topic: Endoscopic Pituitary / Anterior Skull Base Approach
text: **Open approaches and facial growth in children**: The skull base reaches mature shape at about 12 years and the face at about 16. Extensive craniofacial osteotomies, periosteal stripping, and radiation can disturb growth centers and cause asymmetry. Permanent teeth usually erupt after age 10, so a Le Fort I down-fracture is avoided in young children. Plan any maxillotomy with a panoramic film or coronal CT to spare tooth buds; midface degloving and transmaxillary routes give wide exposure while preserving dentition. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1931, 1940)

**Fibrous dysplasia treatment thresholds**: Fibrous dysplasia is diagnosed by imaging without biopsy: CT shows an expansile ground-glass lesion that respects cortex and foramina. On MRI it is low on T1 and T2 and can look alarming, so a CT should follow an incidental MRI finding. Malignant change (osteosarcoma, fibrosarcoma) is about 0.4% and more likely after radiation, so radiation is avoided. Treat only symptomatic disease (deformity, cranial neuropathy, pain). Headache seldom resolves with surgery. Chen-Noordhoff zones guide extent: zone 1 (fronto-orbital, zygoma, upper maxilla) gets total resection, while zones 2-4 (hair-bearing cranium, central skull base, tooth-bearing jaws) get conservative or partial contouring. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1934-1935)

**Fibrous dysplasia and the optic canal**: The optic canal is involved in up to 90% of sphenoid fibrous dysplasia. Asymptomatic patients are observed with serial vision checks, because about 97% keep stable vision without surgery. Prophylactic decompression left only 87% stable, so it can cause the loss it aims to prevent. Give steroids for acute visual decline while arranging decompression, which can be done endonasally; partial decompression is often enough. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1935)

**Origin and associations**: Angiofibroma occurs almost only in males aged about 12-21. Current evidence favors a vascular malformation or hamartoma from incomplete regression of the first branchial arch artery, rather than a true neoplasm. It is more common in familial adenomatous polyposis. Intracranial extension occurs in 10-20%, through bone erosion or along the pterygoid canal, foramen rotundum or superior orbital fissure; true dural invasion is rare. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1936)

**Residual tumor and ending surveillance**: Supply from internal carotid branches (vidian, cavernous) cannot be embolized and predicts more blood loss and staged surgery. Small residuals at the skull base or intracranially can be watched with imaging, because most do not grow and many involute. Regrowth is usually treated endoscopically, and radiation is generally not used. Surveillance can usually stop in the early to mid 20s, after adolescence ends. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1936)

topic: Neonatal Nasal Obstruction and Congenital Nasal Masses
text: **Dermoid with skull base extension**: Nasal dermoids make up about 61% of congenital midline nasal masses, and 5-45% extend intracranially at the foramen cecum or crista galli. A bifid crista on CT is suggestive but not diagnostic, because the infant crista may be unossified; MRI is the study of choice. Incomplete excision of the cyst or tract recurs in 50-100%. Excise a skin punctum, use an external rhinoplasty approach for extracranial disease, and follow an intracranial tract endonasally, drilling the skull base to dura and marsupializing any extradural part. If a dural tract biopsy shows dermal elements, a craniotomy is needed for complete removal. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1931-1932)

topic: Neonatal Nasal Obstruction and Congenital Nasal Masses
text: **Cephalocele classification and approach**: Congenital cephaloceles present at a mean age of 2, almost always contain brain (meningoencephalocele), and nearly always need repair. Acquired ones are usually posttraumatic meningoceles. Frontonasal lesions (through the fonticulus frontalis) are best repaired externally. Frontoethmoidal and fronto-orbital lesions, and basal cephaloceles (transethmoidal, sphenoethmoidal, transsphenoidal, spheno-orbital, sphenomaxillary), suit an endonasal approach. Age is not a contraindication (repairs reported at 1.5-23 months), but repair in infants without a leak can wait. Confirm the sac holds no vessels or pituitary before removing the gliotic intranasal tissue with bipolar cautery, then close the defect as an underlay, overlay, or combined graft. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1932-1933)

**Pediatric traumatic leaks**: A skull base fracture occurs in 5-14% of pediatric head injuries, most often in the temporal bone (63%). CSF leaks complicate 12-30% of skull fractures. About 80% close spontaneously, most within 72 hours, and closure is more likely in very young children and with temporal bone fractures. Meningitis develops in 10-26% of persistent leaks (median about 11 days after injury) and carries about 10% mortality, so repair leaks that persist beyond a few days. Comminuted fractures, associated midface fractures, and lateral frontal sinus extension favor open repair. Beta-2 transferrin testing needs about 0.5 mL and the protein stays detectable for at least 7 days at room temperature. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1938)

topic: Endoscopic CSF Leak Repair / Nasoseptal Flap
text: **Postoperative leak after endonasal skull base surgery**: Postoperative leaks follow up to 5% of endonasal skull base operations when vascularized flaps are used. Risk rises with obesity, a spontaneous-leak presentation, blood-CSF mixing, craniopharyngioma, and large defects that open a cistern or ventricle. Clues are unilateral watery rhinorrhea, the reservoir sign, a double-ring sign, and persistent or increasing pneumocephalus. Early return to the OR (within about 24 hours) works well. Lumbar drains are reserved for recurrent or high-flow leaks or raised CSF pressure, because routine diversion has not been shown to prevent leaks. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1939)

topic: Head and Neck Sarcomas, Chordoma and Chondrosarcoma
text: **Pediatric chordoma and skull base malignancy**: In children the clivus is the most common chordoma site. Younger patients have faster growth and worse outcomes, especially under age 5. Metastases occur in 10-20% clinically (up to 43% at autopsy), and overall 5-year survival is about 54%. Radiation is advised for large or subtotally resected tumors. Across pediatric skull base malignancy (bimodal peaks at 3.5 and 17.5 years), histology predicts survival: SCC and salivary cancers do worst, high-grade sarcoma, esthesioneuroblastoma and chordoma are intermediate (60-70% at 5 years), and low-grade sarcoma does best. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1937)

**Pediatric sinonasal malignancy profile**: In a single-center series, pediatric sinonasal cancer presented at a median age of 12. The maxillary sinus was the most common site, followed by ethmoid, nasal cavity, sphenoid and nasopharynx. Rhabdomyosarcoma made up over 70% of maxillary sinus tumors and 34% overall, followed by SCC and esthesioneuroblastoma. Treatment follows adult principles: resect with negative margins when feasible, then chemoradiation. In parameningeal RMS, surgery is mainly for diagnosis, debulking and salvage. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1937)

**Pediatric mucoceles**: Mucoceles are rare in children and should prompt a search for cystic fibrosis with polyps, fibrous dysplasia, trauma, or prior surgery. In children they are usually unilateral and frontoethmoidal, then maxillary, sphenoid and posterior ethmoid. Rule out a meningocele, neuroblastoma, lymphoma or rhabdomyosarcoma that can look like an expansile sinus lesion. Wide endoscopic marsupialization with mucosal preservation has low recurrence. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 115, p 1935-1936)

**Language referral indicators by age**: Refer for full speech-language evaluation when a child falls at or below about the 10th percentile. At 12 months, the trigger is no response to at least one familiar word in a familiar setting, or little interest in communicating with a caregiver. At 24-36 months, it is fewer than 50 words or no two-word combinations (Language Development Survey); 50-60% of these toddlers still score at or below the 10th percentile at ages 3-5. A 3-year-old speaking mainly single words, or a 4-year-old who cannot hold a simple conversation in roughly three-word utterances, should be referred. Verify hearing on the day of testing, because transient conductive loss is common. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 116, p 1945-1946)

**Intelligibility and sound development milestones**: By 24 months a child uses about 10 consonants, mostly at the start of words. By 36 months most vowels are correct and final consonants appear. By 48 months most consonants are present, but late sounds (r, l, s, sh, th) may still be in error. Refer if parents estimate that a stranger understands less than 50% of the child's speech at 22 months, less than 75% at 37 months, or less than 100% at 47 months. Speech delay affects about 15.6% of 3-year-olds and 3.8% of 6-year-olds, with a male predominance. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 116, p 1947-1948)

**Childhood apraxia of speech features**: Apraxia of speech is a motor planning disorder, while dysarthria is a disorder of motor execution. Apraxia shows many inconsistent sound errors, abnormal prosody, disrupted transitions between sounds and syllables, and difficulty with volitional nonspeech oral movements. It can occur without a confirmed neurologic lesion. It needs intensive motor-based therapy and is not an ENT surgical problem. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 116, p 1948)

**Prevalence and prognosis of language disorders**: About 12-15% of English-speaking children have some language disorder, and 5-7% have specific language impairment (no neurologic, sensory, cognitive or emotional cause). Family history of speech, language or reading problems is a risk factor. Prognosis for complete mastery is guarded: in a longitudinal study, over 70% of children with language disorders at age 5 still had language, cognitive and academic deficits in adolescence. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 116, p 1946-1947)

**Stuttering natural history and when to treat**: Stuttering usually begins at about 2.5-5 years. Prevalence is under 1%, with a lifetime incidence of about 5%. About 75% of young children recover, usually within 6-12 months of onset (sometimes 18-24 months), but full recovery becomes much less likely after about age 7. The male to female ratio is near 1:1 to 2:1 at onset and 3-4:1 in adults, because more girls recover. About 30% also have a speech sound disorder. Refer or treat when there is a family history, stuttering for 3-6 months or more, rising frequency, physical tension or struggle, negative reactions, or a coexisting speech or language disorder. Fluent speech in the office does not rule it out, and parent reports are reliable. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 116, p 1950-1953)

**Post-adenoidectomy and post-palatoplasty VPI**: In this text, VPI after adenoidectomy occurs in about 1 in 1200 children. Risk rises with a repaired cleft or submucous cleft, oromotor delay, generalized hypotonia, intellectual disability, a family history of clefting or VPI, and preoperative nasal regurgitation or hypernasality; superior-half (partial) adenoidectomy reduces it. Even after palatoplasty, 20-30% of cleft patients still have VPI. Very large tonsils whose upper poles project between the velum and pharyngeal wall can also cause VPI. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 117, p 1963-1964)

**Pharyngeal flap: airway safety and technique**: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is the most common problem complicating recovery from a pharyngeal flap. Remove enlarged tonsils and adenoids first and wait 4-6 weeks. In retrognathic children, especially those who needed a tracheotomy in infancy, get a sleep study and consider waiting for growth; otherwise the flap may need takedown, CPAP or tracheotomy. The superiorly based flap is raised on prevertebral fascia with its base near the C1 arch and is sized to the gap. A flap that is too narrow leaves VPI, and one that is too wide or whose ports scar down causes hyponasality and OSA. Poor lateral wall motion before surgery is not a contraindication. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 117, p 1968)

**Small gaps: augmentation and injection**: For small gaps, an obstructing flap is excessive. A rolled pharyngeal flap (muscle rolled into a bulge under replaced mucosa) or posterior wall injection (autologous fat, collagen, hydroxyapatite) suits gaps of no more than about 2 mm AP, or tenuous closure such as in wind instrument players. Injected materials last only about 3-6 months, though the speech benefit can persist. None is FDA approved for this site. Teflon is abandoned because of infection, granuloma, migration and embolic risk. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 117, p 1968-1969)

**Sphincter pharyngoplasty, Furlow and revision**: Sphincter pharyngoplasty transposes superiorly based palatopharyngeus myomucosal flaps into a transverse incision at the level of closure. It suits poor lateral wall motion or deep lateral recesses when central closure is present, and it carries much lower OSA risk than a pharyngeal flap. Furlow double-opposing Z-plasty rebuilds the levator sling and lengthens the palate, mainly for submucous cleft. A failed flap can be redone 6-12 months later, lined with nasal mucosa flaps from the soft palate. Reassess resonance objectively 3-6 months after any VPI operation. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 117, p 1969)

**Prosthetic management**: A speech bulb obturator fills the velopharyngeal port when the velum is too short. A palatal lift holds a long but poorly moving velum up and back, typically in neurologically impaired patients with poor timing and coordination. Prostheses can be tuned under nasendoscopy and suit poor surgical candidates. Drawbacks are frequent refitting as the child grows, poor tolerance, and loss of the device. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 117, p 1967-1968)

**Instrumental assessment specifics**: Nasometry calculates nasalance, the ratio of nasal to total (nasal plus oral) acoustic energy. Multiview videofluoroscopy needs frontal and base views because the lateral view misses a unilateral gap. Nasendoscopy is done after topical decongestant and 2% lidocaine, through the middle meatus, viewing the port from above during recorded connected speech. It requires some cooperation, and adding laryngoscopy screens for compensatory vocal nodules. A Passavant ridge occurs in about 20% of people and usually sits below the plane of closure. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 117, p 1962, 1966-1967)

**Nodules in children**: Nodules are the most common cause of childhood dysphonia (about 50% of dysphonic children; 56% in a 599-patient series), with a prepubertal male predominance. Most resolve with voice therapy, hydration and patience, and even children 4 and younger can benefit from direct therapy. Surgery is not first-line and is considered only for persistent nodules that impair intelligibility in a motivated family. On stroboscopy, preserved mucosal wave favors a nodule, while an adynamic segment suggests a cyst or other lesion. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 118, p 1953, 1978-1979)

**Pediatric medialization ladder**: Left fold palsy after PDA ligation causes a breathy voice and aspiration of thin liquids. Injection medialization can be done even in infants, using temporary gels for immediate airway protection or fat or calcium hydroxylapatite for longer effect; check the swallow afterward with a modified barium swallow. School-aged children start with voice therapy. Younger children get injection if therapy fails, while older children and adolescents can have framework surgery with implants that can be upsized as the larynx grows (adolescents may tolerate it under local anesthesia). Ansa-to-RLN reinnervation adds tone. Voice therapy is still needed after surgery, because compensatory hyperfunction persists after the gap is closed. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 118, p 1979-1980)

**Evidence behind early identification**: Permanent congenital hearing loss affects about 2-3 per 1000 births. Before universal screening, children were typically identified at 18-30 months. Yoshinaga-Itano's Colorado data showed that children identified before 6 months and given intervention within 2 months of diagnosis had language quotients close to normal, regardless of degree of loss (mild through profound) and of whether the family used spoken or signed language. A two-stage OAE then automated ABR protocol is preferred in well-baby nurseries. Genetic causes account for about 50% of congenital loss. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 119, p 1987-1989)

**Pediatric hearing aid candidacy and timing**: Bilateral thresholds above 25 dB HL of any type (conductive, mixed or sensorineural) warrant amplification. Children with mild, unilateral or fluctuating loss may also qualify, especially if they struggle academically; decide in the context of cognition, comorbidities and school performance, not thresholds alone. Do not wait for complete behavioral audiometry: fit infants from click and 500 Hz tone-burst ABR thresholds and adjust as data accrue. BTE aids with soft earmolds are standard. Earmolds must be remade often as the canal grows, and new feedback usually means a poorly fitting mold that needs replacing. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 120, p 1996, 2006)

**Pediatric verification: DSL v5 and RECD**: Pediatric fittings are prescribed with DSL v5 (or NAL-NL2), which aim for higher audibility because young children need more speech level to learn language. Because small ear canals produce much higher SPL than a 2-cc coupler, the real-ear-to-coupler difference (RECD) is measured and used to predict real-ear output from coupler measurements, with accuracy similar to probe microphone testing. Maximum output is set from OSPL90 and prescriptive targets rather than from loudness discomfort judgments that infants cannot give. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 120, p 2008)

**Classroom acoustics and binaural fitting**: Recommended classroom SNR for children with hearing loss is at least +15 to +30 dB, but typical classrooms run -6 to +6 dB. Reverberation should be no more than 0.4 seconds, and the SNR falls with every doubling of speaker distance. Omnidirectional aids do not improve SNR, so remote microphone (FM) systems, preferential seating, and acoustic treatment are key, and IDEA requires amplification services at no cost to the child. Bilateral fitting is standard: binaural summation adds about 3 dB, and it avoids head shadow loss of high-frequency consonant cues from the unaided side. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 120, p 2006, 2010)

**Intraoperative testing and activation**: Intraoperative testing usually includes impedance telemetry (short and open circuits) and electrically evoked compound action potentials on selected electrodes. It is done during flap closure, so it adds no anesthesia time. Absent responses call for an intraoperative radiograph of array position. Tell the audiologist if any electrodes are outside the cochlea so they are not activated. ECAP thresholds predict the shape of the comfort level profile. Activation is 1-4 weeks after surgery, in two visits that build progressively louder maps (T and C/M levels). Maps are revisited about every 3 months until stable, then every 6 months, with magnet strength checked each visit to prevent flap breakdown. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 122, p 2040-2041)

**Age at implantation and language outcomes**: In the CDaCI cohort, a receptive language score typical of a hearing 2.3-year-old was reached at 3.4 years by children implanted under 18 months, 4.7 years by those implanted at 18-36 months, and 5.3 years by those implanted after 36 months (expressive scores were similar). Using sign language before implantation did not slow spoken language growth in children implanted by 18 months. When residual hearing exists, a 3-6 month hearing aid trial builds auditory awareness and device routines. With no residual hearing on ABR or behavioral testing, aids are futile and visual-gestural interaction is the better use of the wait. Meningitis with early ossification is the clearest reason to implant under 12 months. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 122, p 2037-2039)

**The contralateral ear**: If the opposite ear benefits from a hearing aid without binaural interference, bimodal use is encouraged; long-term aid users often rely on it for intonation and music. If it cannot support speech recognition, consider a second implant. Bilateral implants improve hearing in noise and soft speech (summation), remove the head shadow, improve overhearing, and allow some localization over time. Simultaneous implants need little ear-specific training, while a sequential second ear often needs therapy with that side alone. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch 122, p 2041-2042)

**Respiratory role of the PCA and CT**: the posterior cricoarytenoid is the only active laryngeal dilator and fires with each breath slightly before the diaphragm. Under partial upper airway obstruction, negative pressure sensed through the superior laryngeal nerve boosts PCA drive while diaphragm force falls. Because the two muscles behave differently, the phrenic nerve is a poor donor for PCA reinnervation. Cricothyroid contraction lengthens both folds (one CT moves both, without rotating the glottis) but does not widen the glottis on inspiration. (Cummings 7e, Ch 53, p 801–802)

**Laryngeal reflex arcs**: the larynx has far more sensory receptors than the lungs. The superior laryngeal nerve carries the afferent limb of the closure (apneic) reflex and of laryngeal cardiovascular reflexes. Stimulation during intubation or extubation, or strong negative pressure in OSA, can cause bradycardia, ectopy and arrhythmia, with the vagus as the efferent limb. In infants the closure reflex can be set off by something as mild as water; its strength rises and then falls over a time course that matches peak SIDS incidence. The cough reflex is damped in deep sleep. (Cummings 7e, Ch 53, p 802–803)

**Recurrent paroxysmal laryngospasm**: sudden episodes of laryngeal closure, often brought on by eating, steam or odors. They usually start during a URI or after RLN surgical trauma. Some cases come from reflux and respond to acid suppression; others reflect a hypersensitive closure reflex. Most resolve on their own within a few months, but a minority become chronic. (Cummings 7e, Ch 53, p 802)

**FEESST thresholds**: an air pulse from the scope port tests the laryngeal adductor reflex. A response at about 3 mm Hg is normal, 6 mm Hg means mild sensory loss, 9 mm Hg means moderate loss, and no response at 9 mm Hg means severe loss. Test each side, because asymmetry points to the side of the lesion. FEES needs no anesthetic and can be done at the bedside, but MBS is better for the oral and upper esophageal phases. (Cummings 7e, Ch 56, p 831)

**Laryngeal dystonia subtypes**: about 80% of cases are adductor and about 20% abductor, and some are mixed. Two rare forms are adductor breathing dystonia and singer's dystonia. In adductor breathing dystonia the folds close on inspiration, causing stridor and dyspnea, but it is self-limited, does not cause hypoxia, and does not need a surgical airway. Singer's dystonia affects only singing in professional singers and may later spread to speech. Meige syndrome combines blepharospasm, oromandibular dystonia and torticollis with SD. Sensory tricks (pinching the nose, pressing the occiput or abdomen) and better voicing after a yawn, sneeze, singing or yelling are typical. (Cummings 7e, Ch 57, p 834)

**Natural history and genetics**: onset of dystonia is bimodal, peaking near ages 8 and 42. Up to 16% of patients whose dystonia starts in the larynx later spread to another body region, so re-examine them periodically. About 10% have a family history. Idiopathic dystonia is a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring normal development, a normal neurologic exam and studies, and no causative drug such as a phenothiazine. Laryngeal dystonia has been linked to DYT1/TOR1A, DYT4/TUBB4, DYT6/THAP1 and DYT25/GNAL. (Cummings 7e, Ch 56, p 831) (Cummings 7e, Ch 57, p 833)

**Botulinum toxin outcome numbers**: in adductor SD, TA injection restores about 60–100% of normal function (mean about 90%) for 3–4 months. Side effects are a mild breathy voice for under 2 weeks (about 45%) and choking on liquids for a few days (about 22%). In abductor SD, PCA injection restores about 70% of normal function, with mild dysphagia or exertional stridor as the cost. Supraglottic squeeze that persists despite therapy can be treated by injecting the supraglottic part of the LCA through the thyrohyoid membrane. Avoid injection in pregnancy and lactation, and be cautious in myasthenia, Lambert-Eaton and motor neuron disease. RLN section has been abandoned: at 3 years only 36% kept some benefit and 3% had a normal voice. (Cummings 7e, Ch 57, p 833–834)

**Botulinum targeting by tremor axis**: for mainly horizontal (glottic) tremor, inject both TA muscles starting at about 1 U per side. For mainly vertical (laryngeal bobbing) tremor, inject both strap muscles at about 2.5–5 U per side. If both are present, alternate the two sites 3–8 weeks apart to avoid dysphagia and aspiration. The toxin lowers tremor amplitude but does not abolish it. Propranolol and primidone work for limb essential tremor but are unreliable for the voice. About 60% of essential tremor patients have a family history. (Cummings 7e, Ch 57, p 836)

**Koufman–Blalock MTD classes**: Class I is an isometric pattern with an enlarged posterior glottic gap, a high larynx and palpable neck tension; it is common with nodules. Class II is lateral (side-to-side) supraglottic constriction with the false folds adducted; at its extreme the patient phonates on the false folds (plica ventricularis), often as compensation after laryngitis or surgery. Class III is anteroposterior constriction in which the epiglottis and arytenoids hide at least 50% of the glottis. Class IV is complete AP contact of the epiglottis and arytenoids. (Cummings 7e, Ch 58, p 848)

**Systemic corticosteroids for performers**: steroids are appropriate when the risk of permanent damage is low: edema from episodic overuse, mild-to-moderate laryngitis, allergic edema, and (empirically) hemorrhage. If the performance is within 24 hours, give dexamethasone 4 mg plus methylprednisolone 60 mg IM; in subacute cases, give a 3–5 day oral burst with a rapid taper. Never use them for the first time just before a performance, because idiosyncratic voice worsening or mood effects can occur; trial them before a studio session instead. Avoid inhaled or topically applied laryngeal steroids, which irritate the mucosa and promote Candida. (Cummings 7e, Ch 58, p 850)

**Medications singers should avoid**: avoid sedating antihistamines and antihistamine-decongestant combinations because they dry the mucosa; treat allergy with nasal steroids, nonsedating agents or immunotherapy. Avoid aspirin because of hemorrhage risk. Avoid topical anesthetic throat sprays: they let the singer overwork an injured fold, so a singer who cannot perform without one should not perform. Menthol dries the mucosa and can become a habit. Guaifenesin may thin secretions. Beta-blockers for stage fright should be used only rarely, never routinely, because they blunt performance. Hydrate to pale urine (at least about 64 oz a day, more when flying). (Cummings 7e, Ch 58, p 848–850)

**When to cancel a performance**: cancel for submucosal hemorrhage, an enlarging varix, a mucosal break (tear), significant systemic illness, or severe laryngitis. Hemorrhage, an enlarging varix and a mucosal break call for absolute voice rest, and a mucosal break also calls for aggressive antireflux therapy and close follow-up for scar, granuloma or polyp. A mild URI or mild-to-moderate edema carries less risk, and the final decision belongs to the performer. (Cummings 7e, Ch 58, p 849–850)

**Vocal fold varix**: varices occur mostly in female professional singers and may enlarge before and during menses, raising the risk of hemorrhage. Assess their functional impact with serial stroboscopy across the menstrual cycle. First-line care is hydration, avoiding caffeine, and voice therapy; hormonal manipulation is unproven. Treat with surgery or laser for recurrent hemorrhage, enlargement, or persistent dysphonia despite maximal behavioral care. In the OR, apply 1:10,000 epinephrine and coagulate the feeding and then the draining vessels with a defocused 1–2 W CO2, KTP or PDL laser, sparing the medial vibratory surface. (Cummings 7e, Ch 58, p 849, 852)

**Post-microflap recovery phases**: give 5–7 days of complete voice rest for limited dissection, or 10–14 days for extensive or revision surgery. Next, with SLP guidance, start at about 5 minutes of talking and double it daily, reaching full conversation by weeks 3–4; repeat stroboscopy at 2–3 weeks. From months 2–3, singing reeducation with a pedagogue follows. Most patients return to professional activity at about 3 months, and follow-up runs to about 24 months. Intubate gently with the smallest tube, done by the surgeon or an experienced anesthesiologist. (Cummings 7e, Ch 58, p 852–853)

**Other surgery in singers**: tonsillectomy, UPPP, adenoidectomy, septoplasty, sinus and turbinate surgery and maxillary expansion can all change resonance. Even mild new hypernasality can damage a singing career. Stage UPPP over months and keep nasal and adenoid surgery conservative. Get a baseline audiogram in all serious singers, and suggest in-ear monitors to prevent oversinging against stage noise (the Lombard effect). (Cummings 7e, Ch 58, p 853)

**Normal values and pitch tasks**: normal amplitude is about one-third to one-half of the visible fold width. Up to 70% of women have a small posterior gap, which is normal only if it stays behind the vocal processes (the cartilaginous glottis). Raising pitch thins the cover and shrinks the vertical phase difference, so small medial-surface lesions or stiffness may show only during high-pitched phonation. For this reason, examine at high and low pitch and at soft and loud intensity. (Cummings 7e, Ch 58, p 843–844)

**High-speed videoendoscopy numbers**: LHSV records about 2000–10,000 frames per second, compared with 25–30 for standard video, and does not depend on a periodic signal. The recommended minimum is 4000 fps, because degrading to 2000 fps changed 16% of perceptual ratings. In one series stroboscopy could not be rated in 63% of patients, while LHSV could be rated in all. Adding LHSV changed diagnosis or management in about 7%. It captures phonation onset and offset, breaks, and left-right asymmetry. (Cummings 7e, Ch 54, p 815–816)

**Narrow-band imaging**: NBI filters white light down to blue and green bands that hemoglobin absorbs, which highlights the microvessels under leukoplakia and directs biopsy to the most suspicious area. The Ni vascular classification reached about 89% sensitivity and 93% specificity. The simpler ELS scheme separates longitudinal vessel changes (benign) from perpendicular changes such as dots and loops (papilloma, dysplasia, cancer); in one study it reached 100% sensitivity and 95% specificity. NBI also finds second primaries in the oropharynx and hypopharynx better than white light. (Cummings 7e, Ch 54, p 817)

**Nasometry and aerodynamics**: nasalance is nasal acoustic energy divided by nasal plus oral energy. Hypernasality is usually perceived above about 25–33% on a passage with no nasal sounds, and hyponasality below about 50% on nasal sentences. Use regional or dialect norms, because nasalance correlates only moderately with perceived hypernasality. High nasal airflow with low intraoral pressure on pressure consonants indicates velopharyngeal incompetence. (Cummings 7e, Ch 55, p 822)

**Controlling the beam**: the surgeon sets power (W), spot size and exposure time. Irradiance (power density, W/cm2) equals power divided by spot area and predicts tissue effect better than power alone. A longer focal length gives a larger spot and greater depth of focus, and defocusing enlarges the spot and lowers irradiance. Computerized scanning pattern generators can cut lateral thermal damage by up to about 75%. Even at standard settings, CO2 heat injury has been shown about 285 µm into the lamina propria. (Cummings 7e, Ch 59, p 857–858, 862)

**Extinction length by laser**: CO2 (10.6 µm) is absorbed by water within about 0.03 mm regardless of tissue color, with negligible scatter; it is invisible and needs a coaxial helium-neon aiming beam. Nd:YAG (1064 nm) passes through clear fluid (extinction about 40 mm in water, 2–4 mm in tissue), scatters up to 40% backward, and coagulates up to about 4 mm deep, so it is not precise. Argon (488/514 nm) passes through clear media and is absorbed by hemoglobin and pigment; white bone reflects it, so a drop of blood is placed on the stapes in stapedotomy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 59, p 860–862)

**Fiber and vascular lasers**: KTP (532 nm) is frequency-doubled Nd:YAG; it targets oxyhemoglobin (peak about 542 nm), passes through fibers and scopes as small as 3 mm, and its pulsed mode is angiolytic. The 585-nm PDL (oxyhemoglobin peak about 577 nm, roughly 400 µs pulses) was the original office laser but is no longer made, leaving KTP as the main office laser for papilloma, polyps, ectasia and varices. Thulium (2013 nm, water) is fiber-delivered, more hemostatic but less precise than CO2, and more ablative than KTP. Er:YAG (2.94 µm) cuts cleanly with almost no hemostasis. Ho:YAG (2.1 µm) is fiber-delivered for sinus work. Photodynamic therapy activates hematoporphyrin with 630-nm red light. (Cummings 7e, Ch 59, p 861–863)

**Nd:YAG tracheobronchial debulking**: before treatment, get flexible bronchoscopy and tracheal CT, and exclude patients whose obstruction is extrinsic compression. Work through a rigid ventilating bronchoscope rather than a flexible scope. This gives airway control, palpation of the tumor-cartilage interface, a tip that can core or tamponade, and room for suction. Coagulate at about 40–50 W in 0.5–1 s pulses with the beam kept parallel to the airway wall, then core out the devascularized tumor with the scope tip. Pair it with CO2 for bleeding or ulcerated tumors. Hemorrhage is the most dangerous complication. (Cummings 7e, Ch 59, p 861)

**Program-level safety**: hospitals need a laser safety officer and a multidisciplinary committee that credentials each user for each laser and reviews complications. Use two suctions, one for smoke and one for the field, with in-line filters. Suction continuously with a closed circuit, but only intermittently with open or jet ventilation, which is held while the laser fires. HPV DNA has been found in laser plume, but clinical transmission has not been documented. Cummings cites FiO2 below 40% with no N2O; current fire-safety guidance is FiO2 of 30% or less. (Cummings 7e, Ch 59, p 865–867)

**Capillary ectasia**: these dilated capillary arcades are seen mostly in female vocal overdoers, which suggests an estrogen effect. They lower vocal endurance and predispose to hemorrhage and hemorrhagic polyp. Stop NSAIDs and aspirin if possible; they do not raise hemorrhage incidence but worsen bruising. Control reflux and split practice into short sessions (e.g., three 20-minute sessions rather than one hour). If symptoms remain unacceptable, spot-coagulate the vessels every few millimeters; leftover dilations usually involute within weeks. (Cummings 7e, Ch 60, p 876–877)

**Hemorrhage and hemorrhagic polyp**: these are more common in men with intermittent severe voice use or noisy workplaces, and few take anticoagulants. A thin, widely spread superficial bruise usually clears within about 2 weeks. A tense, blister-like hematoma can be drained through a tiny incision to prevent a chronic hemorrhagic polyp, coagulating the feeding Reinke-space capillaries at the same time. An end-stage pale polyp is trimmed superficially. The prognosis after precise surgery is excellent. (Cummings 7e, Ch 60, p 877–878)

**Mucous retention vs epidermoid cyst behavior**: a mucous retention (ductal) cyst arises just below the free margin and projects medially, so it is often mistaken for a nodule or polyp. It limits the voice less than its appearance suggests and need not follow voice overuse. An epidermoid cyst projects less, is harder to see when small, and limits the voice more than expected, with upper-range diplophonia and an abrupt breakdown at a specific pitch. When a cyst ruptures, a small opening leaves an open cyst; an opening as large as the cyst leaves a sulcus. Two parallel sulci from one cyst form a mucosal bridge. (Cummings 7e, Ch 60, p 878, 881)

**Sensitive singing-voice signs**: the speaking voice is an insensitive test for small nodules. Look instead for loss of soft high notes, delayed onset with momentary air escape, need for longer warm-ups, reduced endurance, and more day-to-day variability than training would predict. At high pitch the nodules may stop vibrating while short segments in front of or behind them still vibrate. Reserve the term nodules for chronic lesions; acute swellings that clear with brief rest are not nodules. (Cummings 7e, Ch 60, p 875)

**Contact granuloma specifics**: the lesion occurs mainly in men, often with a habitually low, held-back voice, throat clearing, and unilateral pain over the mid-thyroid cartilage referred to the ear. The opposite vocal process often fits into the cleft of a bilobed lesion. Start empiric antireflux therapy even without symptoms. Most granulomas mature, become pedunculated and fall off within 3–6 months. Office options are depot steroid injection into and around the base, or inhaled triamcinolone or mometasone, reassessed every 6–8 weeks. Surgery is a last resort because recurrence is predictable; if needed, remove only a mature pedunculated lesion and leave the base. (Cummings 7e, Ch 60, p 885–887)

**Intubation granuloma**: this lesion is more common in women, attaches directly to the vocal process, is often bilateral, and CT often shows arytenoid sclerosis. The voice can sound normal. Check fold motion first. With normal motion, use antireflux therapy and inhaled steroid. With impaired motion, which suggests posterior glottic injury or arytenoid fixation, consider microlaryngoscopic excision with steroid injection. Long intubation can also cause tissue loss, posterior glottic incompetence and interarytenoid synechia. (Cummings 7e, Ch 60, p 887)

**Iatrogenic postoperative dysphonia**: this usually follows stripping or vaporization, with adherence of mucosa to ligament or a margin divot. First-line treatment is voice building rather than rest: vigorous singing across the full range for about 10 minutes, 2–3 times a day, using /oo/ and starting from whatever pitch works. It can help even more than a year out. Wait 9–12 months before revision. Remove an iatrogenic granuloma only if it persists beyond about 6 months. Limited elevation of mucosa along a line of adherence can relieve diplophonia, whereas collagen injection gives only modest, inconsistent gains. (Cummings 7e, Ch 60, p 885)

**Clinical clues and mucosal-sparing reduction**: the typical patient is a talkative, middle-aged woman who smokes and is called 'sir' on the phone. Her range is virilized, sometimes down to a bass range, and large polyps can cause an inspiratory snore. Small polyps are revealed by inspiratory phonation, which pulls the edema into the glottis. Polyp reduction that spares mucosa restores voice within about 10 days. Stripping causes weeks of aphonia and a thin, high voice, so leaving some residual polyposis is preferable. (Cummings 7e, Ch 60, p 882–884)

**Benign laryngeal neoplasms**: polypoid granulation tissue, which follows biopsy, intubation or trauma, is the most common vascular lesion of the larynx, and true pyogenic granuloma does not occur there. Adult hemangiomas sit at or above the glottis, are cavernous and bluish, cause hoarseness but not airway distress, and are best observed; the CO2 laser cannot coagulate vessels this large. Rhabdomyoma (pharynx or larynx) is cured by local excision and must be told apart from granular cell tumor and rhabdomyosarcoma. Lipoma favors the aryepiglottic fold and epiglottis, and incomplete removal regrows. Solitary laryngeal neurofibromas are more common than NF1-associated ones. (Cummings 7e, Ch 60, p 894–896)

**Adult-onset phenotype**: adult disease is more often solitary or localized and may take a flat carpet form, a velvety surface with little projection but visible red dots from the fibrovascular cores. NBI helps reveal it. Adult disease is usually less aggressive, and occasionally one excision cures it. HPV 16/18 in papillomas carries a higher risk of malignant transformation. In one cohort, RRP occurred in about 7 per 1000 births to mothers with condylomas. (Cummings 7e, Ch 60, p 892)

**Laryngeal TB in modern series**: in a review of 60 cases, hoarseness was nearly universal, lesions were granulomatous or ulcerative, and the true and false vocal folds were the most common sites. 47% had active pulmonary TB, 33% inactive pulmonary TB, and 15% isolated laryngeal disease. Isolated laryngeal TB tends to be focal, unilateral and atypical, so it mimics carcinoma; biopsy with AFB stains is required. More than a third of patients with disseminated leprosy in India have laryngeal involvement. (Cummings 7e, Ch 61, p 902)

**Candida and chronic bacterial laryngitis**: Candida laryngitis appears as diffuse white speckling of the folds or supraglottis. It belongs in the differential of laryngeal leukoplakia along with keratosis, thick mucus and cancer, even in immunocompetent patients. Treat laryngeal or refractory disease with systemic fluconazole, and switch to itraconazole for fluconazole-resistant strains. Chronic bacterial laryngitis, such as purulent chondritis after intubation injury or relapsing polychondritis (often S. aureus), can present with hoarseness and stridor lasting more than a month and needs drainage plus prolonged antibiotics. (Cummings 7e, Ch 61, p 900–901)

**Less common bacterial and viral causes**: Arcanobacterium haemolyticum causes 0.5–2.5% of bacterial pharyngitis in people aged 10–30, with a rash in 25–50%. It grows best on human blood agar and is missed on sheep blood plates discarded at 48 hours; treat with erythromycin. Gonococcal pharyngitis follows fellatio. Culture deep in the crypts on Thayer-Martin medium, and treat with IM ceftriaxone plus chlamydia coverage (coinfection is about 45%). Group C and G strep can cause glomerulonephritis but not rheumatic fever. HSV-1 causes about 6% of pharyngitis in college students. (Cummings 7e, Ch 61, p 899–900)

**Adult supraglottitis**: adult cases are often less fulminant. In one series only 3 of 23 adults needed airway intervention; the rest were managed with humidification, IV antibiotics, close monitoring and, sometimes, steroids. Decide on the airway from the patient's overall appearance, the flexible laryngoscopic view, and airway factors (habitus, mouth opening, neck extension). If intervention is needed, intubate in a controlled setting or perform an awake tracheotomy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 61, p 900)

**Neurodegenerative causes of inspiratory obstruction**: in multiple system atrophy (Shy-Drager type), vocal fold abduction fails on inspiration and worsens during sleep, alongside autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension, impotence, sphincter dysfunction, anhidrosis). Many patients need tracheotomy, and the disease can progress quickly. (Cummings 7e, Ch 57, p 838)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Margin trial evidence**: The WHO trial (612 patients, melanomas up to 2 mm) found 1 cm and more than 3 cm margins gave equal disease-free and overall survival, but tumors 1.1-2.0 mm had a 3.3% local recurrence with the narrow margin. The Intergroup trial (740 patients, 1-4 mm) found 2 cm equal to 4 cm for local recurrence and 10-year survival. The UK trial (900 patients, 2 mm or thicker) found 1 cm versus 3 cm gave identical mortality but more pooled local, in-transit and nodal recurrence with 1 cm. No randomized trial covers melanomas thicker than 4 mm, and margins wider than 2 cm add no benefit there. Excision depth is full-thickness skin and subcutaneous fat. Fascia or periosteum is taken only if invaded or if a prior biopsy violated that plane. (Cummings 7e, Ch 80, p 1131)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Melanoma of unknown primary**: 2-8% of melanomas present with no identifiable primary. About two-thirds present with regional nodal disease and one-third with distant disease (subcutaneous tissue, lung, brain). Search with a total-body skin and mucosal examination, ask about a lesion that regressed or was removed before, and re-review old pathology slides. Isolated nodal disease is staged as stage III once workup shows no distant spread, and stage for stage the prognosis matches that of a known primary. (Cummings 7e, Ch 80, p 1126, 1130)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Therapeutic nodal dissection by primary site**: For clinically evident nodes from primaries anterior to a coronal plane through the external auditory canals (anterolateral scalp, temple, lateral forehead, cheek, ear), do a parotidectomy plus modified radical neck dissection. In one series parotid-basin recurrence was 13% after superficial and 0% after total parotidectomy, so some surgeons do a total parotidectomy. Preserve the spinal accessory nerve, internal jugular vein and sternocleidomastoid unless tumor involves them. Primaries on the chin or neck do not need a parotidectomy. Posterior scalp and occipital primaries need a posterolateral neck dissection (levels II-V plus postauricular and suboccipital nodes). (Cummings 7e, Ch 80, p 1131-1132)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Sentinel node pitfalls in the head and neck**: Excise the primary before running the gamma probe, because the primary sits so close to the basins that its shine-through can hide the sentinel node. Frozen section of melanoma sentinel nodes has a 5-10% false-negative rate and is not recommended, so send each node for permanent serial sections with immunohistochemistry. In one series 21% of positive nodes were negative on the first H&E. Clinical prediction of drainage disagreed with lymphoscintigraphy in 34% of head and neck cases. MSLT-I data suggest a learning curve of about 55 cases to reach 95% accuracy. Elective neck dissection gave no survival benefit in randomized trials and has been replaced by sentinel node biopsy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 80, p 1132-1133)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Clinical vs pathologic stage trap (AJCC 8)**: A T1b N0 melanoma is clinical stage IB but pathologic stage IA once nodes are pathologically negative, and only one clinical stage III group exists. Pathologic stage III is split into IIIA-IIID by T and N. T4b with N3a/b/c is IIID, and T0 with N1b/c is IIIB. Stage 0 and T1 do not need pathologic node evaluation for pathologic staging. Untreated distant disease has a median survival of only 6-8 months and a 5-year survival around 6%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 80, p 1129-1130)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Staging imaging by stage**: For stage 0-II, history and examination are enough, with imaging only for positive review-of-systems findings. Routine chest x-ray is not cost-effective: asymptomatic pulmonary metastasis is about 0.1%, with a 15% false-positive rate. In-transit disease is melanoma more than 2 cm from the primary, and like satellite disease it is stage III. Clinically suspicious nodes or in-transit lesions need FNA, LDH and optional baseline imaging. Stage IV needs LDH, PET/CT and brain MRI, plus BRAF and KIT mutation testing. (Cummings 7e, Ch 80, p 1127)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Risk numbers and congenital nevi**: Starting tanning-bed use before age 35 raises melanoma risk by up to 75%, and WHO classifies tanning beds as a group I carcinogen. More than 100 nevi in adults or more than 50 in children raises risk. After one melanoma, 5-10% develop a second primary, and up to 8% have multiple primaries at diagnosis. BRAF is mutated in about 42% (mostly V600E), NRAS in 25% and c-KIT in 19%. Congenital nevi are small (under 1.5 cm), medium (1.5-19.9 cm) or giant (20 cm or more). Small and medium nevi carry a 0-4.9% lifetime risk and rarely need prophylactic removal. Giant nevi carry a 4.5-10% risk, 70% of these cancers appear before age 10, and they can start below the dermoepidermal junction. (Cummings 7e, Ch 80, p 1125-1126)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Systemic therapy trial numbers**: In CheckMate 067 (advanced melanoma), 3-year overall survival was 58% with nivolumab plus ipilimumab, 52% with nivolumab and 34% with ipilimumab. In CheckMate 238 (resected stage IIIB-IV), adjuvant nivolumab beat ipilimumab for 12-month recurrence-free survival (70.5% vs 60.8%), with grade 3-4 toxicity of 14.4% vs 45.9%. About 60% of patients on ipilimumab have immune-related adverse events, most often diarrhea. PD-1 monotherapy produces responses in about 40% of patients and is contraindicated in transplant recipients. T-VEC is an attenuated HSV injected into unresectable lesions. It gave a 16.3% durable response rate vs 2.1% with GM-CSF and can cause responses in lesions that were not injected. Dacarbazine is the only approved chemotherapy, with response rates of only 10-20%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 80, p 1135-1136)

**Two-stage saliva formation**: Acinar cells make an isotonic, plasma-like primary fluid. Basolateral Na-K-2Cl cotransporters and Na/K-ATPase load chloride into the cell, and a rise in calcium opens basolateral K and apical Cl channels. Chloride enters the lumen, sodium follows between cells, and water follows osmotically. The ducts then reabsorb Na and Cl and secrete K and bicarbonate, so the final saliva is hypotonic. At high flow there is less time for duct modification, so Na, Cl and the Na:K ratio rise. Bicarbonate also rises with flow, from as low as 5 mEq/L at rest to above plasma (27 mEq/L), which raises buffering. (Cummings 7e, Ch 81, p 1141-1142, 1145)

**Autonomic receptor signaling**: Parasympathetic input dominates and gives high-volume, low-protein saliva. Acetylcholine acts on acinar M3 receptors through Gq, phospholipase C and IP3 to release calcium and drive fluid secretion, which is how pilocarpine and cevimeline work. Sympathetic input gives low-volume, protein-rich saliva: norepinephrine acts on beta receptors through Gs, cAMP and protein kinase A to trigger exocytosis of proteins such as amylase. Alpha-1 receptors act through calcium. The fight-or-flight response, anticholinergic drugs (including most antidepressants) and losing about 8% of body water reduce or stop flow. (Cummings 7e, Ch 81, p 1142-1144)

**Salivary flow norms and hypofunction**: Normal unstimulated whole saliva is 0.1 mL/min or more (average about 0.3), and normal stimulated flow is 0.2 mL/min or more (up to about 7). Daily output is about 1-1.5 L, and stimulated saliva makes up 80-90% of it. The cutoff between normal and hypofunction lies at an unstimulated flow of about 0.12-0.16 mL/min. Because the normal range is wide, a 50% drop from the patient's own baseline is a more reliable definition. About 30% of people report some dry mouth. Flow peaks in the late afternoon and is lowest during sleep. (Cummings 7e, Ch 81, p 1144)

**Saliva chemistry behind submandibular stones**: Calcium in submandibular saliva (3.4-4.4 mEq/L) is almost twice that of parotid saliva (1.4-2 mEq/L), and mucins are most concentrated in sublingual and minor gland saliva, then submandibular, and lowest in parotid saliva. Statherin, a small tyrosine- and proline-rich phosphoprotein, keeps calcium phosphate in supersaturated solution. That helps remineralize enamel and inhibits salivary calculus. (Cummings 7e, Ch 81, p 1145-1147)

**Dry mouth in older adults**: About 65% of people over 60 who complain of xerostomia have objective salivary hypofunction. Healthy, unmedicated adults over 80 have less unstimulated whole saliva, but stimulated parotid flow appears preserved, though studies conflict. Polypharmacy (especially anticholinergics), dehydration and systemic disease are the main reversible causes, so review medications before attributing dryness to age. Aging glands show acinar atrophy, fibrosis, fat replacement, duct dilation and oncocytic change after about 70, more in the submandibular than the parotid gland. (Cummings 7e, Ch 81, p 1144, 1148)

**P1 CAEP biomarker**: The P1 cortical auditory evoked potential reflects input reaching the thalamus and primary auditory cortex. Its latency is about 300 ms in infancy, falls steeply over the first 2-3 years and reaches adult values by age 12-16. Later N1/P2 components (higher-order cortex) emerge in preadolescence. Children implanted before 3.5 years reach normal P1 latency within 6-8 months of implant use. About half of those implanted at 3.5-6.5 years do, while those implanted after 7 years stay delayed even 7-10 years later and rarely develop N1/P2. P1 can also confirm objectively that a hearing aid is benefiting the cortex in infants who cannot give behavioral responses. (Cummings 7e, Ch 132, p 1997-2000)

**Cross-modal reorganization predicts outcome**: In poorly performing pediatric implant users, visual and touch stimuli activate temporal (auditory) cortex. Good performers keep visual processing in visual cortex. Demographic factors such as age at implantation explain less than half of the variation in pediatric implant outcomes. Visual and somatosensory takeover also occurs in postlingually deafened adults and even in mild-moderate age-related hearing loss, along with extra frontal-lobe recruitment that suggests increased listening effort. Fewer than 10% of adults with hearing aids or implants receive tailored auditory rehabilitation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 132, p 2004-2010)

**Using cortical potentials in ANSD**: ANSD accounts for about 5-15% of children with sensorineural hearing loss. Behavioral thresholds and the absent ABR do not predict whether a hearing aid will work, so the aided P1 cortical potential can show whether amplification is reaching the cortex. A delayed or abnormal P1 despite consistent aid use supports moving to cochlear implantation. Children with ANSD implanted before age 2 had better outcomes than those implanted later, a slightly earlier window than in congenital deafness. (Cummings 7e, Ch 132, p 2001)

**Hearing loss and dementia numbers**: In cohort studies, mild hearing loss doubles dementia risk, moderate loss triples it and severe loss raises it about fivefold, and an effect is seen from as young as 55. Over 11 years of follow-up, hazard ratios rose from 1.89 to 4.94 from mild to severe loss, and each 25 dB of loss equaled about 7 years of cognitive aging. The 2017 Lancet Commission ranked age-related hearing loss as the largest potentially modifiable dementia risk factor. Cummings 7e notes that randomized proof that treatment prevents decline was still lacking at the time. (Cummings 7e, Ch 133, p 2013); (Cummings 7e, Ch 132, p 2007)

**Epidemiology and disparities**: About two-thirds of US adults 70 and older (about 23 million) have clinically significant loss (better-ear PTA over 25 dB HL). Prevalence roughly doubles each decade: about 13% at 40-49, 29% at 50-59 and nearly 90% at 80 and older. Men are affected more, especially at high frequencies. Darker skin pigmentation, which tracks with strial melanocyte density, is protective. Cardiovascular risk factors have inconsistent support. Only 15-20% of affected older adults own hearing aids and about 20% use them regularly, with use near 10% among older Black and Mexican American adults compared with about 21% among white adults. (Cummings 7e, Ch 133, p 2012, 2014)

**Access barriers in older adults**: In 2016 the average monthly Social Security benefit was $1360, against about $4700 for a pair of hearing aids, which traditionally cost $2000-4000 per device. Traditional aids are not covered by Medicare. Hearing aid manuals average close to a 10th-grade reading level, while inadequate health literacy is below 6th grade, and only about 3% of older adults have proficient health literacy. The OTC Hearing Aid Act (signed August 2017) created an FDA over-the-counter category, and in trials self-fitted or low-cost devices with counseling gave benefits similar to conventional fitting. (Cummings 7e, Ch 133, p 2011-2012, 2015-2017)

**Implanting older adults**: At many centers most adult recipients are over 70, and octogenarians and nonagenarians are routinely implanted. Complication rates do not differ significantly from younger patients, and more than 80% still use the device after 10 years. Each additional year of age at implantation raises the rate of stopping regular use by about 7.8%. Older age also independently reduces speech-score gains, although age and duration of deafness are hard to separate. Implantation improves quality of life, depressive symptoms and loneliness, and in some cohorts cognition, so refer when hearing first meets criteria rather than waiting. (Cummings 7e, Ch 133, p 2018)

**Age-related vestibular loss and falls**: Dizziness or imbalance affects 20-30% of older adults and more than half of those over 80. On the NHANES modified Romberg test, 35% of US adults 40 and older and 85% of those 80 and older have objective vestibular dysfunction. Lifetime prevalence of vestibular vertigo is 7.8%. Dizziness raises fall risk 2-3 fold, and up to 12-fold in symptomatic vestibular dysfunction, and vestibular asymmetry contributes to wrist and hip fractures. The American Geriatrics Society recommends a multifactorial fall-risk assessment for any older patient with a fall or a gait or balance disorder. Vestibular rehabilitation works but is underused, and internet-delivered programs reduced dizziness for up to 6 months in a randomized trial. (Cummings 7e, Ch 133, p 2019-2020)

**Masking rules with numbers**: Interaural attenuation is about 0 dB for bone conduction, 35-50 dB for supra-aural headphones and 60-65 dB for insert earphones, and it is greater at higher frequencies. Inserts therefore let you mask harder with less overmasking. Mask air conduction when the test-ear air threshold exceeds the non-test ear's air or bone threshold by the interaural attenuation. Mask bone conduction whenever thresholds are asymmetric. For speech, mask when the test-ear SRT differs from the non-test ear's SRT or PTA by 45 dB or more, or when word-recognition testing is presented 45 dB or more above them. Unmasked crossover produces a shadow curve. (Cummings 7e, Ch 134, p 2024)

**Pseudohypacusis checks**: SRT and the 500/1000/2000-Hz PTA should agree within about 5 dB. An SRT much better than the PTA suggests functional loss, as do normal voice level and articulation in someone claiming severe bilateral loss. Every unilateral loss should get a pure-tone Stenger test. The same tone is played to the better ear about 10 dB above threshold and to the poorer ear about 10 dB below the admitted threshold. A patient with a true loss still responds, because the tone is heard in the good ear. A malingerer perceives the tone only in the 'bad' ear and denies hearing it. Many patients with functional loss also have a real underlying loss, so true thresholds still need to be established. (Cummings 7e, Ch 134, p 2037)

**Canal volume and reflex decay numbers**: Normal equivalent ear-canal volume is 0.5-1.0 mL in children and 0.6-2.0 mL in adults. Volumes above about 2.0 mL in children or 2.5 mL in adults with a flat tracing mean a perforation or a patent tube. In reflex decay testing, a tone 10 dB above reflex threshold is held for 10 seconds, and it is abnormal if amplitude falls to half or less within 5 seconds. Test at 500 and 1000 Hz, because decay at higher frequencies is common in normal ears. Absent contralateral reflexes with intact ipsilateral reflexes point to a lesion of the crossed brainstem pathways. (Cummings 7e, Ch 134, p 2025-2026)

**ABR retrocochlear criteria**: One center's click criteria for abnormality are I-III 2.3 ms or more, III-V 2.1 ms or more, I-V 4.4 ms or more, and an interaural wave V difference of 0.4 ms or more. Published cutoffs vary, and about 0.2-0.4 ms is quoted for the interaural difference. The I-III interval is the most sensitive and is least affected by cochlear loss. An absent wave V with a replicated wave I or III is a definitive sign of retrocochlear disease. High-frequency loss over about 40-45 dB delays click wave V without any tumor. 1000-Hz tone pips avoid this: mean wave V latency was 6.7 ms in cochlear loss vs 7.6 ms in acoustic neuroma with identical audiograms. (Cummings 7e, Ch 134, p 2034)

**ECochG SP/AP numbers and third windows**: Normal click SP/AP ratios are usually 0.35-0.4 or less, and a ratio above about 0.4-0.5 suggests endolymphatic hydrops. Superior semicircular canal dehiscence also raises the SP/AP ratio (mean about 0.62 in affected ears in one series), and it normalizes after successful repair, so ECochG can help confirm a third window and monitor plugging. Elevated SP/AP is therefore not specific for Meniere disease when there are low-frequency air-bone gaps or sound-induced vertigo. (Cummings 7e, Ch 134, p 2029-2032)

**VEMP numbers**: In dehiscence, cervical VEMP thresholds are abnormally low, 65 dB HL or less. In confirmed cases the mean threshold was about 67 dB (plus or minus 10) vs about 82 dB HL (plus or minus 5) in unaffected ears. Cervical VEMP tests the saccule and inferior vestibular nerve, and ocular VEMP tests the utricle and superior vestibular nerve, so together they can show which nerve division is involved. For example, ocular VEMP is lost after superior vestibular nerve section while cervical VEMP remains. (Cummings 7e, Ch 134, p 2032)

**Balloon test occlusion technique and limits**: After full four-vessel angiography and heparinization, a nondetachable balloon is inflated in the ICA at the planned occlusion level for about 30 minutes, with serial neurologic exams, and deflated at once if a deficit appears. Neurons work normally above about 20-25 mL/100 g/min of cerebral blood flow, so a patient just above that threshold may pass the clinical test and still infarct with later hypotension. Adjuncts include SPECT perfusion, xenon CT, PET, CT/MR perfusion, EEG or evoked potentials, stump pressures, transcranial Doppler and a hypotensive challenge. Deficits can still follow a passed test, from hypoperfusion, clot propagating from the stump or emboli at occlusion. (Cummings 7e, Ch 136, p 2065)

**Embolization of jugular paragangliomas**: Paragangliomas are about 48% temporal bone, 35% carotid body and 11% vagal, and about 10% are multiple. Jugulare tumors are compartmentalized, with each compartment fed by its own external carotid branch. The ascending pharyngeal and posterior division of the middle meningeal arteries are most common, then the stylomastoid branch and posterior auricular artery. Vertebral and cerebellar branches supply foramen magnum or intradural extension. Before particle embolization (for example 100-500 µm microspheres or 150-300 µm PVA) of a branch that may supply the facial nerve, such as the stylomastoid artery, inject 1% preservative-free lidocaine as a provocative test. A negative test is reassuring. If the ICA must be sacrificed, a passed balloon occlusion test allows preoperative ICA occlusion. Glomus tympanicum is usually small enough to resect without embolization. (Cummings 7e, Ch 136, p 2065-2068)

**Angiographic patterns of neck paragangliomas**: A carotid body tumor sits in the bifurcation and splays the internal and external carotids apart. It is fed by many tiny branches from the distal common and proximal internal carotid and by ECA branches (ascending pharyngeal, superior thyroid, lingual, facial). A vagal paraganglioma arises at C1-C2 and pushes the high cervical ICA forward without splaying the bifurcation, with supply mainly from the ascending pharyngeal artery and sometimes the thyrocervical, costocervical or vertebral branches. Some surgeons avoid preoperative embolization of carotid body tumors because the inflammation it causes may blur dissection planes. (Cummings 7e, Ch 136, p 2068)

**Embolization technique details**: Do bilateral selective internal and external carotid angiography. If a bleeding site is seen, embolize all feeders and collaterals with the microcatheter placed beyond branches that supply cranial nerves (middle and accessory meningeal). If no site is seen, embolize the distal internal maxillary and facial arteries on both sides. 150-400 µm particles control bleeding without devascularizing facial tissue, and distal rather than proximal occlusion lowers rebleeding through collaterals. Cummings reports 91-97% success with 0-3% complications. Other sources quote lower success and about 1% stroke. Embolization can also spare frail elderly patients prolonged posterior packing. (Cummings 7e, Ch 136, p 2071)

**Potassium recycling pathway and its diseases**: Potassium leaves hair cells, is taken up by supporting cells (KCC3/KCC4) and passes through epithelial gap junctions (connexin 26, 30 and 31) to the outer sulcus and root cells. Type II fibrocytes of the spiral ligament take it up via Na/K-ATPase and NKCC1. It then moves through connective-tissue gap junctions to strial basal and intermediate cells, whose KCNJ10 (Kir4.1) channels generate the endocochlear potential. Marginal cells take K up basolaterally (NKCC1, Na/K-ATPase) and recycle chloride through ClC-K channels that need barttin. Marginal cells then secrete K into endolymph through KCNQ1/KCNE1. Clinical links: Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome (KCNQ1/KCNE1, long QT), Bartter syndrome type IV (BSND, deafness with renal salt wasting), DFNB1 (GJB2/GJB6) and Pendred/DFNB4 (pendrin, bicarbonate secretion and pH control in the spiral prominence and endolymphatic sac). (Cummings 7e, Ch 148, p 2266-2267)

**Mechanotransduction complex**: Deflecting the bundle toward the tallest stereocilia stretches the tip links (cadherin 23 above, protocadherin 15 below) and opens transduction channels. The channel complex at the lower end of the link includes TMC1/TMC2, LHFPL5 (TMHS), TMIE and CIB2, and myosin VIIa, harmonin and SANS anchor the upper end. Gene correlates: TMC1 (DFNB7/11 recessive, DFNA36 dominant), LHFPL5 (DFNB67), TMIE (DFNB6) and CIB2 (DFNB48/USH1J). Myosin XVa (DFNB3) and whirlin set stereocilia length, and myosin VI causes DFNA22/DFNB37. Calcium entering through the channel is pumped out by PMCA2, and reduced PMCA2 function worsens CDH23-related and noise-induced loss. (Cummings 7e, Ch 148, p 2252-2253, 2258-2261)

**Synaptopathy genes**: Many ANSD genes act at the inner hair cell ribbon synapse. Depolarization opens CaV1.3 channels (CACNA1D), whose loss causes SANDD syndrome: sinoatrial node dysfunction and deafness. Calcium activates otoferlin, the vesicle-fusion calcium sensor. OTOF causes DFNB9, including temperature-sensitive variants where hearing worsens with fever. Electrical ABRs are preserved, so these patients do well with implants. VGLUT3 (SLC17A8) loads glutamate into vesicles and causes progressive DFNA25. DIAPH3 causes dominant AUNA1. True neural forms include Charcot-Marie-Tooth types 1A (PMP22) and 1B (MPZ). Low-spontaneous-rate fibers have high thresholds, wide dynamic ranges and contact the modiolar side of inner hair cells. (Cummings 7e, Ch 148, p 2261-2263)

**Gene-phenotype pearls from cochlear molecular biology**: TECTA (tectorin) causes DFNA8/12, a congenital, nonprogressive loss often worst in the mid frequencies (cookie-bite), while recessive DFNB21 is severe to profound. In KCNQ4 (DFNA2A), outer hair cells cannot extrude potassium, stay chronically depolarized and degenerate from base to apex, giving progressive high-frequency loss. GJB3 (connexin 31) causes DFNA2B. Usher gene map: USH1B MYO7A, USH1C harmonin, USH1D CDH23 (also DFNB12), USH1F PCDH15 (also DFNB23), USH1G SANS, USH1J CIB2, USH2A usherin, USH2C ADGRV1, USH2D whirlin, USH3A clarin-1. POU3F4 (DFNX2/DFN3) causes stapes fixation with a perilymph gusher, a wide internal auditory canal and progressive SNHL. (Cummings 7e, Ch 148, p 2247, 2258, 2261, 2267)

**GPA ear disease and ANCA yield**: The ear is involved in roughly 20-60% of GPA and can be the first or only site; it is unusual among autoimmune diseases in affecting both the middle ear (eustachian tube obstruction, effusion, granulation) and the inner ear, with SNHL in up to about a third of those with hearing loss. PR3/c-ANCA is more than 95% specific, and is positive in over 90% of active systemic disease but in only about 65-70% of limited (ear or head-and-neck only) disease, so a negative ANCA and a nondiagnostic small ear biopsy do not exclude it; repeat biopsy and clinical correlation are often needed. (Cummings 7e, Ch 151, p 2295-2297; Ch 156, p 2368)

**Paget disease hearing loss is not ossicular fixation**: Hearing loss occurs in a large minority to about half of patients with skull involvement and is usually mixed, with a downsloping bone-conduction curve and fairly flat air thresholds; the facial nerve is spared. Temporal bone studies show the conductive component is not caused by stapes or ossicular fixation and the SNHL is not from cochlear nerve compression; the loss tracks reduced mineral density of the cochlear capsule on quantitative CT. Stapes or ossicular surgery is therefore rarely worthwhile; bisphosphonates (or calcitonin) treat the disease and may stabilize SNHL. Clues favoring Paget over otosclerosis: onset in the sixth decade, larger downsloping SNHL, enlarging calvarium, tortuous superficial temporal artery, and high alkaline phosphatase. (Cummings 7e, Ch 151, p 2304; Ch 152, p 2321)

**Stapes surgery in osteogenesis imperfecta**: OI can mimic otosclerosis (early-onset conductive loss, high tympanometric compliance, childhood fractures that stop after puberty, blue sclerae). At surgery the footplate is typically thick, soft and chalky but fixed, the crura may be thin or fractured, and the incus long process and malleus may be fragile. Stapedectomy can match otosclerosis results but is delicate: crimping can fracture the incus, so a platinum-ribbon (rather than stainless-steel wire) prosthesis is preferred. Hearing loss occurs in about 30-50% of type I, about 50% of type III and 10-30% of type IV. (Cummings 7e, Ch 151, p 2303-2304)

**Fibrous dysplasia of the temporal bone: management**: About 100 temporal bone cases are reported (70% monostotic, 23% polyostotic, 7% McCune-Albright), presenting in the second-third decade as painless bony swelling with canal stenosis. Surgery is limited to biopsy and relief of function; restenosis after simple canalplasty is common, and a canal-wall-down mastoidectomy with wide canalplasty and skin grafting gives more durable patency. Radiotherapy is contraindicated because it raises the risk of sarcomatous change (baseline about 0.4%). Follow long term for facial nerve involvement and progression to SNHL. (Cummings 7e, Ch 151, p 2305-2306)

**Osteopetrosis and recurrent facial palsy**: Any child or young adult with recurrent Bell-like facial palsy should be imaged for osteopetrosis: in the dominant adult (Albers-Schonberg, often CLCN7) form the temporal bone is sclerotic with narrowed eustachian tube, EAC and IAC, ossicles jammed by periosteal overgrowth and obliterated window niches, and each palsy tends to leave more residual weakness; total facial nerve decompression has been advocated. In the malignant recessive infantile form (often TCIRG1), the tympanic facial nerve is consistently dehiscent and may herniate into the oval window niche, and bone marrow transplant is the only effective treatment. (Cummings 7e, Ch 151, p 2305-2307)

**Plasma cell and myeloid tumors of the temporal bone**: Multiple myeloma often replaces petrous marrow and makes punched-out lytic lesions that can rarely present with hearing loss, vertigo, otalgia or facial palsy. A solitary plasmacytoma of the temporal bone (M-protein in under 30%) is indolent and is treated with local radiation of about 40 Gy, with serial serum/urine protein studies and skeletal survey to detect conversion to myeloma. Granulocytic sarcoma (chloroma) is an extramedullary myeloid tumor that may precede, coincide with or follow AML/CML and can first present in the temporal bone. Leukemic infiltrates and hemorrhage in the middle and inner ear cause effusion, suppuration, mixed loss, sudden SNHL, vertigo and facial palsy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 151, p 2300-2302)

**Temporal bone metastases and meningeal carcinomatosis**: Metastases arrive hematogenously, most often from breast, then lung, prostate and skin; they favor the petrous apex and IAC while the otic capsule resists invasion, and prostate or breast deposits may be osteoblastic. Meningeal carcinomatosis commonly presents with rapidly progressive SNHL that mimics a CPA tumor when unilateral or immune-mediated inner ear disease when bilateral; diagnose with CSF cytology. (Cummings 7e, Ch 151, p 2301-2302)

**IgG4-related disease of the mastoid**: IgG4-RD (usually men in their sixties-seventies, often multisystem) can involve the mastoid and look like chronic suppurative otitis media, though a mass lesion is more typical. Histology shows a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4-positive plasma cells, storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis, and it is easily missed unless the pathologist is asked to look. It responds well to corticosteroids, so making the diagnosis spares repeated surgery. (Cummings 7e, Ch 151, p 2310)

**Multiple sclerosis and the ear**: SNHL occurs in about 4-10% of patients with MS and is often sudden and unilateral, recovering over days to weeks; word recognition may be poor out of proportion to thresholds and acoustic reflex patterns can be abnormal. ABR abnormalities (prolonged latencies, poor morphology, rate-sensitive changes) are common, and MRI may show plaques in the cochlear nucleus or inferior colliculus. Vertigo in MS usually reflects central vestibular pathway plaques with normal end organs. (Cummings 7e, Ch 152, p 2318; Ch 151, p 2309)

**Hematologic and vascular causes of SNHL**: SNHL is reported in about 22% of patients with sickle cell disease and may be sudden during crises. Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia causes hyperviscosity with progressive or sudden SNHL that may respond to alkylating agents or plasmapheresis; cryoglobulinemia and polyarteritis nodosa (necrotizing small-medium artery vasculitis, SNHL sometimes preceding systemic disease, facial palsy) are other causes. Cardiopulmonary bypass slightly raises the risk of sudden SNHL (emboli or hypoperfusion). AICA occlusion gives vertigo, SNHL, facial palsy, ipsilateral facial pain-temperature loss and Horner syndrome because AICA usually supplies the labyrinthine artery. (Cummings 7e, Ch 152, p 2319-2320)

**Lupus and Susac syndrome**: SNHL is reported in 15-66% of patients with SLE, typically bilateral, symmetric and high-frequency, often subclinical and unrelated to disease severity.
