Susac syndrome (RED-M: retinopathy with branch retinal artery occlusions, encephalopathy with corpus callosum lesions, deafness from microangiopathy) mostly affects women aged 20-40; the loss is fluctuating, asymmetric and worst in the low-mid frequencies because the apical cochlear arterioles are occluded. Neurologic features often burn out over 2-4 years, but hearing loss usually persists; treatment is immunosuppression, with cochlear implantation if needed. (Cummings 7e, Ch 156, p 2368-2369; Ch 151, p 2309)

**Lyme facial palsy: antibiotics yes, steroids no**: Facial palsy is the most common otologic manifestation of Lyme disease (about 3-11% of cases, bilateral in about 25%) and occurs in early disseminated (second-stage) disease, sometimes as the only neurologic sign. Recovery is usually spontaneous and complete over weeks to months; antibiotics (doxycycline first line) do not change the palsy outcome but are given to treat the infection and prevent late arthritis and neurologic disease. Corticosteroids have not shown benefit, and one retrospective series found worse long-term outcomes with more synkinesis when steroids were added. A red-violet earlobe nodule (borrelial lymphocytoma) is another second-stage ear sign. (Cummings 7e, Ch 151, p 2298-2299)

**Otologic disease in HIV/AIDS**: Pneumocystis jirovecii can cause subcutaneous EAC masses or aural polyps from the canal, drum or middle ear with conductive loss and otorrhea, may be the first sign of AIDS, and responds to oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. SNHL is found in roughly 30% of HIV-positive patients and sudden SNHL is about twice as common as in controls; causes include HIV neurotropism, otosyphilis or CMV reactivation, cryptococcal or tuberculous meningitis, toxoplasmosis and ototoxic drugs. Temporal bone series show the ear is particularly prone to CMV infection (about a quarter of AIDS bones) and occasional labyrinthine cryptococcosis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 151, p 2309; Ch 155, p 2363)

**Natural history and prognostic factors**: Incidence is about 5-20 per 100,000 per year with a peak in the sixth decade; bilateral involvement is rare. Without treatment roughly 30-65% recover partially or fully, and most recovery happens in the first 2 weeks; little meaningful recovery occurs after 3 months. Worse prognosis: more severe or profound loss, flat or downsloping configuration, vertigo (especially with a downsloping loss), poor word recognition, and age (children and adults over 40 do worse); upsloping and midfrequency losses do best. Vertigo accompanies about 40%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 152, p 2323-2324)

**Vestibular schwannoma yield and MRI alternatives**: About 10-20% of vestibular schwannomas present with sudden SNHL, and roughly 3-10% of sudden SNHL patients who undergo MRI harbor one; no clinical feature reliably separates them, and recovery (spontaneous or on steroids) does not exclude a tumor. Gadolinium MRI is the most sensitive test and is more cost-effective than ABR followed by MRI, because ABR misses small tumors. When MRI is impossible (e.g., pacemaker), fine-cut temporal bone CT with contrast can detect lesions larger than about 1.5 cm. (Cummings 7e, Ch 152, p 2324)

**Steroid evidence and dosing**: Steroids remain standard despite mixed RCT data: Wilson's double-blind trial found 78% complete or partial recovery with steroids versus 38% with placebo in nonprofound losses (all midfrequency losses recovered regardless, and losses over 90 dB showed no benefit), while later RCTs and Cochrane-style meta-analyses found no clear effect. A common regimen is prednisone about 1 mg/kg/day (maximum 60 mg) as a single morning dose for 10-14 days with a taper, after counseling on side effects; intratympanic steroids suit patients with diabetes, glaucoma or cataracts. (Cummings 7e, Ch 152, p 2325-2326)

**Hyperbaric oxygen and other adjuncts: magnitude of benefit**: A 2012 Cochrane review found hyperbaric oxygen raised the chance of a 25% improvement in pure-tone average (RR about 1.39) but not of a 50% improvement, with an absolute gain of about 16 dB of uncertain clinical meaning. Vasodilators, dextran, pentoxifylline, heparin, carbogen, diatrizoate and multi-drug 'shotgun' regimens have not beaten spontaneous recovery in controlled studies, and a Cochrane review of four low-bias RCTs found no added benefit of antivirals with steroids. (Cummings 7e, Ch 152, p 2326-2327)

**Infectious causes worth targeting**: Syphilis accounts for 2% or fewer of sudden SNHL but can occur at any stage and should be reconsidered in HIV. Lyme titers were positive in about 21% of sudden SNHL in one large study, yet treated seropositive patients did no better than seronegative ones; Cummings notes Lyme does not appear to cause inner ear disease in North America, so testing is reserved for European or strongly suggestive exposures. About 28% report a viral URI in the prior month; mumps SNHL is almost always unilateral, starts 4-5 days after parotitis and can occur without parotitis, and Lassa fever causes sudden SNHL in about two-thirds of patients. (Cummings 7e, Ch 152, p 2314, 2324; Ch 156, p 2366)

**Intratympanic steroid technique**: With the patient supine and head turned so the ear faces the ceiling, inject enough to fill the middle ear (about 0.3-0.5 mL) through an anesthetized drum, then keep the head still for 15-30 minutes without swallowing, talking or yawning so drug stays on the round window. Typical agents are dexamethasone (about 10-24 mg/mL) or methylprednisolone 62.5 mg/mL; methylprednisolone reaches the highest perilymph levels but can burn, which a small amount of 1% lidocaine reduces. Injection doses are variable because drug leaks down the eustachian tube; a tympanostomy tube helps repeated dosing, and Gelfoam or wick devices can prolong round window contact. Salvage works best started soon after oral therapy fails, ideally within about 2 weeks of failure. (Cummings 7e, Ch 158, p 2385-2388)

**Radiation-induced SNHL**: When the cochlea is in the field, about half of patients develop SNHL (about 50% after nasopharyngeal cancer RT, 53% after parotid RT, 14-23% after pediatric brain tumor RT). Fractionated doses below about 45 Gy are generally tolerated, with risk rising above 45-60 Gy, especially with cisplatin (nasopharyngeal cancer cochlear doses over about 48 Gy), older age and preexisting loss. Onset is delayed 0.5-2 years and progressive, so audiometric follow-up for at least 10 years is advised; stereotactic radiosurgery cochlear doses as low as about 4 Gy are linked to worse hearing at 1 year. (Cummings 7e, Ch 152, p 2317-2318; Ch 157, p 2379)

**Opioid and PDE-5 inhibitor hearing loss**: Abuse of hydrocodone-acetaminophen (also reported with propoxyphene, methadone and heroin) can cause rapidly progressive, usually bilateral, severe-to-profound SNHL that does not respond to corticosteroids; these patients do very well with cochlear implants. Acetaminophen itself may be the culprit. After an FDA review of 29 reports, PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, vardenafil, tadalafil) were linked to sudden, usually unilateral, partial SNHL with full recovery in about a third, though causation is unproven. (Cummings 7e, Ch 152, p 2315-2316; Ch 157, p 2377)

**Platinum ototoxicity risk factors and drug differences**: Cisplatin risk rises with age under 5 years (and older age), male children, cumulative dose over about 400 mg/m2, noise, other ototoxins, cranial irradiation, renal impairment, anemia and low albumin; loss is bilateral, symmetric, permanent, high frequency first, and can be delayed because platinum is retained in the cochlea. Nearly all patients given 150-225 mg/m2 show loss on extended high-frequency testing, and the 8-kHz shift after two cycles predicts later need for amplification. Cisplatin injures outer hair cells first, while carboplatin preferentially damages inner hair cells and is more ototoxic at high doses (about 80% of children after high-dose regimens) than once thought; oxaliplatin is rarely ototoxic. (Cummings 7e, Ch 157, p 2371-2372, 2376; Ch 152, p 2316)

**Loop diuretics, macrolides and deferoxamine**: Furosemide hearing loss (about 6%) is usually temporary, linked to plasma levels above about 50 mg/L, rapid infusion, renal failure and aminoglycosides; bumetanide is less ototoxic and torsemide has no clinical ototoxicity. IV erythromycin loss is dose related (about 16% at 2 g/day versus 53% at 4 g/day in transplant patients) and usually reverses in 1-3 weeks; azithromycin and clarithromycin can rarely cause permanent loss. Deferoxamine causes high-frequency SNHL in over a third of thalassemia patients (worst near 6 kHz), so audiograms every 6 months are recommended, and hearing may recover with dose reduction. (Cummings 7e, Ch 157, p 2376-2379; Ch 152, p 2316)

**Aminoglycoside vestibulotoxicity: course and testing**: Vestibular toxicity typically declares itself over 1-2 days, after which imbalance and oscillopsia are present with any head movement; improvement may begin around 2 months but recovery is rarely complete. On rotary chair testing the low-frequency responses are lost first and most severely, and test improvement (mostly high frequency) often exceeds clinical recovery. Risk rises with bacteremia, fever, liver or renal dysfunction, loop diuretics and mitochondrial 12S rRNA variants; therapeutic peak/trough levels do not guarantee safety. (Cummings 7e, Ch 157, p 2371)

**Ototoxicity monitoring protocol**: Match monitoring to risk: low-risk short aminoglycoside courses can use pre- and post-treatment audiograms with weekly symptom checks, while long high-risk courses (e.g., amikacin) warrant weekly or biweekly conventional plus extended high-frequency audiometry. Because aminoglycoside damage can continue after the drug stops, obtain the final audiogram a few weeks after therapy ends. For cisplatin, test at baseline and before each cycle; DPOAEs detect early cisplatin and deferoxamine injury sooner than pure-tone audiometry. (Cummings 7e, Ch 157, p 2380)

**Analgesics and salicylates**: Aspirin causes dose-dependent, reversible SNHL (up to moderate-severe) and tinnitus, which appears reliably around 6-8 g/day and resolves within about 72 hours of stopping; it acts on outer hair cell motility (prestin) without killing hair cells. Large cohort studies link regular (2 or more days a week) acetaminophen and NSAID use to hearing loss, with the strongest effect in men under 50 (about 99% higher risk with acetaminophen, 61% with NSAIDs, 33% with aspirin); in women, ibuprofen and acetaminophen but not aspirin were associated. (Cummings 7e, Ch 152, p 2315; Ch 157, p 2378)

**NIOSH versus OSHA and sound weighting**: OSHA's permissible limit is 90 dBA for 8 hours with a 5-dB exchange rate, whereas the NIOSH recommended limit is 85 dBA for 8 hours with a 3-dB exchange rate (allowed time halves with every 3-dB rise), which is more protective. A-weighting discounts energy below about 1 kHz to mirror quiet-level hearing and is the US regulatory standard; C-weighting is nearly flat and better reflects loud low-frequency sound. A personal dosimeter integrates level and time for workers who move around, and impulse noise such as gunfire needs a peak-reading meter. (Cummings 7e, Ch 154, p 2343-2344)

**NIHL course and susceptibility**: Occupational NIHL is bilateral and symmetric, starts at 3-6 kHz with the deepest notch at 4 kHz, progresses fastest in the first 10-15 years and almost never becomes profound; about 25% of US adults have a notch (15 dB at 3, 4 or 6 kHz). Acoustic trauma is a single exposure causing permanent shift without a preceding temporary shift and is often asymmetric. Conductive loss protects the cochlea, an absent acoustic reflex predisposes to injury (the reflex protects mainly at 2 kHz and below), and tinnitus after exposure is a warning sign; 50-70% of persistent tinnitus is associated with NIHL. No otoprotective drug is FDA approved for noise. (Cummings 7e, Ch 152, p 2317; Ch 154, pp 2348, 2354; Ch 153, p 2331)

**Defining asymmetry and imaging yield**: Definitions of asymmetric SNHL vary (AAO-HNS: 15 dB or more average difference at 0.5-3 kHz); the 'rule 3K' (15 dB or more interaural difference at 3 kHz) captured nearly all vestibular schwannomas while limiting MRIs. Unilateral tinnitus alone has a low MRI yield (only 4 of 542 schwannoma patients with symmetric hearing presented with tinnitus alone), but yield rises as asymmetric loss or cranial neuropathy is added. For pulsatile tinnitus, CTA/CTV is the usual first study and finds a relevant abnormality in about 20-30%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 153, p 2330)

**Somatic and typewriter tinnitus**: Somatic tinnitus is perceived in the ear, modulated by an ipsilateral somatic trigger (jaw, neck, eye or limb movement) and has no new hearing complaint; about a third of TMJ patients can modulate their tinnitus, and treating TMJ or myofascial trigger points may help. Typewriter tinnitus is an intermittent staccato clicking ('popcorn' or Morse code) triggered by movement or sound, attributed to vascular compression of the cochlear nerve; it responds to carbamazepine, whereas tensor tympani/stapedius tenotomy does not help, so distinguish it from middle ear myoclonus. (Cummings 7e, Ch 153, p 2331-2332)

**Device benefits and therapies to avoid**: Cochlear implantation improves tinnitus in about 38-85% of recipients (up to 93% suppression after 2 months), including the contralateral ear, though new or worse tinnitus occasionally occurs, more often with bilateral implants. For tinnitus, fit hearing aids with open domes, a wide bandwidth and digital noise reduction off. Intratympanic steroids and lidocaine are ineffective (lidocaine causes severe vertigo), anticonvulsants and gabapentin failed trials, benzodiazepines are discouraged, and ginkgo biloba has antiplatelet effects with reported serious bleeding with anticoagulants, so warn patients taking blood thinners. (Cummings 7e, Ch 153, p 2334-2335)

**Tinnitus numbers**: Tinnitus affects up to 50 million US adults (about 30% of those over 55); about 28% of acute tinnitus (under 6 months) resolves spontaneously, and only about 20% find it bothersome enough to seek care. Subjective nonpulsatile tinnitus is about 90% of referrals, pulsatile about 11% (86% subjective, 14% objective), and objective tinnitus only about 1.5% overall. Severe tinnitus is often accompanied by depression or anxiety, and suicide has been reported, so screen and refer. (Cummings 7e, Ch 153, p 2329, 2336)

**Hyperacusis prevalence, associations and TRT outcomes**: Hyperacusis affects about 6-8% of normal-hearing people and 18-80% of tinnitus patients, and its severity does not track audiometric thresholds, which separates it from recruitment. Associations include loss of the stapedial reflex with facial palsy, migraine, Lyme disease, benzodiazepine withdrawal and Williams syndrome; nearly half have a psychiatric disorder. Tinnitus retraining therapy raised loudness discomfort levels by about 12.5 dB and widened the dynamic range by about 11 dB, and helped hyperacusis (63%) more often than tinnitus (47%). (Cummings 7e, Ch 153, p 2332-2333)

**Post-meningitic ossification and imaging**: Up to 35% of children develop hearing loss after bacterial meningitis, and up to 70% of those with SNHL show some labyrinthine ossification, which can begin within days to 3 weeks; pneumococcus causes more SNHL, but ossification rates do not differ by organism. Steroids at diagnosis were associated with less labyrinthitis ossificans in one study. Use heavily T2-weighted MRI to show early fibrous obliteration that CT misses, and expedite implant evaluation (bilateral simultaneous implantation may be offered). Cryptococcal meningitis, the most common fungal meningitis, causes SNHL in up to 30%, with organisms in the IAC and modiolus. (Cummings 7e, Ch 155, p 2360-2362)

**Congenital syphilis, rubella, toxoplasmosis and HSV**: Infants of mothers with reactive treponemal tests need a quantitative RPR/VDRL; an infant titer more than fourfold the mother's suggests severe disease and needs CSF analysis plus HIV testing, and CDC treatment is 10 days of IV aqueous penicillin G. Rubella infection in the first trimester carries the highest risk, yet 10-20% of infants infected later develop SNHL (bilateral, often cookie-bite, from cochleosaccular degeneration). Congenital toxoplasmosis (about 1 in 10,000) causes hearing loss in up to 26%, and neonatal HSV in about 10%, though routine HSV screening for unexplained neonatal SNHL is not recommended. (Cummings 7e, Ch 155, p 2359-2360)

**No diagnostic antibody test**: The anti-68-kD (HSP-70) antibody test lacks the accuracy to rule AIED in or out, and serum TNF is too insensitive to screen, so diagnosis stays clinical: rapidly progressive SNHL that clearly responds to steroids. Labs serve to find secondary AIED: CBC, ESR, CRP, RF, ANA, ANCA, anti-dsDNA, SSA/SSB, antiphospholipid antibodies, complement and thyroid studies, plus a treponemal test (FTA-ABS or MHA-TP) and gadolinium MRI; formal vestibular testing adds little. In recurrent unilateral loss that seems steroid responsive, holding steroids for up to 2 weeks helps separate Meniere disease, which often recovers on its own. (Cummings 7e, Ch 156, p 2366-2367)

**Steroid course and steroid-sparing evidence**: Start prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 4 weeks as early as possible, because damage can become irreversible within about 3 months; nonresponders are tapered over 7-10 days, and responders taper over 4 weeks to 10-20 mg/day, restarting full dose for relapse (patients who eventually wean average about 9 years of treatment). A large RCT did not support methotrexate maintenance, and two etanercept trials showed safety but no efficacy; cyclophosphamide carries infection, marrow, bladder, fertility and cancer risks, and plasmapheresis remains experimental. In Cogan syndrome cochlear ossification can follow, so implant early in nonresponders. (Cummings 7e, Ch 156, p 2367-2368; Ch 152, p 2320)

**Autoinflammatory inner ear disease**: A newer concept is innate-immune (autoinflammatory) SNHL driven by gene mutations that cause excess IL-1 beta, as in Muckle-Wells syndrome (cryopyrin-associated, with urticarial rash and amyloidosis). Such hearing loss may respond to IL-1 blockade such as anakinra, although supporting data are limited. (Cummings 7e, Ch 156, p 2369)

**Intratympanic gentamicin protocols compared**: In a meta-analysis, titration dosing (daily or weekly until vestibular symptoms or hearing change) gave the best complete vertigo control (about 82%), low-dose one-or-two-injection regimens the worst (about 67%), multiple daily dosing the most hearing loss (about 35%) and weekly dosing the least (about 13%). Because the vestibular deafferentation reaction appears 3-5 days after an injection, space injections at least a week apart; adult 40 mg/mL gentamicin is often buffered to about 30 mg/mL. Severe hearing loss usually shows up within the first month, and poor pretreatment hearing is the main risk factor. (Cummings 7e, Ch 158, p 2390-2391)

**IT steroids versus gentamicin and spontaneous remission**: In a double-blind trial, intratympanic methylprednisolone cut vertigo attacks by about 90% versus about 87% for gentamicin, so a nonablative steroid series is a reasonable first step when hearing must be preserved, with gentamicin for those who accept hearing risk or cannot return for repeat injections. Interpret all vertigo outcomes against the 60-80% spontaneous remission of Meniere disease over 2-8 years; a single sustained-release dexamethasone dose (OTO-104) also reduced vertigo in an early RCT. (Cummings 7e, Ch 158, p 2386-2387)

**Vibrant Soundbridge (semi-implantable middle-ear implant)**: an electromagnetic floating mass transducer (FMT) is clipped to the long process of the incus through a transmastoid approach. It can instead be coupled to the round window, the stapes, or the footplate (vibroplasty) for conductive or mixed loss. FDA criteria are age 18 or older, moderate-to-severe SNHL (PTA up to about 70 dB), normal middle-ear anatomy, word recognition of at least 50%, and no retrocochlear disease. Mean functional gain is about 30 dB. Current models are conditional at 1.5 T but not 3 T MRI. (Cummings 7e, Ch 159, pp 2401–2402)

**Totally implantable piezoelectric devices (Esteem, Carina)**: in the Esteem, a sensor on the malleus/drum picks up sound and a driver on the stapes moves it. The incus is partly removed to stop feedback between them, so device failure or removal leaves a maximal conductive loss. Its nonrechargeable battery is replaced surgically about every 5 years, and the device is not MRI compatible. The Carina uses a subcutaneous microphone with a piezoelectric driver on the incus and leaves the ossicles intact. Both are for adults with moderate-to-severe SNHL. (Cummings 7e, Ch 159, pp 2404–2406)

**Percutaneous bone-anchored implant audiologic limits**: the bone-conduction PTA (0.5–3 kHz) should be 45 dB HL or better for a standard head-worn processor, up to 55 dB for a Power processor and up to 65 dB for a Super Power processor. In long-term series, 89% with BC PTA under 45 dB improved, compared with 61% at 46–60 dB and only 22% above 60 dB. For single-sided deafness, the hearing ear needs an AC PTA of 20 dB HL or better. Contraindications include age under 5 (FDA) and BC thresholds worse than 65 dB. An indication sometimes missed is otosclerosis, tympanosclerosis or atresia when repair is unwise, such as in an only-hearing ear. (Cummings 7e, Ch 159, pp 2410–2411)

**Abutment and osseointegration complications**: soft-tissue reactions are graded with the Holgers scale (0–4); grade 2–4 reactions occur in about 2–38%. Skin overgrowth of the abutment is the most common complication (about 7%, usually about 1 year after surgery). Failure to osseointegrate is second (0–18%). Its risk factors are a thin skull, young age, syndromic patients and prior radiation, which favor a two-stage operation, with hyperbaric oxygen sometimes used after radiation. Revision rates are about 2–35% in adults and up to 44% in children. A linear incision without soft-tissue reduction, using an abutment that stands at least 3 mm above the skin, does not raise skin complications and shortens surgery. (Cummings 7e, Ch 159, p 2410)

**Transcutaneous bone-conduction options**: *passive* systems (BAHA Attract, Sophono Alpha 2) use implanted magnets under intact skin. Skin thinned to about 4–6 mm if needed. They give better cosmesis and skin health, but the skin attenuates the signal, so output is about 10–15 dB less than a percutaneous abutment. *Active* Bonebridge places a floating mass transducer in a 9-mm bony well, so osseointegration is not needed. It is FDA approved from age 12 for conductive or mixed loss (BC PTA up to 45 dB) and for SSD (hearing ear 20 dB or better). It is 1.5 T MRI conditional but leaves an artifact of up to about 15 cm. (Cummings 7e, Ch 159, pp 2411–2412)

**Prescription, verification and validation**: gain targets come from prescriptive formulas, mainly NAL-NL2 and DSL v5.0, which is favored for children. Ear-canal resonance varies between people, so the delivered output must be verified at the drum with real-ear probe-microphone measurement. Speech mapping with soft, average and loud speech is now standard. Benefit is then validated with self-report tools: HHIE (handicap), APHAB (benefit), COSI (patient-chosen goals), and IOI-HA or the Glasgow Hearing Aid Benefit Profile (quality of life). (Cummings 7e, Ch 164, pp 2462–2464)

**Binaural versus monaural fitting**: symmetric loss should be fitted with two aids for localization, better speech in noise and better sound quality. Aiding only one ear in bilateral loss puts the unaided ear at long-term risk of declining speech recognition (deprivation). When only one aid can be fitted, aid the better ear. Aiding a very poor-discrimination ear can cause binaural interference that lowers overall understanding. When the poorer ear cannot be aided usefully, route its signal to the better ear (CROS/BiCROS). (Cummings 7e, Ch 164, pp 2462–2463)

**Hard-to-fit configurations and older listeners**: a precipitous high-frequency loss, with or without cochlear dead regions, is hard to fit; frequency-lowering (transposition or compression) moves high-frequency cues into audible regions. Rising (low-frequency) losses are uncommon (under 2%) and pick up a lot of background noise when aided. Word recognition worse than the thresholds predict, as in hydrops, retrocochlear tumors or ANSD, limits benefit. In older adults with central auditory decline, add directional microphones, noise reduction and remote microphones. Dexterity and cognition guide the choice of style. (Cummings 7e, Ch 164, pp 2455–2456, 2465)

**Pediatric fitting and nonprescription devices**: a child's small ear canal leaves little residual volume, so the same aid produces a higher SPL at the drum than in an adult. Individual real-ear measures are therefore essential and must be repeated as the child grows. Children are always fitted bilaterally with the controls disabled, and gain must cover fluctuating loss from effusion. Personal sound amplification products (PSAPs) are not FDA devices for treating hearing loss and are distinct from FDA-regulated OTC hearing aids for adults with perceived mild-to-moderate loss. (Cummings 7e, Ch 164, pp 2455, 2464–2465)

**Cummings referral and trial criteria**: refer *adults* when unaided thresholds are 70 dB HL or worse at 1 kHz and above in the better ear, unaided word discrimination is under 60%, or communication frustration persists despite aids. Consider *children* when the better ear has unaided thresholds over 90 dB at 2 kHz and above or aided thresholds over 35 dB (especially at 4 kHz), when ABR is absent in both ears (or absent in one and elevated in the other), when loss is progressive into the profound range, when severe ANSD is present, or when parents are concerned about progress. Recent adult trial criteria were PTA of 70 dB or more, aided open-set sentence scores under 50% in the implant ear and 60% or less in the other ear, and 1–3 months of hearing-aid use. There is no upper age limit. (Cummings 7e, Ch 160, pp 2413, 2416–2417)

**Electric-acoustic (hybrid) candidacy**: candidates have low-frequency thresholds no worse than 60 dB HL through 500 Hz and an average of 75 dB HL or worse at 2, 3 and 4 kHz. CNC scores are 10–60% in the implant ear and no better than 80% in the other ear. Short arrays (about 10, 15 or 20 mm) are inserted atraumatically, usually through the round window. Delayed loss of the preserved hearing occurs in up to 40%, mostly in the first year. If it happens, the patient can use the electric mode alone or be reimplanted with a standard-length array for better coverage. (Cummings 7e, Ch 160, p 2417; Ch 161, pp 2431–2432; Ch 162, p 2442)

**Jervell and Lange-Nielsen before CI surgery**: JLNS is found in about 6 per 1000 deaf children, and perioperative arrhythmic deaths have occurred during CI surgery. Obtain an ECG and refer to cardiology and genetics for syncope, atypical seizures, or a family history of sudden death or long QT; a normal QT does not exclude JLNS. Anesthesia precautions: correct magnesium, calcium and potassium; use total IV anesthesia with propofol, because sevoflurane prolongs QT; give beta-blockade; extubate deep; and have transvenous pacing and a pediatric cardiologist available. Consider omitting epinephrine from the local injection. (Cummings 7e, Ch 161, pp 2425–2426)

**Cochlear nerve deficiency (CND) on imaging**: about 20% of congenitally deaf patients have an inner-ear malformation, and the cochlear nerve can be small or absent even when the IAC on CT is normal. MRI is therefore needed in ANSD (where CND causes up to about 18–20%), in children with SSD, and after meningitis. Suspect CND when the IAC is 1.5 mm or narrower or the bony cochlear nerve canal is under 1.4 mm. Fewer than 20% of CND ears benefit meaningfully from a CI. Michel aplasia and a proven absent nerve are absolute contraindications. (Cummings 7e, Ch 160, p 2415; Ch 161, pp 2426, 2433)

**Timing after meningitis**: ossification starts next to the round window and moves apically. Hearing can partly recover, which argues for some observation, sometimes up to 6 months. However, fibrosis and new bone can form within a month. Get MRI at about 1 month and then every 2–3 months. Loss of T2 fluid signal in the cochlea (sometimes seen first in the horizontal semicircular canal) means recovery is unlikely and implantation should not wait. CT plus MRI detects fibrosis better than either alone. (Cummings 7e, Ch 161, pp 2433–2434)

**Etiology and expected outcome**: autoimmune inner ear disease and bilateral Ménière disease usually do very well after CI, because neurons survive and deafness is short. TORCH infection, prematurity, hyperbilirubinemia and other causes of central processing deficits call for tempered expectations; TORCH can also displace the facial nerve. Bilateral temporal bone fractures should be implanted early, before cochlear fibrosis. When nerve injury is suspected, promontory electrical stimulation with electrically evoked ABR checks whether the nerve works before CI is chosen over an ABI. (Cummings 7e, Ch 160, p 2414)

**CI in chronic otitis media or an open cavity**: implant only into a dry ear. *Dry perforation*: myringoplasty first, then CI about 3 months later. *Cholesteatoma or unstable cavity*: radical mastoidectomy with eustachian tube obliteration and blind-sac canal closure, with or without obliteration, then CI 2–6 months later. *Stable cavity*: single-stage obliteration and implantation. Closing the canal can bury cholesteatoma, which needs long-term monitoring. Otitis media itself is not more frequent after implantation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 160, pp 2414–2415)

**Cummings ear-selection logic**: implant the better or uninvolved ear when the worse ear has an imaging problem (dysplasia, ossification, facial-nerve or vascular anomaly, poor pneumatization) or a medical one (chronic otitis, trauma, prior surgery, tumor or Gamma Knife). Also favor the better ear when the worse ear has been anacusic or unaidable for more than 10 years. Otherwise implant the worse ear, which keeps a hearing aid in the better ear (bimodal); outcomes with either ear are similar. Up to 35% of adults over 40 and 70% of children with profound SNHL already have vestibular dysfunction. Some centers implant the ear with weaker vestibular function to protect balance in the better labyrinth. (Cummings 7e, Ch 161, pp 2425–2427; Ch 162, p 2441)

**Pneumococcal vaccination details**: a 2003 CDC study found pneumococcal meningitis in 0.6% of implanted children, about 30 times the rate in age-matched controls. Risk is highest with labyrinthine dysplasia, prior meningitis and the old positioner arrays. The book schedule is a PCV series plus PPSV23 at age 2 for children; vaccine-naive adults get a conjugate vaccine followed by PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later. CI recipients are not at extra meningococcal risk. Note: ACIP has since replaced PCV13 with newer conjugate vaccines (PCV15/20/21), so follow the current CDC schedule. (Cummings 7e, Ch 161, pp 2427–2428)

**Why two ears help (bilateral CI, bimodal, SSD)**: *head shadow* is a physical effect and gives the largest benefit. *Squelch* and *summation* are central processes worth about 2–3 dB of signal-to-noise ratio. Horizontal localization error averages about 50–67 degrees with one CI and 24–29 degrees with two, compared with about 14 degrees in normal listeners. About 20% of users have bilateral devices. In SSD, a CI improves hearing in noise, localization and tinnitus more than a bone-conduction device or CROS, which cannot restore localization. CI for SSD was off-label when the book was written and has since been FDA approved (2019, from age 5). (Cummings 7e, Ch 159, p 2411; Ch 161, p 2435; Ch 162, p 2442)

**Pediatric timing evidence**: children implanted before 12 months reach language comprehension and expression comparable to hearing peers and better than children implanted at 12–24 months. Implantation from about 6 months is therefore supported, limited mainly by diagnosis and the hearing-aid trial. Early-implanted children show normal cortical auditory evoked potential latency in about 96%, compared with about 5% of late-implanted children. Cortical recovery is minimal after about age 5. Up to 70% of early-implanted children taught without sign language reach age-appropriate spoken language, compared with 39% of those taught ASL. (Cummings 7e, Ch 161, pp 2432, 2438)

**Tight periosteal pocket technique**: make a 3–4 cm incision 1 cm behind the postauricular crease and dissect in the avascular areolar plane. Seat the receiver-stimulator in a tight subperiosteal pocket between the temporoparietal and lambdoid sutures, with no bone well or tie-downs. In 227 cases there was no migration, whereas drilling a seat has caused dural exposure, CSF leak, epidural or subdural hematoma and sinus thrombosis; parietal bone is only about 1 mm thick in young children. The skin flap must be no thicker than about 6–8 mm. Avoid surgical thinning, which exposes hair follicles and invites biofilm; a depot triamcinolone injection can thin a thick flap after surgery. Do not use monopolar cautery near an existing implant. In Down syndrome, avoid excessive head rotation because of cervical instability. (Cummings 7e, Ch 161, pp 2428–2429)

**Choosing the cochlear opening and insertion vector**: in a survey, 86% of surgeons used a round window approach, 9% an extended round window and 5% a bony cochleostomy anteroinferior to the window. When the round window membrane is angled more than 45 degrees inferiorly (about 10% of ears), it looks smaller than a 1-mm burr; an extended or bony opening is then safer. Precurved perimodiolar arrays placed through the round window tend to strike the modiolus, causing translocation or tip foldover. For round window insertion, emphasize the inferior vector, because the modiolus lies directly anterior. A burr touching the endosteum produces about 130 dB, so avoid contact. Insert over 30 seconds or longer, not the usual 3–10 seconds, and pack fascia all the way around the array. (Cummings 7e, Ch 161, pp 2430–2431)

**Pharmacologic hearing preservation**: give a single IV dexamethasone dose (about 0.1–0.2 mg/kg in children, 4–8 mg in adults). Dexamethasone-soaked sponges can also be placed at the round window. Put a drop of hyaluronic acid on the opening, but never inject it into the scala. Most residual hearing is lost later through inflammation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, fibrosis and new bone, not from the immediate mechanical injury. This is the rationale for steroids even in ears with no usable hearing. (Cummings 7e, Ch 161, pp 2428, 2431)

**Gusher and lumbar drain timing**: expect a gusher in any malformation visible on imaging; it can also occur with membranous dysplasia when the bony labyrinth looks normal. Insert the array through the clear fluid and pack muscle or fascia tightly into the opening. Do not place a lumbar drain before the seal is made: it lowers CSF pressure and hides whether the seal holds. A drain is also unnecessary once the leak is sealed. (Cummings 7e, Ch 161, p 2433)

**Ossified cochlea strategies**: in the 1990s, 3–9% of pediatric candidates had ossification, which in about 90% was limited to the area next to the round window; drill through it to the patent basal turn. If the scala tympani is blocked, insert a full-length array into a patent scala vestibuli. If both scalae are ossified beyond the ascending turn, use a complete drill-out or a split (double) array and set low expectations. Small wedges from the long process of the incus or malleus help hold the array in place. Post-meningitic ears need higher stimulation levels and more reprogramming over time, which raises the risk of facial-nerve stimulation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 161, p 2434)

**Complication benchmarks**: overall CI complication rates fell from about 39% in 1991 to under 10%, and postoperative facial paresis is now under 1%. Revision rates are 3.8–7% in adults and 8–12.5% in children. Damaged or misplaced electrodes account for about 1.2% of revisions. Tinnitus improves in 50–90% of patients but is new or worse in up to 28%. An electrode that crosses between scalae carries about a 16% risk of causing or worsening tinnitus. (Cummings 7e, Ch 161, pp 2435–2436)

**Vestibular effects of implantation**: patients rarely volunteer complaints, but up to 75% report vestibular symptoms when asked. These are usually mild and resolve with central compensation, and gait may even improve. Techniques not designed for hearing preservation reduce caloric responses in more than 90% and abolish VEMPs in about 40%, although most patients have no symptoms. This matters more with bilateral implantation and in older adults. (Cummings 7e, Ch 161, pp 2437–2438)

**Revision causes and tip foldover**: in a series of 2827 implants placed with bone seats, 8.3% were revised. The causes were device failure (58%), receiver-stimulator migration (23%) and infection (17%). Tip foldover is more common with delicate perimodiolar arrays. The surgeon cannot see it during insertion, it usually causes no aversive sensations, and it lowers performance. Overlap on spread-of-excitation testing suggests it, but imaging diagnoses it best; treatment is to deactivate the overlapping contacts or replace the array. Fluctuating performance in patients with autoimmune hearing loss or systemic autoimmune disease may respond to steroids. (Cummings 7e, Ch 161, pp 2436–2437)

**Far-advanced otosclerosis (FAO): stapedotomy or CI?**: FAO means air-conduction thresholds over 85 dB with no measurable bone conduction. Overall, a CI gives better results than stapedotomy plus a hearing aid. Exceptions are ears with good cochlear reserve, where a successful stapedotomy performs about as well. A prior stapedotomy does not harm CI outcomes. In otosclerotic ears, expect facial-nerve stimulation, pain or dizziness from current flowing through spongiotic bone; this is more common with straight than perimodiolar arrays. Expect scalar translocation and gusher as well. Get both CT and MRI, because CT tends to overestimate scalar obstruction. (Cummings 7e, Ch 161, pp 2434–2435)

**Hearing rehabilitation in NF2**: if the cochlear nerve is anatomically intact (untreated or radiated tumor, or after hearing-preservation surgery), try a CI first; it gives open-set speech in up to about 70%, which an ABI rarely achieves. Assess nerve status with promontory stimulation no sooner than 6–8 weeks after surgery. An absent response does not rule out CI benefit. About one third of ears develop cochlear ossification after translabyrinthine surgery, which favors a CI placed at the same operation. If the nerve is lost, place an ABI at the first-side resection as a 'sleeper' device. (Cummings 7e, Ch 163, p 2449)

**Compensation and hyperventilation clues**: slow tumor growth lets the brain compensate gradually, so many patients only notice brief imbalance on quick turns toward the tumor side. Patients whose vestibular function is preserved until surgery often have severe postoperative vertigo and an ocular tilt reaction, with vertical diplopia from skew. Hyperventilation can transiently restore conduction in a demyelinated nerve (schwannoma, vascular compression, MS). The result is an excitatory nystagmus whose fast phase beats toward the affected ear, whereas peripheral hypofunction usually beats away from it. (Cummings 7e, Ch 165, pp 2490, 2493; Ch 166, p 2505)

**CONFLICT on caloric cutoffs, plus caloric mechanics**: Cummings counts unilateral weakness over 20% and directional preponderance over 25% (Jongkees formulas) as significant, with each lab setting its own norms. The patient lies with the head up 30 degrees, and convection produces about 75% of the response. Warm water excites the horizontal canal (ampullopetal flow). Directional preponderance usually reflects a spontaneous nystagmus that adds to or subtracts from each irrigation; without one, it may be a central sign. (Cummings 7e, Ch 166, pp 2508–2509)

**Rotary chair: indications and time constant**: rotary chair is best for suspected bilateral loss, monitoring vestibulotoxic drugs, children who do not tolerate calorics, after meningitis, and genetic hearing-loss workups; it is not affected by the canal or cerumen. The cupula returns with a time constant of about 10 seconds, but velocity storage stretches the VOR time constant to about 20 seconds. Peripheral loss shortens the time constant and causes low-frequency phase lead and reduced gain. Bilateral loss lowers both gain and time constant. A compensated unilateral loss can have normal gain and phase, leaving only an asymmetry. (Cummings 7e, Ch 165, p 2488; Ch 166, pp 2509–2510)

**Posturography and subjective visual vertical**: the sensory organization test has six conditions. In conditions 1–3 the platform is fixed (eyes open; eyes closed; visual surround sway-referenced). In conditions 4–6 the platform is sway-referenced (eyes open; eyes closed; both sway-referenced). Falls on conditions 5 and 6 are the 'vestibular pattern'. A bedside version (CTSIB: foam plus a lantern over the head) correlates with it. After acute loss of utricular function, the subjective visual vertical is tilted about 10–15 degrees toward the lesioned side, but the test does not show which ear is affected unless done during off-axis rotation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 166, pp 2512–2513)

**Skew deviation and the ocular tilt reaction**: skew is a vertical misalignment not explained by an ocular muscle palsy. Detect it with the alternate cover test or a Maddox rod. With peripheral or vestibular-nucleus lesions (below the decussation), the lower eye is on the side of the lesion. Above the decussation (MLF or INO, midbrain), the higher eye is on the lesion side, and the head tilts toward the lower eye. The full ocular tilt reaction is head tilt, skew and conjugate ocular torsion. A fourth nerve palsy is worst with the eye down and in (Bielschowsky head tilt), whereas skew changes little with gaze and may lessen when supine. (Cummings 7e, Ch 165, p 2490; Ch 166, pp 2500–2501)

**Saccade and pursuit localization**: overshoot or undershoot dysmetria points to the dorsal vermis or fastigial nuclei. In Wallenberg syndrome, saccades overshoot toward the lesion and undershoot away from it, and vertical saccades drift toward the lesion; superior cerebellar peduncle lesions do the opposite. Slow horizontal saccades suggest pontine disease (e.g., SCA2); slow vertical saccades suggest the midbrain (PSP, Huntington, Niemann-Pick). Square-wave jerks (5 degrees or less) are prominent in PSP and cerebellar disease. Ocular flutter (horizontal) and opsoclonus (multidirectional) suggest encephalitis or paraneoplastic disease such as neuroblastoma. Flocculus lesions impair ipsilateral pursuit, and sedatives, anticonvulsants and age also degrade pursuit. Normal saccade latency is about 200 ms. (Cummings 7e, Ch 166, pp 2501–2502)

**Central nystagmus patterns and their drugs**: *downbeat*: Chiari malformation or cerebellar degeneration; treat with 4-aminopyridine. *Upbeat*: pontomedullary or pontomesencephalic junction, or fourth ventricle. *Periodic alternating* (horizontal nystagmus reversing about every 2 minutes): cerebellar nodulus; treat with baclofen. *Pendular*: MS, or oculopalatal tremor after brainstem stroke; may respond to memantine or gabapentin. *Purely torsional*: vestibular nuclei (e.g., syringobulbia). *Seesaw*: midbrain. *Convergence-retraction*: Parinaud syndrome. *Dissociated, abducting-eye nystagmus*: INO. *Rebound nystagmus*: cerebellar disease. Nystagmus outside the plane of the stimulated canal ('perverted') is central. (Cummings 7e, Ch 166, p 2500)

**Bedside signs of acute unilateral loss**: spontaneous horizontal-torsional nystagmus beats toward the intact ear and is suppressed by fixation, so look with Frenzel lenses. *First-degree* nystagmus appears only on gaze toward the fast phase, *second-degree* also in primary gaze, and *third-degree* in every direction. After about 30 passive head shakes, the initial nystagmus beats toward the intact side and may then reverse. Mastoid or suboccipital vibration also drives nystagmus toward the intact side. An abnormal head impulse needs a fast thrust of only 10–20 degrees; the corrective saccade appears after thrusts toward the lesion. (Cummings 7e, Ch 165, p 2482; Ch 166, pp 2499, 2503–2504)

**Expected course after acute loss**: spontaneous nystagmus resolves within days. Most patients have no vertigo at rest and can walk (perhaps with help) by about 2 weeks, and walk unaided and resume daily activities by about 1 month. Head-shaking and gaze-evoked nystagmus last longer, and fast head turns toward the lesion fail permanently if the nerve does not recover. Posterior canal BPPV develops later in 15–30% of patients, so new positional vertigo after recovery should prompt a Dix-Hallpike test rather than a diagnosis of relapse. (Cummings 7e, Ch 165, pp 2492–2493)

**Why compensation works and when it fails**: after unilateral loss, the ipsilateral vestibular nuclei fall silent. Resting activity rebalances over 1–3 weeks, but the dynamic asymmetry (abnormal head impulse) persists. Adaptation needs error signals such as retinal slip; through cerebellar learning (climbing-fiber driven long-term depression) these raise VOR gain. Exercises that provoke visual-vestibular mismatch are therefore essential, and recovery is helped by sensory substitution, cervico-ocular reflex potentiation and preprogrammed saccades. A stable deficit can be compensated but a fluctuating one cannot. This is why ablation (gentamicin, neurectomy, labyrinthectomy) helps intractable Ménière disease when the other ear is stable. New CNS insults can cause decompensation later. (Cummings 7e, Ch 165, pp 2491–2493)

**Vertebral artery dissection**: Dissection is easy to miss because dizziness is its most frequent symptom (about 58%) and most patients have no neck pain, so no single symptom rules it out. It causes only about 2% of ischemic strokes overall but a large share of strokes under age 45 (mean onset about 46 years), and trauma, chiropractic manipulation or connective-tissue disease is present in fewer than half. Diagnose with CT or MR angiography; antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy is first line, with endovascular treatment as an option. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, p 2545)

**AICA versus PICA territory numbers**: The labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery arises from the AICA in about 80% of people, so an AICA (lateral pontomedullary) infarct causes combined vestibular and auditory loss in about 60%, often with ipsilateral facial weakness, tinnitus and contralateral pain-temperature loss; vertigo can linger for weeks because central compensation pathways are damaged. A lateral medullary (Wallenberg) infarct spares hearing because it lies caudal to the cochlear nerve entry zone and cochlear nuclei. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, p 2543)

**Cerebellar infarction and hemorrhage**: A cerebellum-only infarct presents with severe vertigo, vomiting and ataxia but few brainstem signs, so it is mistaken for acute labyrinthitis; prominent gait ataxia and gaze-evoked nystagmus are the clues, and early MRI can be falsely negative. After a latent interval of about 24 to 96 hours, cerebellar swelling can compress the brainstem and progress to coma and death unless surgical decompression is done, so admit and observe. Cerebellar hemorrhage (mortality about 20%-74%) is shown on noncontrast CT, which should be the first study to exclude blood. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, pp 2543-2545)

**Central positional vertigo and fourth-ventricle masses**: Positional vertigo can come from lesions of the dorsolateral fourth ventricle or dorsal vermis. Suspect it when positional nystagmus has a short or no latency, an atypical direction (for example pure downbeat), appears in several positions, does not fatigue, and fails to respond to repositioning maneuvers. Fourth-ventricle tumors (medulloblastoma in children, ependymoma, epidermoid) can cause headache, vomiting and vertigo with head-position change from intermittent CSF obstruction (Bruns syndrome). Dizziness occurs in about 81% of posterior fossa tumors. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, pp 2544, 2547)

**Vertebrobasilar insufficiency treatment**: Vertebrobasilar ischemia is usually atherosclerotic (vertebral origin in men of European descent; intracranial disease more often in African American, Asian and female patients) and seldom causes vertigo alone without diplopia, ataxia, numbness, weakness or bulbar symptoms. Nonacute care is risk-factor control. For symptomatic 50%-99% intracranial stenosis, aspirin works as well as warfarin with less bleeding and is preferred; warfarin is reserved for cardioembolic stroke. Get CT first to exclude hemorrhage, and route acute stroke to neurology for thrombolysis decisions. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, p 2543)

**Chiari malformation**: Chiari I is defined by cerebellar tonsils more than 5 mm below the foramen magnum on sagittal MRI. It is an incidental finding in about 3.6% of people, and symptoms usually begin at age 25-35: occipital headache brought on by cough, sneeze, bending or lifting, arm weakness and sensory loss, ataxia (24%-49%) and, less often, vertigo (8%-18%) or downbeat nystagmus. Lower cranial nerve involvement can bring the patient to ENT with dysphagia, aspiration or hoarseness. About a third do not improve after decompression. Chiari II appears in infancy with hydrocephalus and myelomeningocele. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, p 2548)

**Craniovertebral junction disorders**: Cervicomedullary compression can cause tinnitus, vertigo, hearing loss, dysphagia and hoarseness, and it can lead to needless ear surgery if missed. In basilar impression (from Paget disease, rheumatoid arthritis, osteomalacia, osteogenesis imperfecta or rickets), the odontoid tip rises above Chamberlain's line (posterior hard palate to the posterior lip of the foramen magnum) or lies behind Wackenheim's clivus-canal line; platybasia alone causes no symptoms. Atlas assimilation often comes with Klippel-Feil fusion. Atlantoaxial instability is seen radiographically in 10%-30% of people with Down syndrome (atlantodens interval 4-5 mm), but only 1%-2% have symptoms. MRI is the key study. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, pp 2547-2548)

**Multiple sclerosis**: Vertigo is the first symptom of MS in only about 5% of patients but occurs in up to 60% at some point, and MS causes about 10% of central acute vestibular syndromes. Plaques in the vestibular nuclei or the CN VIII root entry zone are the usual cause, and other signs such as internuclear ophthalmoplegia usually point to a central lesion. BPPV is still the most common cause of vertigo in people with MS, so do positional testing. MRI shows white-matter lesions in over 90% of cases, and CSF oligoclonal bands are common. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, pp 2548-2549)

**Hereditary, degenerative and paraneoplastic ataxias**: Familial episodic ataxia is autosomal dominant. Stress-triggered attacks of vertigo and ataxia last minutes to hours, start between childhood and early adulthood, and respond markedly to acetazolamide. Friedreich ataxia (autosomal recessive GAA expansion in frataxin, onset usually before age 20) combines sensory neuropathy with areflexia, Babinski sign, cardiomyopathy and diabetes, with square-wave jerks and low VOR gain. Late-onset cerebellar atrophy shows rebound and vertical nystagmus. Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration progresses rapidly over months, sometimes with opsoclonus-myoclonus, from anti-Purkinje antibodies (small cell lung, breast or ovarian cancer, Hodgkin lymphoma), and it often appears before the cancer is found. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, p 2549)

**Mal de debarquement versus PPPD and motion sickness**: After disembarking, a rocking feeling ('land sickness') is normal: it fades within 6 hours in more than 90% of people and within about 48 hours in most others. Mal de debarquement syndrome is rocking or swaying (not spinning) that lasts at least a month after a cruise, flight or long drive. It mostly affects women in their 40s and can last months to years. Unlike PPPD and motion sickness, symptoms improve while riding in a vehicle and return when motion stops. Meclizine and scopolamine do not help; benzodiazepines (clonazepam), amitriptyline, readaptation to passive motion and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation may help. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, p 2550)

**Precipitants and diagnostic stance**: PPPD is diagnosed by positive Barany criteria, not by exclusion. Precipitants are peripheral or central vestibular disorders in about 25%-30%, vestibular migraine attacks in 15%-20%, panic attacks or generalized anxiety with prominent dizziness in about 15% each, concussion or whiplash in 10%-15%, and autonomic disorders in about 7%. Coexisting conditions are common and need treatment alongside the PPPD. The maladaptive mechanism is keeping high-threat postural strategies (stiffening, visual dependence) after the trigger resolves. Treat with a three-part plan: PPPD-specific gentle vestibular therapy, SSRIs or SNRIs, and cognitive behavioral therapy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, pp 2541-2542; Ch 170, p 2570)

**Prophylaxis doses and drug-class details**: Start with lifestyle measures (migraine diet, regular sleep, aerobic exercise), and add prophylaxis if symptoms persist after 6-8 weeks. Typical starting and target doses: propranolol 60 mg/day to 120-180 mg/day; nortriptyline 5-10 mg/day up to 50-200 mg/day (less sedating than amitriptyline, which is 10-25 mg at bedtime up to 50-100 mg); venlafaxine 37.5 mg/day to 75-225 mg/day; gabapentin 300 mg/day to 1200-2400 mg/day in divided doses; zonisamide 25 mg/day up to 100-400 mg/day, often better tolerated than topiramate. Only beta-blockers without intrinsic sympathomimetic activity work (acebutolol does not). Verapamil has a modest effect, and diltiazem has none. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, pp 2538, 2540)

**Epidemiology and timing numbers**: Migraine affects about 25% of women, 15% of men and 5% of children, and the female excess in vestibular migraine may reach 4:1, with mean onset in middle age. Vertigo comes before the headache in only about 15%; it occurs during the headache in about 47% and in the headache-free interval in about 36%. Motion sickness is much more common with migraine (about 51% vs 20% with tension headache). The lifetime prevalence of migraine is 56% in Ménière disease versus 25% in controls. At about 9 years of follow-up, the diagnosis was confirmed with a positive predictive value of 85%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 168, pp 2537-2540)

**Uncompensated stable lesion versus unstable labyrinth**: Before offering ablative surgery, decide whether symptoms come from poor central compensation after a stable lesion or from a fluctuating labyrinth. A single severe crisis followed by milder, motion-provoked or continuous unsteadiness suggests a stable but uncompensated lesion, so treat with rehabilitation. Spontaneous spells as bad as or worse than the first, or fluctuating SNHL, point to unstable disease. In the Michigan series of uncompensated vestibular neuritis, rehabilitation gave complete or dramatic improvement in 72%, versus 25% dramatic improvement, 25% no improvement and 5% worsening after vestibular nerve section. No improvement after 4-6 weeks of supervised therapy makes an unstable labyrinth (hydrops, fistula) more likely. (Cummings 7e, Ch 169, pp 2556-2557)

**Cochleosacculotomy and endolymphatic sac surgery details**: In cochleosacculotomy, a 3-mm right-angle pick is passed through the round window to fracture the osseous spiral lamina, creating a permanent endolymph-perilymph shunt. It relieves vertigo in about 70% but causes high-frequency SNHL in about 25% and profound loss in about 10%, so it is an alternative to labyrinthectomy in elderly patients who already have poor hearing. The endolymphatic sac always lies below Donaldson's line (drawn along the horizontal semicircular canal through the posterior canal), bounded by the sigmoid sinus, jugular bulb and mastoid facial nerve. A Cochrane review of two RCTs found no significant benefit from sac surgery. A sac-to-subarachnoid shunt is conceptually flawed and raises CSF leak risk. (Cummings 7e, Ch 169, pp 2554-2555)

**Plugging outcomes and intraoperative ECochG**: Plugging is more reliable than resurfacing. It relieves vertigo and lowers superior semicircular canal VOR gain by about 44%, with a modest 10% fall in ipsilateral posterior canal gain. Hearing improvement is less predictable than relief of the auditory symptoms. The ECochG SP/AP ratio is usually high, rises further when the dehiscence is exposed, and normalizes right after an adequate plug, so it can guide surgery. Do not suction perilymph at the defect. Plug with fascia or periosteum supported by bone chips or bone pate. Use a transmastoid route for poor craniotomy candidates. (Cummings 7e, Ch 169, pp 2553-2554)

**Exploration technique**: When possible, explore under local anesthesia with sedation so that the patient can do a Valsalva maneuver. Remove posterosuperior canal bone until the oval window is fully seen, and take down the round window overhang and mucosal folds. Clear fluid that reaccumulates in a niche is often transudate or pooled local anesthetic, not perilymph, so it does not confirm a fistula. Inspect fissures in front of the oval window and below the round window. Routinely patch the round window niche even when exploration is negative, but be conservative at the oval window to avoid a conductive loss. Explore early for penetrating trauma or suspected stapes subluxation; for suspected chronic fistula with stable hearing, try vestibular rehabilitation first. Beta-2 transferrin testing of middle-ear fluid is not recommended. (Cummings 7e, Ch 169, p 2554)

**Functional outcome measures and fall-risk cutoffs**: Track self-report and performance measures. DHI (0-100) scores self-perceived handicap, with 100 meaning severe. On the ABC scale, below 85% identifies likely fallers. On the Dynamic Gait Index, a score under 19/24 correlates with falls in older adults living in the community. A Functional Gait Assessment score of 22/30 or less predicts falls with 100% sensitivity and 72% specificity. A Timed Up and Go over about 11 seconds signals higher fall risk, and gait speed below 0.6 m/s suggests poor aging. If posturography is not available, the modified CTSIB tests four 30-second stances: eyes open or closed, on a firm or foam surface. (Cummings 7e, Ch 170, pp 2567, 2571)

**Static versus dynamic compensation and decompensation**: Static compensation rebalances resting activity in the vestibular nuclei and relieves the worst vertigo and vomiting within 24-72 hours. Dynamic compensation (adaptation, habituation, substitution) is much slower. Gaze stability must work up to head frequencies of about 10 Hz, while posture needs only below about 4 Hz. Substitution strategies include the cervico-ocular reflex, smooth pursuit, and covert or overt compensatory saccades. VOR x1 and x2 exercises can produce either true gain recovery or more saccades. Compensation is fragile: inactivity, fatigue, a change in medication, general anesthesia or an intercurrent illness can cause relapse without any new labyrinthine disease. Habituation exercises usually relieve positional symptoms within 2-6 weeks. (Cummings 7e, Ch 170, pp 2565-2566, 2572)

**Electrodiagnostic test criteria and pitfalls**: These tests apply only to complete paralysis, from about day 3 (after Wallerian degeneration) until recovery begins or excitability is lost. A nerve excitability test difference above 3.5 mA suggests degeneration, though 38% of such patients still recover fully. On the maximal stimulation test, an equal response predicts complete recovery in about 92%, and a markedly reduced or absent response predicts incomplete recovery in about 86%. ENoG compares the nasolabial CMAP between sides; healthy sides differ by about 3%, and test-retest error is about 20%, so average repeated trials. Degeneration above 90% within 14 days leaves only about a 30% chance of spontaneous good recovery. Always follow over 90% ENoG with voluntary EMG: motor units or polyphasic potentials mean dyssynchrony (false-positive ENoG) and an excellent prognosis. Patients who cannot cooperate are treated as complete and tested with MST after 72 hours. (Cummings 7e, Ch 171, pp 2579-2582)

**Late EMG and nerve-repair failure**: Fibrillation potentials appear 10-14 days after denervation and predict incomplete recovery in about 81%. Polyphasic reinnervation potentials can appear as early as 4-6 weeks, before visible movement, and predict fair to good recovery. After 14 days, EMG predicts outcome better than ENoG. After a nerve repair or anastomosis, no clinical recovery and no polyphasic potentials by 15 months (18 months at the latest) means failure, and another procedure such as hypoglossal-facial transfer should be considered. (Cummings 7e, Ch 171, pp 2581-2582)

**Grading reliability and FNGS 2.0**: House-Brackmann is AAO-HNS endorsed and weights maximal effort, but full agreement among examiners ranges from only about 33% to 80%, and it handles regional and secondary deficits poorly. Facial Nerve Grading System 2.0 scores the brow, eye, nasolabial fold and oral commissure separately (1-6 each) and adds a secondary-movement score for synkinesis and contracture. In acute palsy, where synkinesis cannot yet exist, grade by percentage of function: II = 75%-99%, III = 50%-75%, IV = 25%-50%, V = 1%-25%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 171, pp 2575-2576)

**Bell palsy evidence numbers**: Untreated, 80%-90% recover completely, and in the Peitersen series none of 1505 untreated patients was left with permanent complete paralysis; patients whose palsy never becomes complete recover in 95%-100%. Steroids raise the chance of complete recovery by about 17%, and starting within 48 hours (829-patient RCT) gave higher recovery and less synkinesis. The AAN estimates that adding an antiviral increases recovery by no more than 7%. Poor prognostic factors include hyperacusis, reduced tearing, age over 60, diabetes, hypertension and severe pain. Transmastoid decompression has been abandoned because the lesion is at the meatal foramen (about 0.68 mm wide, versus 1.02-1.53 mm elsewhere in the canal). (Cummings 7e, Ch 172, pp 2589, 2591)

**Middle fossa decompression for Bell palsy**: The criteria are ENoG degeneration over 90% within 14 days of complete paralysis plus no voluntary EMG motor units. In the Iowa and Gantz series, about 91%-92% reached HB I-II after middle fossa decompression of the meatal foramen, labyrinthine segment and geniculate, versus about 42% with steroids alone. Find the IAC about 60 degrees anterior to the blue line of the superior semicircular canal. Only about 120 degrees of the lateral IAC circumference can be opened safely, because the cochlea may lie within 1 mm below and the superior canal ampulla just behind. Bill's bar separates the nerve from the superior vestibular nerve. Risks include about a 30-dB conductive loss, SNHL, CSF leak and, most serious, AICA injury, so offer it only where the approach is done routinely. (Cummings 7e, Ch 172, p 2592; Ch 173, pp 2603-2605)

**Bilateral facial paralysis**: Simultaneous or sequential bilateral palsy (0.3%-2% of cases) is far more often systemic than unilateral palsy. Causes include Guillain-Barre syndrome (CN VII is the third most often involved cranial nerve after IX and X; high CSF protein with a normal cell count), Lyme disease, sarcoidosis and Heerfordt syndrome, leukemia, syphilis, bacterial meningitis, mononucleosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, benign intracranial hypertension, and brainstem or prepontine tumor. Work up with a full neurologic exam, lumbar puncture with cytology, VDRL, Lyme serology, autoantibodies and MRI. Eye care is critical, and the disability is far greater than with unilateral palsy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 172, p 2594)

**Recurrent, familial and progressive palsy**: About 9%-11% of Bell palsy patients have had a prior episode, on either side, and familial cases make up 6%-8%. A second palsy on the same side revealed a tumor in about 20% (8 of 40), so image recurrent ipsilateral palsy. Slowly progressive weakness is not Bell palsy. Palsy that progresses beyond 3 weeks, or shows no return of function by 6 months, should be presumed to be tumor (facial schwannoma, hemangioma, meningioma, perineural metastasis) until proven otherwise, with CT and gadolinium MRI and serial imaging if the first studies are negative. (Cummings 7e, Ch 172, p 2594; Ch 173, p 2609)

**Pregnancy, barotrauma and other special settings**: Bell palsy is about 3.3 times more common in pregnancy, mainly in the third trimester or just after delivery; preeclampsia is about 6 times more frequent among these patients, outcomes may be worse, and prednisone is considered low risk late in pregnancy. Facial baroparesis is a transient palsy, sometimes with taste loss, on ascent in a plane or car (about 8000-10,000 ft) or when diving. It is caused by middle-ear pressure acting on a dehiscent nerve and is prevented with a tympanostomy tube. In Kawasaki disease, facial palsy may mark more severe disease. In HIV, early palsy resembles Bell palsy, but consider lymphoma, zoster and Guillain-Barre syndrome. (Cummings 7e, Ch 172, pp 2595-2597)

**Lyme and otitis media palsy**: Facial palsy occurs in 0.9%-4.5% of Lyme disease and can come before seroconversion or occur without erythema migrans or a known tick bite; confirm a positive ELISA with IgM and IgG immunoblots. Treat with oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily or amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 14-21 days. Adding corticosteroids was associated with worse long-term facial outcomes than antibiotics alone. Otitis media causes about 3.1% of acute palsies. In acute otitis media, give parenteral antibiotics and do a wide myringotomy without manipulating the nerve. Palsy with chronic otitis, usually gradual, suggests cholesteatoma and needs surgery, with decompression that leaves the perineurium intact. (Cummings 7e, Ch 172, pp 2596-2597)

**Congenital versus birth-trauma palsy numbers**: Neonatal facial palsy occurs in about 0.23% of live births, and about 78% is due to birth trauma, split evenly between forceps and nonforceps deliveries (pressure from the maternal sacrum). Facial bruising, swelling or hemotympanum favor trauma. Other cranial neuropathies or a prolonged ABR I-III or I-V interval favor a developmental cause. Congenital unilateral lower lip palsy (absent depressor labii inferioris) is the mildest form. In CHARGE syndrome, 75% have at least one cranial neuropathy (CN VIII about 60%, VII 43%, IX/X 30%). (Cummings 7e, Ch 172, pp 2592-2593)

**Prognosis and timing numbers**: VZV causes about 4.5%-9% of peripheral facial palsies and is the second most common cause. Incidence rises sharply after age 60 as cell-mediated immunity declines. Complete recovery occurs in only about 16%-22% overall: about 10% after complete paralysis versus about 66% after incomplete paralysis. The rash appears before the palsy in about 25%, and these patients do better, while in about 10% the vesicles appear well after the palsy. Zoster sine herpete shows fourfold-raised anti-VZV IgG and responds better to prednisone plus an antiviral than to prednisone alone. Combined steroid and antiviral therapy is the consensus. (Cummings 7e, Ch 172, pp 2589, 2592)

**Facial nerve decompression timing in trauma**: Most fracture-related nerve injury is in the perigeniculate region, at the distal labyrinthine segment and geniculate ganglion, where traction from the greater petrosal nerve concentrates force. Fisch's criterion is ENoG degeneration over 90% within 6 days of onset. Surgery can be delayed up to about 3 weeks after an immediate palsy so that edema and hematoma settle. For long-standing paralysis, where electrical testing is no longer valid, wait about 12 months unless CT shows gross canal disruption, then explore if there is no clinical or EMG recovery. Take care with middle fossa exploration: 14 of 15 patients had MRI evidence of temporal lobe contusion. For an unexpected palsy after ear surgery, loosen packing and let local anesthetic wear off, then re-explore urgently if function does not return. (Cummings 7e, Ch 172, pp 2594-2595)

**Facial EMG signals, train time and setup**: Bursts are brief, near-instant discharges from direct contact or stimulation. Trains are prolonged irregular discharges (like popcorn) from stretch, heat or irrigation and are potentially more harmful. Total train time over about 10 seconds has been linked to worse immediate and long-term function, though this is disputed. A nerve that responds at the brainstem to 0.05-0.1 mA at the end of the case predicts an excellent outcome. On transcranial facial MEPs, a final-to-baseline amplitude ratio above 50% correlates with good immediate function. Place needles in the orbicularis oculi and oris, drape so the whole face is visible, tape the tube to the opposite side, use the largest diamond burr that fits with constant irrigation near the canal, and use bipolar cautery only. (Cummings 7e, Ch 171, pp 2582, 2585; Ch 173, pp 2599-2600)

**Neurorrhaphy and graft technique**: Cut the nerve ends at about 45 degrees to expose more endoneurial tubules, and trim the epineurium back only about 0.5 mm. Place three or four 10-0 nylon epineurial sutures, because the facial perineurium will not hold sutures; inside the fallopian canal a graft can be laid in without sutures if it cannot be displaced. Any tension calls for an interposition graft. The graft should be 10%-20% larger in diameter than the facial nerve. The great auricular nerve gives about 7-10 cm. The sural nerve, behind the lateral malleolus next to the lesser saphenous vein, gives up to 35 cm with little deficit. Repair the branches to the orbicularis oculi and upper-lip elevators first. (Cummings 7e, Ch 173, p 2609; Ch 174, p 2613)

**When to stop waiting**: Native facial muscle becomes irreversibly unreceptive about 18-24 months after denervation. After skull base surgery with an anatomically intact nerve, the traditional wait was a year. However, no recovery by 6 months predicted permanent paralysis with about 97% sensitivity and specificity, and patients who were not operated on ended at a mean HB V at 18 months versus HB III with surgery. The reconstructive ladder is: observation, primary neurorrhaphy, interposition graft, nerve transfer, regional muscle transfer, free muscle transfer, then static procedures. (Cummings 7e, Ch 174, p 2613)

**Donor nerve specifics**: Classic hypoglossal-facial transfer gives strong tone but causes tongue atrophy and mass movement and requires conscious effort. A jump graft keeps tongue function in about 87%, and the mini-hypoglossal transfer uses only the superior 40% of the nerve. A cross-facial nerve graft (usually sural, 15-20 cm) is the only source of a spontaneous emotional smile. Axons take about 6-9 months to cross it, so it works alone only if denervation is under about 6 months, and it is usually paired with a gracilis transfer. The masseteric nerve needs about 3 cm of mobilization, has about twice the motor axons of a buccal branch, and restores tone and motion in about 3-6 months. About 75% learn an effortless smile without clenching by 2 years. It has replaced the mini-hypoglossal as the 'babysitter' to keep muscle alive during 6-24 months of denervation while a cross-facial graft matures. (Cummings 7e, Ch 174, p 2614)

**Eyelid and lower-lid rehabilitation details**: An upper-lid weight is first-line for paralytic lagophthalmos. Platinum is denser than gold, so the implant is about 10% smaller, migrates and extrudes less, and shows less. Size it with a weight taped over the medial limbus in 0.2-g steps (most patients need 0.8-1.0 g) and place it between the orbicularis and the tarsus. A weight does not work with a negative vector or proptosis. Palpebral springs give a brisker blink, but about 33% need replacement at an average of 43 months. Medial ectropion signals severe loss of support and is the hardest to repair (medial canthopexy or spindle). Lateral laxity responds to a lateral tarsal strip or canthopexy. Consider dynamic eyelid muscle transfer when the orbicularis has been denervated for more than 18-24 months. (Cummings 7e, Ch 174, pp 2616-2617)

**Regional transfers and lower-face balancing**: The temporalis (trigeminal nerve, deep temporal artery) is the most common regional transfer. Gillies' original antidromic flip over the zygomatic arch leaves a temporal hollow and midface bulk. Orthodromic temporalis tendon transfer or lengthening temporalis myoplasty avoids this. Digastric transfer to the orbicularis oris treats isolated marginal mandibular palsy or balances an upward temporalis pull. For lower-lip asymmetry, try chemodenervation of the healthy side first. If it helps, offer selective marginal mandibular neurectomy or depressor labii resection. For platysmal banding, excise a segment of platysma rather than simply dividing it. Brow botulinum toxin lasts only 3-4 months as a bridge, and endoscopic brow lift is ineffective in elderly patients. (Cummings 7e, Ch 174, pp 2616, 2621-2622)

**IAC and CPA nerve relationships**: The IAC is about 1.2-1.4 cm long. At the fundus the falciform crest and Bill's bar divide it into quadrants: facial nerve anterosuperior, superior vestibular posterosuperior, cochlear anteroinferior and inferior vestibular posteroinferior; the singular nerve exits through its own foramen. Going medially, the cochlear and vestibular fibers rotate about 90 degrees, so at the porus and in the CPA the vestibular fibers lie superior to the cochlear fibers (the plane used in retrosigmoid or retrolabyrinthine vestibular neurectomy). At the brainstem, CN VII lies 1-2 mm anteroinferior to VIII. The labyrinthine segment meets the IAC at about 120 degrees, the first genu turns at about 75 degrees, the tympanic segment is about 11 mm, and the mastoid segment, the longest, is about 13 mm. (Cummings 7e, Ch 175, pp 2631-2632; Ch 173, p 2599)

**Balloon test occlusion limits**: When a tumor involves the ICA, an awake balloon test occlusion of the cervical ICA (about 15 minutes of serial neurologic checks) identifies patients at high stroke risk: any deficit is a failure. False negatives are common. Even after passing, ischemic stroke from hypoperfusion occurs in about 2%-20% after operative ICA occlusion. Add-ons such as a hypotensive challenge, stump pressure, SPECT, xenon CT, transcranial Doppler and EEG have not been shown to reduce delayed stroke. Preserve the ICA whenever possible. Patients at high risk who need sacrifice should be considered for bypass, and preoperative embolization of vascular tumors reduces bleeding. (Cummings 7e, Ch 176, p 2638)

text: **Limits of a purely endonasal approach**: Before the vascularized nasoseptal (Hadad-Bassagasteguy) flap was introduced in 2006, CSF leak rates after expanded endonasal surgery were about 20%-30%; with the flap they fell to about 5%. A purely endonasal approach is contraindicated when tumor involves the nasal bones, the anterior table of the frontal sinus, the skin over the dorsum or frontal sinus, or the orbit to a degree that needs exenteration. Relative contraindications are superficial soft-tissue involvement, the need for vascular reconstruction and very long expected operations. Disease lateral to the mid-orbital roof, or no usable septal flap, pushes toward a combined endoscopic and craniotomy approach. (Cummings 7e, Ch 176, pp 2641, 2647-2648)

text: **Sphenoid variant rates and intercarotid distances**: The optic nerve bulges into the sphenoid sinus in about 57% of specimens, its canal is dehiscent in about 6%, and about 1% have no bony canal at all. The cavernous carotid makes a prominent bulge in about 67% and is dehiscent in about 6%; V2 is prominent in about 48% (dehiscent in 5%) and the vidian nerve in 18%. The carotids are closest just below the tuberculum sellae (mean about 14 mm, range 10–17 mm), about 20 mm apart at the sellar face, and about 17 mm apart at the clivus, so the suprasellar corridor is the narrowest. (Cummings 7e, Ch 177, p 2664)

text: **Matching the endonasal module to the target**: Transcribriform (unilateral or bilateral, with ethmoid artery division and often a Draf III) is for olfactory-groove meningioma, esthesioneuroblastoma, CSF leak, encephalocele and sinonasal malignancy. Transtuberculum-transplanum is for planum and tuberculum meningiomas, craniopharyngioma, Rathke cleft cyst and suprasellar adenoma, and the nasoseptal flap is raised before the bony work. Transclival is for clival and retroclival lesions such as chordoma. The craniocervical (odontoid) corridor mainly treats extradural compression from basilar invagination (for example rheumatoid), plus foramen magnum meningioma and chordoma with inferior extension. (Cummings 7e, Ch 177, pp 2671–2675)

topic: Endoscopic Pituitary / Anterior Skull Base Approach
text: **Landmarks that protect the carotid in extended approaches**: In transpterygoid exposure, finding the vidian canal early leads you to the carotid at the junction of its petrous and paraclival segments. When the nasopharynx and longus muscles are taken down to reach C1 and the odontoid, stay medial to the eustachian tube, because the parapharyngeal ICA runs directly posterolateral to it. (Cummings 7e, Ch 177, pp 2671, 2675)

topic: Endoscopic Pituitary / Anterior Skull Base Approach
text: **Complication benchmarks**: A 1997 US survey of transsphenoidal pituitary surgery found carotid injury in 1.1%, CNS injury in 1.3%, vision loss in 1.8%, CSF fistula in 3.9%, meningitis in 1.5% and mortality of about 0.9%. In a 700-patient expanded endonasal series, neurovascular complications occurred in about 1%. Optic injury usually happens at the superolateral sphenoid wall or posterior ethmoid. During transplanum work, vision can also be lost from injury to the superior hypophyseal artery. Blindness from orbital hematoma can reverse if it is decompressed promptly. (Cummings 7e, Ch 177, pp 2676–2677)

topic: Endoscopic Pituitary / Anterior Skull Base Approach
text: **Postoperative instructions after a dural repair**: For about 30 days, no moderate or strenuous exertion, straining, nose blowing or closed-mouth sneezing, and use stool softeners and a high-fiber diet. Packing may stay 7–10 days after extended approaches. Saline irrigations and debridement every 2 weeks, with the first surveillance imaging at about 3 months once the cavity has healed. Be ready to recognize and treat acute anterior pituitary insufficiency and other transient or permanent endocrine problems from stalk manipulation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 177, pp 2676–2677)

**House-Brackmann-based intervention thresholds**: Observe a facial nerve tumor without intracranial compression while function is HB I–II. Consider bony decompression of the IAC or fallopian canal once function falls to HB III–IV. Reserve resection with cable grafting (frozen-section margins) for HB V–VI. When the involved segment is under about 1 cm, primary end-to-end repair is sometimes possible. Stereotactic radiation has controlled nearly 100% of tumors in small series, with tinnitus and facial twitching as reported side effects. (Cummings 7e, Ch 178, p 2683)

**Classic history and surprises**: The typical story is facial weakness that creeps in over months to years rather than days to weeks, but sudden palsy, fluctuating paresis and hemifacial spasm all occur.
