A gray-white mass behind the posterosuperior drum with conductive loss suggests tympanic-segment disease. The tumor usually runs farther along the nerve than exam or imaging predicts. Enhancement of the nerve alone is not diagnostic, because inflammation such as Ramsay Hunt also enhances, so correlate clinical, CT and MRI findings. (Cummings 7e, Ch 178, pp 2682–2683)

**The CPA 'acoustic' that is really a facial schwannoma**: On imaging, a facial schwannoma in the CPA or IAC looks the same as a vestibular schwannoma. Clues are erosion of the anterosuperior IAC or the labyrinthine facial canal, enlargement of the geniculate fossa, early facial twitching or weakness, and a reduced ENoG response on the tumor side (it stays normal in vestibular schwannoma until the tumor is very large). Warn every patient having CPA schwannoma surgery of about a 1% chance that the tumor arises from CN VII. (Cummings 7e, Ch 179, pp 2706–2707)

**Approach and preparation details**: A tympanicum tumor can come out transcanal only if all of its borders are visible through the drum. Otherwise use a mastoidectomy with an extended facial recess. Glomus jugulare is usually removed through a Fisch type A infratemporal approach, staged if the intracranial component is large. Embolize 24–48 hours before resection. Consider preoperative permanent balloon occlusion or stenting when the tumor infiltrates the wall of the horizontal petrous carotid. Normal preoperative lower cranial nerve function does not prove the nerves are free of tumor. Preserve the nerves whenever possible, because losing them can mean tracheostomy and gastrostomy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 178, pp 2681–2682)

**Radiation by Fisch class**: Conventional radiotherapy and stereotactic radiation control about 90% to nearly 100% of temporal-bone paragangliomas. One series reported a 25% failure rate at a median of 27 months, so long follow-up matters. A systematic review found that Fisch A/B tumors confined to the middle ear are best treated surgically, with little morbidity. Fisch C/D tumors had fewer complications and similar or better control with radiation. About 1–3% secrete catecholamines, so check urine metanephrines before surgery to avoid an intraoperative hypertensive crisis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 178, pp 2682, 2698; Ch 181, p 2753)

**Jugular foramen schwannoma strategy**: These tumors arise in the pars nervosa, anteromedial to the jugular bulb. Unlike the irregular erosion of a paraganglioma, they cause smooth, well-corticated enlargement of the foramen. A mainly intracranial tumor is removed most easily through a suboccipital (retrosigmoid) approach. Intraforaminal and dumbbell tumors need a Fisch infratemporal approach. Avoid transposing the facial nerve when possible, because of permanent weakness. Stereotactic radiosurgery has controlled more than 94% in several series. In one Gamma Knife series, 20% of affected lower cranial nerves improved and 77% stayed stable. (Cummings 7e, Ch 178, p 2682; Ch 179, p 2707; Ch 181, p 2753)

**Defect pattern and repair principles**: Tegmen defects fall into two size groups, small ones under 5 mm and large ones over 10 mm, and they are often multifocal. Ectopic arachnoid granulations probably help cause spontaneous cases. Choose an approach (transmastoid, middle fossa or combined) that shows every possible leak site. Layered composite grafts (soft tissue plus a rigid support such as bone, cartilage or cement, plus sealant) re-leak less often than single-layer repairs. Patients with a CSF leak are a recommended group for pneumococcal immunization. (Cummings 7e, Ch 178, p 2686)

topic: Temporal Bone Malignancy and Temporal Bone Resection
text: **Resection extent and outcome nuances**: A sleeve resection is enough only for superficial cancer limited to the cartilaginous canal. Bony canal disease needs at least a lateral temporal bone resection. Obliterate the cavity with fat, a temporalis flap and eustachian tube packing when postoperative radiation is planned, to avoid osteoradionecrosis. Subtotal resection has about a 5% perioperative mortality. Dural involvement of 1 cm or less without brain invasion did not change disease-free survival, but parenchymal invasion sharply worsens survival. Total resection adds questionable benefit once high-grade tumor reaches the petrous apex, ICA or cavernous sinus. (Cummings 7e, Ch 178, pp 2688, 2690–2691)

**Symptom order and the sudden-loss rule**: In descending order, the common symptoms are SNHL, tinnitus, dysequilibrium and facial hypesthesia, with a median duration of about 2 years. About 1% of patients with sudden SNHL turn out to have a vestibular schwannoma, and up to 20% of tumors present with sudden loss, so image every unexplained sudden or asymmetric loss even after full recovery. Patients rarely report imbalance, but on the Fukuda stepping test they often turn more than 90 degrees toward the tumor, and the head impulse test may show catch-up saccades to that side. (Cummings 7e, Ch 179, p 2701)

**Imaging and test details**: Contrast CT can miss tumors under about 1.5 cm, whereas gadolinium MRI detects lesions as small as 1.5 mm. Watch for false positives from vessels or neuritis. Noncontrast high-resolution T2 sequences can screen and can follow known tumors, detecting a 2-mm change about as reliably as contrast MRI (except in cystic tumors) without repeated gadolinium. Calorics (superior nerve) and cVEMP (inferior nerve) can suggest which nerve the tumor comes from, which bears on hearing-preservation odds, but are not screening tests. About 85% of schwannomas meet the bone at an acute angle, while about 75% of meningiomas meet it at an obtuse angle. (Cummings 7e, Ch 179, pp 2702–2703)

**Translabyrinthine steps that protect nerves**: Leave an island of bone over the sigmoid sinus (Bill's island) and divide the mastoid emissary vein. Finish all bone work before opening dura, skeletonizing the IAC through about 270 degrees. Expose the inferior border first, using the cochlear aqueduct as the inferior limit to protect the lower cranial nerves, and the superior border last, because the facial nerve is most at risk there. At the fundus, Bill's bar marks the facial nerve: reflect and divide the superior vestibular nerve lateral to it to find the plane, and debulk large tumors from inside before dissecting the capsule off CN VII. Close by removing the incus, cutting the tensor tendon, packing the eustachian tube, and filling the defect with strips of abdominal fat. (Cummings 7e, Ch 179, pp 2716–2719)

**Realistic hearing-preservation counseling**: In a pooled review of 621 attempted hearing-preservation operations, hearing was preserved in only about 33%, and much less often when useful or serviceable hearing is the standard rather than any measurable hearing. About 56% of patients later lose much of the hearing that was saved. Hearing preservation is unlikely by any approach once the tumor is over about 2 cm. Because translabyrinthine removal has a slightly higher facial-nerve preservation rate, many eligible patients choose it. (Cummings 7e, Ch 179, pp 2716, 2726)

**Postoperative complications**: After translabyrinthine surgery, CSF rhinorrhea occurs in under 5% and usually stops with a fresh compression dressing. A persistent leak usually seals after about 3 days of lumbar drainage, or closing the ear canal with eustachian tube obliteration works at once. Meningitis appears at a mean of about postoperative day 8. Vital-sign changes during brainstem dissection signal AICA-territory ischemia, so pause. Changes that persist or recur mean the operation should end, because complete AICA loss causes Atkinson syndrome (lateral pontine tegmental infarction, often fatal). When facial palsy and corneal anesthesia occur together and the palsy is expected to last more than about 6 months, protect the eye early with a gold weight or spring and a brow lift. (Cummings 7e, Ch 179, p 2727)

**Radiosurgery dose and selection limits**: Cutting the marginal dose below 16 Gy dropped facial neuropathy to about 15%, and at 13 Gy or less facial injury is rare and usually transient. Keeping the cochlear dose under about 4 Gy helps preserve hearing. Even so, PTA usually falls 15–20 dB over the first 6–12 months and keeps declining for years. Radiation is generally contraindicated for tumors over about 3 cm in the posterior fossa, or with brainstem compression or non-auditory cranial neuropathies, because of swelling, hydrocephalus and radionecrosis. Cystic tumors respond less predictably. (Cummings 7e, Ch 181, pp 2750–2751)

**Pseudoprogression numbers**: About 23% of tumors swell after radiation, usually 2–4 mm (occasionally up to 10 mm), mostly 6–24 months after treatment but sometimes up to 5 years. About half lose central enhancement. Do not call treatment a failure before about 2–3 years. The swelling itself can raise the risk of hydrocephalus, hearing loss and facial or trigeminal symptoms. (Cummings 7e, Ch 181, p 2749)

**Late radiation risks and salvage surgery**: Hydrocephalus occurs in about 3.4–5.6% and is treated with a VP shunt. Malignant change in a sporadic tumor is roughly 1 in 1000 (about 0.1–0.3%), but about 4.7% in NF2, a 10-fold rise. Half of reported cases are in NF2, so avoid radiation in children and tumor-prone syndromes when possible. Failures can occur after 5 years, so follow-up is lifelong. Surgery after failed radiation is harder: the tumor is densely stuck to the facial nerve in 89% vs 63%, and HB I–II results fall to 37% vs 70%, which favors planned subtotal removal. (Cummings 7e, Ch 181, pp 2751–2752)

**Extended posterior fossa approaches**: Retrolabyrinthine gives limited CPA access without the IAC (biopsy, small lesions) and needs no cerebellar retraction. Transcochlear opens the petrous apex and clivus with full petrous carotid exposure, at the cost of hearing and usually temporary facial palsy from posterior rerouting. Transotic gives similar exposure without moving the facial nerve, which then limits the corridor. Extended middle fossa treats petroclival lesions, especially meningiomas, that spare the otic capsule and IAC in hearing patients. The combined petrosal approach gives the widest middle-plus-posterior fossa exposure for large petroclival tumors with good hearing. (Cummings 7e, Ch 179, pp 2718, 2725–2726)

**Telling the cystic apex lesions apart**: Cholesterol granuloma is about 20 times more common than apex epidermoid but is still uncommon (about 1 for every 35 vestibular schwannomas). It is the only apex lesion bright on both T1 and T2, with smooth borders and no restricted diffusion. Epidermoid is T1 dark, T2 bright, scalloped and diffusion-restricting. Mucocele is T1 dark and T2 bright with only rim enhancement. Asymmetric marrow in a non-pneumatized apex is T1 bright but does not expand, enhance or stay bright on T2, and it darkens with fat suppression. Leave it alone. (Cummings 7e, Ch 179, pp 2709–2710)

**Two theories of cholesterol granuloma**: The classic obstruction-vacuum theory holds that a blocked air cell develops negative pressure, effusion and hemorrhage, followed by a foreign-body reaction to cholesterol. The newer Jackler-Cho theory holds that advancing pneumatization exposes marrow that bleeds into the cells. The second theory better explains why granulomas form in well-pneumatized bones. Either way, the cyst cannot usually be removed completely, so treatment aims at durable drainage. (Cummings 7e, Ch 178, p 2685; Ch 179, p 2710)

**Choosing a drainage route**: The transcanal infracochlear route between the jugular bulb and carotid gives dependent drainage into the middle ear. A blocked tube can be revised through an office myringotomy, but the route needs carotid exposure and slow canal healing. The infralabyrinthine route can be impossible with a high jugular bulb, and revision needs formal reexploration. A middle fossa catheter to the mastoid preserves hearing and stays patent long-term. An endoscopic transsphenoidal approach is the preferred hearing-sparing route when the cyst abuts the posterolateral sphenoid wall with favorable pneumatization. Keep it open with a silicone stent or a small nasoseptal flap. Translabyrinthine drainage is reserved for dead ears. (Cummings 7e, Ch 179, pp 2710, 2725–2726; Ch 177, p 2671; Ch 178, p 2686)

**Stimulation mapping protocol**: Before dissecting, confirm the whole system works: stimulate CN XI in a retrosigmoid case or the mastoid facial nerve in a translabyrinthine case. For a large tumor, map the exposed surface at 0.3 mA, then 0.5 mA and 1.0 mA. No response at 1.0 mA means the nerve is not on that surface. Once a response appears, drop to 0.1–0.2 mA to narrow the area. With small tumors (CPA part 1 cm or less), find the nerve at the brainstem, set the threshold, and sweep the capsule at three or more times threshold before cutting. Use up to 1.0 mA to clear tissue you are about to cut or cauterize. (Cummings 7e, Ch 180, pp 2732–2733)

**What end-of-case stimulation can and cannot predict**: A proximal (brainstem) threshold of 0.04–0.05 mA or less predicts good function, but delayed palsy can still occur. A 0.05-mA threshold with a CMAP of 240 µV or more predicted good 1-year function with about 98% probability, as did a proximal-to-distal amplitude ratio above about 0.6. Absent responses do not reliably predict a poor outcome when the nerve is anatomically intact. Never base reanimation on intraoperative tests. If no recovery has begun by about 12 months, it is unlikely. (Cummings 7e, Ch 180, p 2733)

**When to stop and accept subtotal resection**: Published stop rules for large vestibular schwannomas include a proximal stimulation threshold rising above 0.3 mA, a rise of at least 0.1 mA over baseline, or loss of about 50–60% of the supramaximal proximal response amplitude. They are promising but not fully validated. (Cummings 7e, Ch 180, p 2733)

**Reading free-run EMG**: Neurotonic bursts show the nerve is close, not that it is injured, and the stimulator should then be used to find it. A trains (sudden, sinusoidal, high-frequency 60–210 Hz) are the only pattern linked to poor postoperative function. An acute transection can be silent, and badly compressed nerves in large tumors may fire little despite handling. Artifacts, such as bimetallic instrument contact, sound crackly rather than popping and show up on several channels at once. EMG cannot be read during electrocautery, which is exactly when thermal injury happens. (Cummings 7e, Ch 180, pp 2734–2735)

**Corticobulbar MEPs and anesthesia**: Transcranial facial MEPs test the whole corticobulbar-facial pathway continuously without touching the nerve, which is valuable before a large tumor exposes it. A true central response disappears with a single pulse (except in hemifacial spasm) and has a latency of about 14 ms. A final-to-baseline amplitude ratio above about 50% predicts good immediate function. MEPs need TIVA with no volatile agents or muscle relaxants. EMG needs no relaxant and no local anesthetic near the stylomastoid foramen. ABR is unaffected by routine anesthesia but gives only delayed feedback, so direct cochlear nerve action potentials are used for near-real-time hearing monitoring. (Cummings 7e, Ch 180, pp 2732, 2737; Ch 179, p 2727)

**Recording sites for other cranial nerves**: Use hook-wire electrodes for the eye muscles: CN III in the inferior rectus or oblique via the infraorbital margin, CN VI in the lateral rectus via the lateral canthus, and CN IV (hardest) in the superior oblique. Their 2–3 ms latency tells them apart from facial contamination. Record V3 from the masseter, which is prone to crosstalk with facial channels. Palatal electrodes do not validly monitor CN IX, which needs the stylopharyngeus. Monitor CN X with ETT surface electrodes (tube rotation gives false lateralization) or postcricoid surface electrodes. Record CN XI from the trapezius (latency 5–7 ms, keep the current low because of movement in head pins) and CN XII from the lateral anterior third of the tongue. (Cummings 7e, Ch 180, pp 2739–2741)

**Intelligibility and sound milestones**: A stranger should understand about 25% of a child's speech at 18 months, 50–75% at 24 months, and 75–100% at 36 months. Early sounds (p, m, h, n, w, b, then k, g, d, t) come first, while r, l and s come much later. English has about 44 phonemes. (Cummings 7e, Ch 183, pp 2767–2768)

**Articulation vs phonologic vs motor speech**: Phonologic disorders follow consistent rules, such as stopping ('dip' for 'zip') or velar fronting ('tup' for 'cup'), so listeners learn the pattern. Nondevelopmental processes such as initial-consonant deletion are red flags. Dysarthria is weakness or poor control (cerebral palsy is the classic pediatric cause) and does not track cognition, so a bright child may need augmentative communication. Childhood apraxia of speech is a motor-planning disorder with no lesion. It shows inconsistent errors, groping, and more errors as words get longer. (Cummings 7e, Ch 183, pp 2767, 2769)

**Do not stop at hearing loss: screen for autism**: Autism affects about 1 in 59 children (4.5 times more often in boys) and can be reliably diagnosed by age 2. About 4% of deaf or hard-of-hearing children also have autism, yet only about a quarter get that diagnosis by age 4. Autism-specific clues are echolalia or pronoun reversal, absent joint attention and pointing, poor imitation of gestures, no pretend play, and language regression. Children with specific language impairment (7–8% at kindergarten) want to communicate and do pretend play. Refer early to a multidisciplinary autism clinic: fewer than 10% stay nonverbal with intervention, and starting before age 5 matters. (Cummings 7e, Ch 183, pp 2769–2770)

**Anesthesia for the bleeding child**: About 3% of children who were easy to intubate become difficult during a post-tonsillectomy bleed. Judge blood loss and volume status (duration, dizziness, tachycardia, hypotension). Get large-bore IV access, start fluid resuscitation before induction, and have crossmatched blood ready, because anesthetic vasodilation can cause profound hypotension. Use rapid sequence induction with cricoid pressure and a cuffed tube, suction the stomach before emergence, and extubate awake. (Cummings 7e, Ch 184, p 2788)

**Perioperative opioid and antiemetic pearls**: Children with OSA had about a 10-fold higher rate of apnea after fentanyl. Children whose oxygen saturation nadir is below 85% need about half the opioid for the same pain relief. Snoring alone has been linked to critical respiratory events under anesthesia, and the 5-item STBUR questionnaire helps predict risk. Codeine is contraindicated after tonsillectomy in anyone under 18 because CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolism has caused deaths. A single intraoperative IV dexamethasone dose reduces PONV and pain and speeds return to diet. (Cummings 7e, Ch 184, pp 2786, 2789)

**Anesthetic hazards in trisomy 21**: Expect marked bradycardia during sevoflurane induction, difficult mask ventilation and intubation (midface hypoplasia, relative macroglossia, short neck), postintubation stridor and bronchospasm. About half have congenital heart disease (mostly AV canal defects), and pulmonary hypertension is more common. Craniocervical instability is found on imaging in 8–63% but causes symptoms in only 1–2%. Routine preoperative cervical films are not advised and a negative film does not exclude instability, so keep the neck neutral and avoid hyperextension in every patient. (Cummings 7e, Ch 184, p 2778)

**Choosing VPD tests**: Perceptual speech analysis by an experienced speech pathologist is still the gold standard. Nasometry (nasal-to-oral sound energy ratio against normative passages) and pressure-flow testing are indirect measures. Speech endoscopy is the usual first-line direct study; most children over about 3 years tolerate it. Pass the scope through the middle meatus rather than along the floor so it sits high in the nasopharynx, and record audio with the video. Speech videofluoroscopy needs at least two, ideally three, views (lateral, frontal, and en face such as Towne or base view), costs radiation, and can miss small fistulas. Closure during swallowing tells you nothing about closure for speech. More than 40% of children with VPD are also dysphonic, which can hide mild VPD. (Cummings 7e, Ch 189, pp 2853-2854)

**Phoneme-specific VPD and other bedside clues**: In phoneme-specific (mislearned) VPD, the child closes the port for most oral sounds but makes /s/, /sh/, /z/ (rarely /f/) as a nasal fricative. It is often mistaken for global VPD, it responds to articulation therapy, and it rarely needs surgery. Hyponasality turns /m/ into /b/, /n/ into /d/ and /ng/ into /g/. Facial grimacing (pinching the nares on oral sounds) is a compensatory sign of VPD. Speech that worsens as a task is repeated over minutes suggests fatigue, as in myasthenia gravis. VPD follows about 1 in 1500 adenoidectomies. Test any child with VPD of unknown cause for 22q11.2 deletion (FISH or chromosomal microarray; FISH can miss deletions under about 40 kb). In one series of VPD after adenotonsillectomy, more than half carried the deletion, 28% without obvious features. (Cummings 7e, Ch 189, pp 2851-2853)

**Prosthetic options**: A palatal lift pushes a palate of adequate length up and back, and a speech bulb (acrylic obturator) fills the port for a short or immobile palate. Gradual bulb reduction can sometimes wean the patient as wall motion improves. Prostheses hang on the maxillary teeth, so they need adequate dentition and a cooperative child. They cannot be used during active orthodontics, with loose deciduous teeth or during rapid maxillary expansion. They suit adolescents and adults, poor surgical candidates, temporary VPD after stroke or brain injury, and patients with OSA, because the device comes out at night. (Cummings 7e, Ch 189, pp 2855-2856)

**Matching the operation to the gap**: Furlow double-opposing Z-plasty or intravelar veloplasty re-orient a longitudinal levator. In the Furlow, both myomucosal flaps are posteriorly based and both mucosal flaps anteriorly based. A superiorly based pharyngeal flap fills the midline and suits sagittal or circular patterns with good lateral wall motion. Sphincter pharyngoplasty (lateral myomucosal flaps inset at the level of maximal palatal excursion) suits coronal or circular patterns with reasonable palatal motion, and narrower flaps with less overlap are used when the palate moves well. A large gap with poor wall motion ('black hole') may need Furlow plus sphincter pharyngoplasty. Posterior wall augmentation (fat, hyaluronic acid, calcium hydroxylapatite, or a rolled pharyngeal flap) is only for a small central gap and often does not last. A randomized trial found no outcome difference between pharyngeal flap and sphincter pharyngoplasty. Every procedure needs postoperative airway monitoring, and CPAP can bridge the airway while edema settles. (Cummings 7e, Ch 189, pp 2856-2858)

topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
text: **Palatoplasty outcome numbers**: Repair before age 1 sharply reduces articulation errors (about 10% vs 86% when repaired later, Dorf and Curtin), and hypernasality is less common with repair before 18 months. Unintended oronasal fistula occurs in about 8.6% overall, mostly at the anterior hard palate or the hard-soft palate junction, and more often with more severe clefts. Fistulas recur in 25-33% after repair. Perioperative airway events occur in up to 23%, so check the tongue and floor of mouth for edema and place a tongue-tip traction stitch before extubation. VPD is the most common complication of palatoplasty, and rates are lower after a double-opposing Z-plasty. Most centers do a single-stage palate repair, because staging to protect maxillary growth has not clearly helped. (Cummings 7e, Ch 188, pp 2843-2844)

topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
text: **Submucous cleft and 22q11.2 numbers**: Submucous cleft palate (bifid uvula, notched posterior hard palate from an absent posterior nasal spine, and midline zona pellucida) occurs in about 1 in 1250. In an occult submucous cleft only the musculus uvulae is deficient, so it is seen only on nasendoscopy. Palpate the palate before adenoidectomy, especially in a child with an isolated cleft lip. Operate only for VPD that fails nonsurgical care. In 22q11.2 deletion (about 1 in 3000 births; the most common syndrome with isolated cleft palate), about 5% have a bifid uvula, 9-11% an overt cleft, 16% a submucous cleft and 32% VPD. Middle ear disease affects 22-88%, and anterior glottic webs can cause dysphonia or post-intubation distress. Most deletions are de novo, though transmission is autosomal dominant. (Cummings 7e, Ch 188, p 2848)

**Cleft ear numbers**: In cleft palate, effusion is present in about 97% of ears by 4 months of age, and about 96% of children need tubes (nearly half need repeat sets). Long-term sequelae are chronic perforation in about 13%, CSOM in 6% and cholesteatoma in 1-3%, and coordinated team follow-up cut cholesteatoma from 9% to 3% in one program. Eustachian tube dysfunction persists 2 years after palatoplasty in about 80%. The mean age at normal hearing and tympanometry is about 7 years, and about 70% of ears normalize with at least 6 years of follow-up. Tympanoplasty results in cleft children (including submucous cleft) match those in noncleft children. Tubes placed before palatoplasty have high otorrhea rates, and speech at age 5 was the same whether tubes went in before or at palate repair. (Cummings 7e, Ch 188, pp 2848-2849)

**Why children reimplant and the vestibular link**: Device failure occurs in about 6-13% of implanted children (2.9% reimplantation over 20 years in one large program). Reimplantation runs 20-52% in children deafened by meningitis. The excess is explained by the vestibular loss and falls that follow meningitis, not by the meningitis itself. Bilateral horizontal canal areflexia raises the odds of device failure about 7.6- to 8-fold, and absent VEMPs and poor balance scores are also more common in children with failures. After reimplantation, about 44% return to their best prior speech score and 40% improve. A child implanted in infancy should expect at least one reimplantation in a lifetime. (Cummings 7e, Ch 192, p 2885; Ch 198, p 2952)

**Securing the receiver in infants**: Small children spend hours lying on beds and car seats, and the repeated head-roll forces can make the receiver-stimulator migrate before it encapsulates. Micro-movement can fatigue the device. A tight subperiosteal (subpericranial) pocket has largely replaced a drilled bed with tie-down sutures, which needs dural exposure in a thin infant skull. Devices with a medial pedestal, titanium pins or screws add retention. Placing the package slightly more anterior and superior, and more upright than the usual 45 degrees, lowers contact with the pillow. In an implanted child with acute mastoiditis and a subperiosteal abscess, early incision and drainage plus myringotomy and tube almost always saves the device. (Cummings 7e, Ch 192, p 2885)

**Etiology mix in pediatric CI candidates**: In North America the three leading causes of pediatric SNHL are autosomal recessive nonsyndromic loss (about 45%, with GJB2 accounting for nearly half of recessive loss), cochleovestibular anomalies (about 25%) and congenital CMV (about 11%). Anomalies can add a conductive component through a third window (EVA, IP-3). Most implant candidates are born to hearing parents. CMV-deafened children with a normal brain MRI do about as well as GJB2 children early on. Those with an abnormal MRI lag in speech perception for up to about 5 years and remain behind in speech production. The best language results come from implantation between 12 and 24 months. (Cummings 7e, Ch 192, pp 2883-2884)

**Vestibular loss in deaf and implanted children**: Up to 70% of children with SNHL have vestibular impairment, and 20-40% have severe bilateral loss. More than 50% of children with unilateral profound SNHL have abnormal vestibular function, usually only on the deaf side. A child with profound SNHL plus vestibular loss of unknown cause should see ophthalmology and genetics with Usher type 1 in mind. Symptomatic congenital CMV damages the vestibular system more often than the cochlea, and the loss can progress. Implantation reduces end-organ function in 0-77% of ears depending on the study. The estimated risk of total bilateral vestibular loss from simultaneous bilateral CI is about 2%, which is worth counseling but is far smaller than the risk from the deafness etiology itself. (Cummings 7e, Ch 198, p 2952)

**Three-part bedside vestibular screen**: You can screen without a lab. (1) Ask about motor milestones (head control, sitting, walking age). (2) Time one-foot standing. Expected times are a brief stand at 30 months, 2 seconds at 36 months, 5 seconds at 4 years, and from age 5 about 10 seconds eyes open (red flag under 8) and more than 5 seconds eyes closed (red flag under 4). (3) Check horizontal canal function with a clinical head impulse test, or in infants 6 months or younger by spinning the caregiver's stool and looking for postrotary nystagmus. Infants this young cannot visually suppress the VOR. Any single abnormal component justifies formal testing. Even a 10-day static-balance exercise program improved standing balance in children with SNHL. (Cummings 7e, Ch 198, pp 2953-2954)

**Failed newborn screen with middle ear fluid**: About 55-65% of infants who fail newborn screening have OME, but the effusion does not exclude SNHL. One series found underlying SNHL in 11%, and only 15 of 64 neonatal effusions had cleared by about 4.8 months. Document counseling that hearing must be rechecked once the effusion resolves. One pragmatic protocol waits about 3 months, then places tubes if fluid persists (sooner in high-risk infants such as Down syndrome or NICU graduates). OAEs are repeated 3-4 weeks after tubes, and a diagnostic ABR is done while the infant can still be tested in natural sleep if OAEs are abnormal. (Cummings 7e, Ch 193, p 2892)

**Getting the CMV test right**: Congenital infection can be proven only with urine or saliva CMV PCR or culture taken in the first 3 weeks of life. Saliva PCR is highly sensitive, but breast milk from a seropositive mother causes false positives (15 of 56 saliva-positive infants were urine-negative in one Finnish study). Collect saliva at least 90 minutes after a feed and confirm any positive result with urine. After 3 weeks, the newborn dried blood spot can be tested. It is only about 34% sensitive but about 99.9% specific, so a positive result confirms congenital CMV while a negative one does not exclude it. Hearing-targeted screening tests every infant who fails the newborn hearing screen, and Utah has mandated it since 2013. About 5% of infants failing an inpatient AABR were CMV-positive in one hospital protocol. Testing for CMV first was the most cost-effective workup for every loss type except ANSD, where imaging came first. (Cummings 7e, Ch 193, pp 2892-2893)

**Transotic CSF leak and recurrent meningitis**: A spontaneous CSF otorrhea or rhinorrhea through a malformed ear needs two openings. One joins the subarachnoid space to the inner ear, most often a defect at the fundus of the IAC (also around the facial nerve or a dilated labyrinthine facial canal). The other joins the inner ear to the middle ear, most often a defect in or next to the stapes footplate. Common cavity carries the highest risk, while a classic incomplete partition is not thought to raise it. Acute otitis media is the usual source of the meningitis (S. pneumoniae in about 71%). Any child with recurrent meningitis and no clear cause needs temporal bone CT, and any child after even one episode needs an audiogram, then CT if SNHL is found. Repair options: with residual hearing, start with tympanotomy and a connective tissue graft over the leak, then consider posterior fossa plugging of the IAC. With a dead ear, remove the footplate and pack the vestibule with muscle (or use a translabyrinthine approach). Eustachian tube closure is a poor choice in children. (Cummings 7e, Ch 194, pp 2911-2912)

**Schuknecht canal types and atresiaplasty vs bone conduction**: Schuknecht type A is isolated meatal stenosis with a near-normal middle ear. Type B is narrowing of the whole canal with more middle ear anomalies; about half have a partial atretic plate. Type C is complete atresia with a favorable middle ear (an atresiaplasty candidate). Type D is complete atresia with poor pneumatization and major ossicular and facial nerve anomalies, and these ears are usually not operated. Canal cholesteatoma occurs in about 1 in 5 stenotic canals and in about 50% by age 20 when the canal is under 4 mm. In a systematic review, atresiaplasty reached a PTA under 30 dB in about 60% (air-bone gap under 30 dB in about 69%) with about 24 dB of gain. Osseointegrated bone conduction devices reached about 96-98% with about 38 dB of gain. (Cummings 7e, Ch 197, pp 2944-2945)

**Preventing AOM beyond antibiotics**: PCV7 cut overall AOM episodes by only about 6-7% but reduced tubes for recurrent disease by about 20%. Serotype replacement followed, and PCV13 (2010) added six serotypes, including 19A. AOM complicates up to 67% of influenza infections in young children, and both injected and live influenza vaccines lower seasonal AOM (AAP: vaccinate everyone 6 months and older). Breastfeeding for at least 6 months is protective. Xylitol gum or syrup works only if given five times a day for 2-3 months and is useless once a cold has started, so adherence limits it. Probiotics are unproven. No licensed vaccine yet targets nontypeable H. influenzae or M. catarrhalis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 199, pp 2963-2964)

**OME adjuncts and limits of tubes**: Nasal balloon autoinflation used three times a day improved effusion clearance at 3 months in a UK primary-care trial of 320 school-age children, but the effect was modest and it has not been shown to reduce tube surgery. Hearing aids are an option for persistent bilateral OME when surgery is contraindicated or declined. Eustachian tube balloon dilation has no supporting evidence in children. The hearing benefit of tubes is modest and fades after about 6-9 months (the usual tube lifespan). Benefit is greatest in young children with heavy infection exposure (daycare) and older children with bilateral loss of 25 dB or worse for at least 3 months. Adding adenoidectomy helps most at age 4 and older and cuts tube reinsertion by about 10%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 199, p 2966)

**Lund-Mackay thresholds in children**: Asymptomatic children average a Lund-Mackay score of about 2.8, so incidental opacification is common (18-45% of children scanned for other reasons). A score of 2 or less has an excellent negative predictive value, and a score of 5 or more strongly predicts CRS (sensitivity about 86%, specificity about 85%). The score also predicts how well adenoidectomy works: in one series, 1-year success was about 65% with scores under 5 (adenoiditis) vs 43% with scores of 5 or more (true CRS). For cultures, middle meatal suction aspirates outperform swabs (87% vs 66% accuracy). Under general anesthesia, maxillary antral puncture remains the gold standard and lets you irrigate at the same time. (Cummings 7e, Ch 200, pp 2974, 2977)

**Stepwise surgery and why FESS fails**: Adenoidectomy alone helped about 61% at 12 months vs about 88% when combined with a maxillary sinus wash, and the wash helps most in children with asthma and high CT scores. Children younger than 7 and those with asthma more often fail adenoidectomy and need FESS. AAO-HNS consensus supports adenoidectomy as the first operation up to age 12, with no consensus for teens 13 and older. There is no consensus that balloon maxillary dilation adds anything beyond irrigation with adenoidectomy, and it raised charges without saving OR time. Conservative pediatric FESS succeeds in about 88%. When revision is needed (13% in one series), the usual findings are adhesions (57%) and a stenotic or missed natural maxillary ostium (52%). Go straight to FESS for CF, polyps, antrochoanal polyp or allergic fungal sinusitis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 200, p 2977)

**Comorbidities to look for**: In one series, 12.1% of children with CRS but no CF carried a single CFTR mutation, compared with an expected 3-4%. Dense biofilm covered 88-99% of the adenoid surface in children with CRS vs 0-6.5% in children with OSA, which helps explain why adenoidectomy works. In a large pediatric CRS cohort, asthma coexisted in about 18%, immune deficiency in about 12% and primary ciliary dyskinesia in 0.2%. Reflux was documented by pH probe in 63% in one study, but routine antireflux therapy is not recommended. (Cummings 7e, Ch 200, pp 2971-2973)

**Medical therapy evidence**: Antibiotic evidence in pediatric CRS is weak. In a placebo-controlled trial after tap and washout, cefaclor and placebo had similar resolution rates (about 65% vs 53%). AAO-HNS consensus nonetheless supports about 21 days when antibiotics are used. In a randomized trial, adding an oral methylprednisolone taper to 30 days of amoxicillin-clavulanate improved symptoms and CT scores over antibiotics alone. Saline irrigation is the mainstay, and more than 80% of children tolerate it. Culture-directed IV antibiotics are not justified on their own, because the reported success came alongside irrigation and adenoidectomy. Reserve antihistamines and leukotriene antagonists for documented allergy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 200, pp 2975-2977)

**Pertussis in the differential**: Pertussis (Bordetella pertussis; milder disease with B. parapertussis and others) is the least well-controlled vaccine-preventable disease in the US, and it is rising with waning immunity and vaccine refusal. A 7-10 day catarrhal phase resembling a cold is followed by paroxysmal coughing with an inspiratory whoop, and the cough can last up to 10 weeks. Infants under 1 year carry the highest morbidity. Unvaccinated young infants may show only mild congestion before gasping, apnea, cyanosis or pneumonia (death in about 1%), often without a whoop. Macrolides do not shorten symptoms after the catarrhal phase but do limit spread, and patients can be contagious for about 6 weeks. Boosters are now recommended for older children and adults. (Cummings 7e, Ch 201, p 2988)

**Bacterial tracheitis numbers**: No clinical, radiographic or laboratory finding reliably predicts bacterial tracheitis, so endoscopy (direct laryngoscopy and rigid bronchoscopy with suctioning of pseudomembranes) is the diagnostic gold standard and is also therapeutic. Between 53% and 91% need intubation. Use a tube half to one size smaller than the age-predicted size, and tracheotomy is rarely needed. Extubate once the child is afebrile, has a leak around the tube and secretions have fallen, typically after about 3 days (up to 7). Pneumonia, in about half, is the most common complication. In croup, the steeple sign is absent in about 50%, and it is not pathognomonic. (Cummings 7e, Ch 201, pp 2983, 2987-2988)

**PANDAS criteria and the tonsillectomy question**: PANDAS requires OCD and/or tics starting between age 3 and puberty, an episodic course with abrupt onset or dramatic flares, a documented temporal link to culture-proven GABHS infection, and neurologic findings (motor hyperactivity, adventitious movements without frank chorea). Supportive features are remission on antibiotics, high streptococcal titers and clumsiness. Steroids, plasma exchange and IVIG have been tried. Tonsillectomy has been proposed, but there is no good evidence that it reduces symptoms or prevents episodes, so PANDAS alone is not a standard indication. (Cummings 7e, Ch 201, pp 2982-2983)

**Arch-specific operative pearls**: Defer excision until acute infection resolves. First-arch lesions are excised through a parotidectomy incision with formal facial nerve identification, because the nerve may be pushed inferiorly. Work type II lesions involve the parotid and the nerve more often. For second-arch lesions, expect a fistula even if none was suspected, and consent for stair-step incisions. The tract runs between the internal and external carotid arteries, over the glossopharyngeal and hypoglossal nerves and beneath the stylohyoid ligament to the tonsil fossa. For suspected third-arch tracts, start with direct laryngoscopy of the piriform sinus. Cannulate the opening to inject dye, and consider endoscopic cauterization of the opening. In a systematic review, about 15% of third-arch anomalies required partial thyroidectomy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 202, p 3000)

**Pediatric HL vs NHL**: Hodgkin lymphoma usually stays in one axial nodal group (cervical, mediastinal, para-aortic) and spreads in order to contiguous nodes. It rarely involves Waldeyer ring or mesenteric nodes and is rarely extranodal. Classic HL is about 95% of US cases, nodular sclerosis is the most common subtype, mixed cellularity favors children under 10, and nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL is 10-15%. NHL involves multiple peripheral nodes, spreads noncontiguously, often involves Waldeyer ring and the mesentery, and often presents extranodally (mediastinum 35-45%, abdomen 25-30%). Pediatric NHL subtypes are Burkitt 35-40%, and lymphoblastic, diffuse large B-cell and ALK-positive anaplastic large cell about 15-20% each. NHL is staged with the St. Jude (Murphy) system rather than Ann Arbor. Prefer abdominal MRI over CT in children. (Cummings 7e, Ch 204, pp 3022-3024)

**JRP and its mimics**: JRP has a bimodal onset (peaks at about 3-6 and about 10 years), nonpurulent secretions from Stensen duct, elevated serum amylase, and sialectasis on ultrasound, MR sialography or sialography. Juvenile Sjögren syndrome usually presents as recurrent parotid swelling (parotid involvement in about 70%) rather than dry eyes and mouth. Check ESR, ANA, RF, anti-SSA/SSB and immunoglobulins, and consider a labial or parotid biopsy. Pneumoparotitis is air insufflated up Stensen duct, either self-induced or from wind instruments, glassblowing, diving, spirometry or coughing. Diagnose it with ultrasound, plain film or CT, treat it by removing the trigger, and reserve duct ligation for chronic cases. Postoperative 'anesthesia mumps' is transient gland swelling after surgery that rarely threatens the airway. (Cummings 7e, Ch 205, pp 3045-3047)

**Sialendoscopy for JRP**: In pediatric sialendoscopy series, JRP is the leading indication (about 69%), followed by stones (about 15%). Ductal perforation is the most common complication. Thresholds for scoping range from two episodes in 6 months to two in a year. Endoscopy typically shows a pale white duct lining that has lost its normal vascular pattern. In a meta-analysis, about 73% had no further episodes after ductal irrigation with steroid (with or without antibiotic). Most children still outgrow JRP by puberty. (Cummings 7e, Ch 205, pp 3040, 3046)

**Acquired subglottic cysts**: The subglottis is the most common site of laryngeal cysts in children. Most are acquired from intubation trauma or suctioning. In one review of 55 cases, all had been intubated as neonates and 94% were born at 24-31 weeks. They mimic subglottic stenosis or hemangioma and can flare acutely with infection. Unroof symptomatic cysts with laser, Bugbee cautery or cold instruments, and keep watching because recurrence is common. Leave small nonobstructing cysts alone, because manipulation can inflame them and cause acute obstruction. (Cummings 7e, Ch 206, p 3063)

**Vallecular cyst vs lingual thyroglossal duct cyst**: Both sit in the vallecula. A true vallecular cyst is a thin-walled laryngeal (ductal) cyst on the lingual surface of the epiglottis. A lingual thyroglossal duct cyst arises from the foramen cecum at the tongue base, sits higher, is not translucent, and may contain thyroid follicles. Both can cause position-dependent stridor, feeding difficulty, choking, cyanotic or breath-holding spells, failure to thrive and a muffled voice. Infection can cause sudden life-threatening obstruction in a neonate, and both may coexist with laryngomalacia. Both are treated by endoscopic marsupialization or excision. (Cummings 7e, Ch 206, pp 3064-3065)

**Fixation tools for young dentition**: MMF has to fit the dentition. Primary dentition lasts to about age 6, mixed dentition about 6-12, and permanent after 12. Under about 2 years there are too few teeth for arch bars, so use a custom acrylic (lingual) splint secured with circummandibular wires, transnasal or piriform wires for the maxilla, or monocortical screws placed to avoid unerupted tooth buds. Risdon cables (twisted 24-gauge wire) are a malleable arch-bar substitute. Resorbable plates are not FDA approved for load-bearing sites such as the mandible. They are bulkier, can cause sterile inflammation, fluid collections or extrusion during hydrolysis at about 6-18 months, and a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence that they match titanium. (Cummings 7e, Ch 191, p 2873)

**Bithermal caloric parameters**: water is delivered at 7°C above and below body temperature (44°C and 30°C) for 30 seconds; air uses ±13°C (50°C and 24°C) for 60 seconds. Unilateral weakness = [(RW+RC)−(LW+LC)]/(sum of all four peak slow-phase velocities); a side difference above roughly 15–30% (lab dependent) is abnormal. Bilateral weakness is suggested when each ear's warm+cool total is under about 12°/s. Directional preponderance over 30% is reportable but of doubtful localizing value. Look in the ear first: remove cerumen, and use air (not water) with a perforation, expecting an exaggerated response on that side. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 322-323)

**Rotary chair, vHIT and scleral coil specifics**: rotary chair tests the horizontal canals of both ears together at about 0.01–2 Hz (peak ~50°/s) and reports phase (often exaggerated in peripheral disease), gain (eye/chair velocity; low bilateral gain = bilateral loss) and symmetry (useful for tracking recovery). It finds residual function when calorics are absent, and off-vertical axis rotation probes the otoliths. vHIT uses a >250 Hz goggle camera; gain of about 1 is normal. Overt (catch-up) saccades after the head stops are typical of an acute loss; covert saccades during the turn suggest a compensated lesion. Goggle slippage limits vHIT above about 150–200°/s. The magnetic scleral search coil remains the gold standard and can record eye movements over 300°/s. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 323-324)

**VEMP and SVV numbers**: VEMPs use a brief, loud (>90 dB SPL) 500 Hz tone burst. cVEMP is an ipsilateral inhibitory potential from the tensed SCM (P13/N23; saccule → inferior vestibular nerve → medial vestibulospinal tract → CN XI). oVEMP is a contralateral excitatory potential under the eye during upgaze (N10; utricle → superior vestibular nerve → MLF → CN III nucleus → inferior oblique). Amplitude asymmetry over 40% (after rectification) is abnormal. Conductive pathology, ossicular problems or age raise thresholds or abolish responses; a third window gives low cVEMP thresholds and oVEMP amplitudes over about 17 µV. VEMPs can be present in a deaf ear. Subjective visual vertical is normally within ±2–3°; tilt is sensitive for acute utricular or brainstem injury, and a bucket test is a cheap version. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 324-325)

**Computerized dynamic posturography**: the Sensory Organization Test measures anterior-posterior sway in six conditions that take away or sway-reference vision and the support surface, to separate visual, somatosensory and vestibular contributions to balance. The Motor Control Test measures automatic responses to sudden forward/backward platform translations, and the Adaptation Test measures responses to toes-up/toes-down platform rotation. CDP measures functional impairment (it tracks Dizziness Handicap Inventory scores) rather than localizing a lesion. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 325)

**When formal vestibular testing is (and is not) needed**: order it when history and examination have not identified the side or site of the lesion, to select and monitor vestibular rehabilitation, to document recovery, to confirm contralateral function before a destructive procedure, and to check whether ablation (gentamicin, neurectomy) worked. Classic posterior canal BPPV with a positive Dix-Hallpike does not need it. No single test is a gold standard, otolith tests give only crude present/absent answers, and a normal battery does not exclude vestibular disease. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 316, 321)

**Bedside VOR tests beyond HINTS**: the head-shake test (about 2 Hz for 15 seconds) produces nystagmus whose fast phase usually beats away from the weaker ear and correlates with caloric asymmetry. Vertical or torsional nystagmus after horizontal shaking (cross-coupling) means a CNS cause must be excluded. Loss of more than 5 Snellen/LogMAR lines of dynamic visual acuity with >2 Hz head shaking suggests bilateral vestibular loss. Failure to suppress nystagmus with fixation during VOR suppression points to the vestibulocerebellum. An abnormal visually enhanced VOR (VVOR) shows combined vestibular, cerebellar and pursuit failure. The head-heave test (a quick lateral head translation) checks the utricle and helps predict recovery after vestibular neuritis. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 318-320)

**ENG/VNG patterns that point central**: spontaneous or positional nystagmus with normal calorics; direction-changing nystagmus or failed fixation suppression; bilaterally reduced calorics with no history of labyrinthine disease, middle-ear disease or ototoxicity; saccadic pursuit or dysmetric saccades, especially with normal calorics; hyperactive calorics (loss of cerebellar inhibition) with an intact drum and no mastoid cavity; and perverted (wrong-direction) caloric nystagmus. Peripheral patterns are unilateral caloric weakness, direction-fixed nystagmus, fatiguing positional nystagmus and intact fixation suppression. Alexander's law grades peripheral nystagmus: first degree only when gazing toward the fast phase, second degree also in primary gaze, third degree in all gaze directions. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 321-322, 326)

**CABV and CANVAS**: cerebellar ataxia with bilateral vestibulopathy (CABV) is progressive imbalance and oscillopsia from vestibulocerebellar atrophy plus bilateral vestibular loss. Adding a non-length-dependent sensory neuropathy (ganglionopathy) makes it CANVAS, a late-onset recessive disorder. It can also occur with SCA3/SCA6, Friedreich ataxia, paraneoplastic disease, cerebellar-type MSA and Wernicke. Signs are marked DVA loss, poor pursuit and optokinetic responses, an abnormal VVOR (the single most informative bedside test), gaze-evoked or downbeat nystagmus and gait ataxia. Work up with MRI, sensory nerve action potentials and VNG/vHIT. Treatment is vestibular rehabilitation, avoiding cerebellar toxins (alcohol, solvents, some antiepileptics) and assistive devices. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 331-333)

**Vestibular hair cells, nuclei and Ewald laws**: type I hair cells are flask-shaped with a chalice afferent (mainly excitatory); type II are cylindrical with many bouton terminals. In the lateral canal the kinocilia face the utricle, so ampullopetal flow excites; in the superior and posterior canals they face away, so ampullofugal flow excites (Ewald's second and third laws). Eye movements occur in the plane of the stimulated canal (first law). Paired canals: left superior with right posterior and vice versa. Nuclei: superior (Bechterew) relays canal-ocular reflexes; lateral (Deiters) drives ipsilateral vestibulospinal 'righting' reflexes; medial (Schwalbe) links eye-head movements via the MLF; descending integrates cerebellar and reticular input. Because inhibition bottoms out at zero firing, a unilateral loss stays visible to fast head impulses even after compensation. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 315-318, 320-321)

**Recurrent vestibulopathy as a differential**: recurrent Ménière-like vertigo spells without hearing loss or neurologic signs (vestibular Ménière). Over about 8.5 years, roughly 60% remit, 15% develop Ménière disease, 10% keep having attacks, 10% develop BPPV and 5% another peripheral disorder. Treat symptoms only. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 329)

**Nystagmus during an attack and ECoG cutoff**: early in a spell, irritative nystagmus beats toward the affected ear. In the paralytic phase it beats toward the healthy ear. In the recovery phase it often reverses toward the affected ear again. The direction therefore depends on timing and does not reliably lateralize. ECoG SP/AP ratio above about 0.35 is considered abnormal. Hydrops can bulge the saccule against the footplate (vestibulofibrosis), producing a positive fistula test with an intact drum; the other causes of that sign are SCDS, otosyphilis and perilymph fistula. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 327-328, 330)

**Course numbers and a red flag**: instability with some head movements can last months, and BPPV follows in up to 15% (often posterior canal, since the inferior division is spared). Fast phase beats away from the affected side, with caloric hypofunction in most patients. If the patient is not clearly improving after 2–3 weeks, rule out a central lesion such as cerebellar infarction. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 16, p 329)

**Non-CMV congenital infections**: *Toxoplasmosis* (about 1/10,000 US births; cat feces/undercooked meat) is mostly silent but classically causes chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcifications. Pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine can prevent the hearing loss. *Congenital rubella* causes cataract, heart defects, retinitis, cognitive impairment and SNHL (up to about half of affected newborns, often bilateral, profound and mid-frequency). Pathology shows cochleosaccular degeneration with a rolled tectorial membrane. *Neonatal HSV* is mostly peripartum (85%) and causes SNHL in about 10%. IV acyclovir is given for 14 days for skin/eye/mouth disease and 21 days for CNS or disseminated disease. *Zika* (flavivirus) causes microcephaly with SNHL. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 17, p 334-337); (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 22, pp 437-438)

**Kernicterus and congenital hypothyroidism**: about 20% of children with kernicterus develop severe hearing loss, usually high-frequency, from injury to the dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei and the colliculi (a retrocochlear/ANSD-type pattern). Exchange transfusion is usually indicated above about 20 mg/dL bilirubin. Cretinism (untreated congenital hypothyroidism) combines growth failure, intellectual disability and mixed hearing loss. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 17, p 337)

**Less common X-linked syndromes**: *Norrie syndrome* (Xp11.4) is retinal pseudotumor/dysplasia leading to congenital blindness, with progressive SNHL starting in the 2nd–3rd decade in about a third, plus intellectual disturbance. *Otopalatodigital syndrome* (Xq28) is hypertelorism, a prominent supraorbital ridge, cleft palate, short stature, broad digits with a wide first toe web, and conductive loss from ossicular malformation (full disease in males). *X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth* (connexin 32/GJB1, Xq13) is peripheral neuropathy with 'champagne-bottle' calves and sometimes SNHL. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 17, p 341-342)

**Congenital footplate fixation vs otosclerosis**: congenital fixation starts in childhood, does not progress, has no family history and gives a flat 50–60 dB conductive loss without a Carhart notch or Schwartz sign. Otosclerosis is usually progressive, familial (dominant with only 25–40% penetrance) and shows a Carhart notch. In congenital middle-ear malformations, the outer-ear deformity does not predict the middle-ear anatomy. Isolated ossicular anomalies with a normal auricle and aerated ear are the most common pattern. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 17, p 339, 357-358)

**EHDI screening protocol details**: in a one-step protocol, either OAE or AABR is used and a failed screen is repeated with the same technology before discharge. In a two-step protocol, OAE is followed by AABR. NICU infants should be screened with AABR only, because OAE misses neural (ANSD) loss. Infants readmitted in the first month with a hearing-loss risk condition are rescreened before discharge. Avoid screening more times than recommended, because each repeat raises the chance of a false pass. A cookie-bite (U-shaped) audiogram suggests hereditary loss. Every child with SNHL should have a urinalysis (Alport) and serial eye examinations (Usher). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 17, p 358-359)

**Prognosis and sound-therapy numbers**: over time about 25% of patients have near resolution, 50% improve substantially and 25% stay the same. Tinnitus pitch and loudness matching does not predict distress or outcome; many patients match at only about 5 dB above threshold. Hearing aids are first line when there is hearing loss, and adding a masker raises the rate of tinnitus control from about 25% to 55%. Tinnitus retraining therapy pairs directive counseling with low-level broadband noise for about 16 hours a day, set just below the level that covers the tinnitus. Habituation takes about a year. rTMS remains investigational. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 18, p 363-364)

**Pulsatile tinnitus sources and SBUTT**: venous causes include a high or dehiscent jugular bulb, sigmoid sinus diverticulum or dehiscence, and aberrant condylar or petrosal veins. Arterial causes include carotid dissection, stenosis or aneurysm, aberrant ICA, dehiscent carotid canal and persistent stapedial artery. Dural AV fistulas, often near the transverse/sigmoid sinus or after craniotomy, can bleed when they drain into cortical veins. Other causes are paragangliomas and other tumors, encephaloceles touching the ossicles, high-output states (anemia, thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy) and IIH. Auscultate with a stethoscope or Toynbee tube. A sudden, brief, unilateral, tapering tinnitus (SBUTT) is normal. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 18, p 361-363)

**Electroacoustic terms and predictors of success**: an aid is described by frequency response (typically up to 3–4 kHz), gain (output/input) and OSPL-90 (output with a 90 dB input). Compression (nonlinear) processing gives more gain for soft sounds than loud ones, which suits recruiting ears. Dynamic range = UCL − SRT, and MCL roughly bisects it. Success is best predicted by word recognition of at least 50% and a wide dynamic range; a narrow range makes fitting hard. Large vents remove the occlusion effect and help in noise but are contraindicated with significant low-frequency loss. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 19, p 366-367)

**Implantable and bone-conduction device details**: electromagnetic middle-ear implants attach a floating mass transducer to the ossicles (usually the incus). A piezoelectric fully implantable device needs incus removal (deliberate discontinuity) to prevent feedback. Downsides are surgery, cost, battery replacement surgery and MRI limits. Percutaneous osseointegrated implants are placed above the temporal line and allowed about 3 months to integrate. For single-sided deafness they need a better-ear PTA of 20 dB HL or better. They remove the head shadow and help in noise but do not restore localization; CI can. Magnetic transcutaneous systems vary in MRI conditionality (about 1.5 T for one design, 3 T for another). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 19, p 367-369)

**Reconstruction outcomes and transformer numbers**: in most series, at least two-thirds of PORPs and at least half of TORPs reach an air-bone gap of 20 dB or less. Incus interposition brings about 66% within 20 dB, and results are stable over time. A cartilage disc under the prosthesis head reduces extrusion, and a footplate shoe stabilizes a TORP. The ideal transformer predicts about 28 dB of gain (about 26 dB from the roughly 20:1 TM/oval-window area ratio plus about 2 dB from the 1.3:1 lever). Measured gain is about 23 dB, peaking near 1 kHz. Mastoid cavities have a shallow middle ear, so short prostheses are needed. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 19, p 369-373)

**Patient situations that change the stapes plan**: osteogenesis imperfecta bone is brittle, so take care not to fracture the tympanic ring while curetting or the incus while crimping. Coexisting hydrops (Ménière) puts a distended saccule under the footplate and raises the risk of a dead ear, so consider amplification. A blind patient, or one with contralateral vestibulopathy, may not compensate for even a minor vestibular injury; get calorics if vestibulopathy is suspected and consider a hearing aid. Patients with mixed loss will likely still need aids. Indications: air-bone gap of at least 25–30 dB (negative 512 Hz Rinne), normal otoscopy and absent or biphasic reflexes; operate on the worse ear. A vestigial persistent stapedial artery can be worked around; a large one means aborting. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 19, p 371-372)

**Textbook audiometric criteria**: adults have bilateral moderate-to-profound SNHL with best-aided sentence scores of 50% or less in the ear to be implanted and 60% or less binaurally. CMS (Medicare) is stricter: 40% or less. Hybrid (electroacoustic) labeling: low-frequency thresholds (500 Hz and below) better than about 60 dB HL with 2–4 kHz PTA of at least 75 dB HL in the implant ear, and aided CNC word scores of 10–60% in that ear. Children: at least 12 months by FDA labeling (earlier is increasingly done), a 3–6 month aid trial (waived for postmeningitic ossification), profound loss at 12–24 months and severe-to-profound loss after 24 months, open-set words of 30% or less (MLNT/LNT). Adult testing uses AzBio, CNC and BKB-SIN. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 20, p 377, 380-381)

**Imaging and ear-selection rules**: heavily T2-weighted MRI (CISS/FIESTA) in the sagittal oblique plane confirms the cochlear nerve and separates fluid from fibrosis or ossification. When the IAC is under about 3 mm, CT of the bony cochlear nerve canal helps: a closed canal supports nerve aplasia. CT also shows obstacles: poor pneumatization, an anterior sigmoid, a high jugular bulb, an anomalous facial nerve and gusher-prone anomalies. Ear choice: adults usually do better in the better ear, but useful residual hearing there favors implanting the worse ear (bimodal). After more than 10 years of prelingual deprivation, choose the better ear. With malformations, implant the less dysplastic side first. Contraindications: labyrinthine or cochlear aplasia, complete ossification, absent cochlear nerve. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 20, p 379-382)

**Binaural benefits and timing**: bilateral CIs give the head shadow effect, binaural summation (redundant input), squelch (the cocktail-party effect, from central processing of interaural time and level differences) and better localization. They also prevent going 'off air' if one device fails. The critical window is birth to about 2 years; missing it lets auditory cortex be taken over by other senses (cross-modal plasticity). Simultaneous implantation beats sequential implantation with a gap over 12 months, but sequential with under 12 months is comparable. Duration of deafness and preoperative speech scores explain about 80% of outcome variance. Postlingual adults commonly exceed 75% open-set sentences, and about 60% use the telephone. Prelingually deaf adults who sign rarely gain open-set recognition. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 20, p 383-384, 389-390)

**Soft-surgery and electrode choices**: preserve low-frequency hearing (thresholds under 80 dB HL are aidable for electroacoustic stimulation). Use a round-window insertion when possible, a flexible lateral-wall array inserted very slowly, no perilymph suctioning, an intact incus buttress and ossicles, no overpacking, and perioperative steroids. Trauma mechanisms: fracture of the osseous spiral lamina or spiral ligament, basal-turn lateral-wall injury, tip deflection through the basilar membrane into the scala media or vestibuli, and over-deep insertion. Perimodiolar arrays sit closer to the modiolus (theoretically lower current, less channel interaction) but are more traumatic. Aim for an angular depth of at least 360–400°. Do not saucerize the posterior/inferior mastoid, because the overhangs hold the coiled lead. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 20, p 383-385)

**Approaches for difficult anatomy**: double posterior labyrinthotomy for a common cavity; suprameatal approach (through a tympanomeatal flap) for a contracted mastoid, narrow facial recess, anomalous nerve or anterior sigmoid; subtotal petrosectomy with ET obliteration and canal closure for hostile anatomy, uncontrollable CSF leak or recurrent meningitis. For ossification (about half of children deafened by neonatal meningitis), drill a basal-turn tunnel through a cochleostomy anterior to the round window, or use scala vestibuli insertion, partial insertion or a split (two-limb) array. Malformed cochleae more often have an anteromedially displaced second genu/mastoid segment. Use fluoroscopy to avoid insertion into the IAC. Check with impedances (high = open circuit, low = short circuit), ECAP/NRT (sets pediatric starting levels) and a modified Stenvers film. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 20, p 385-387)

**Complication numbers and fixes**: lifetime hard device failure is about 4%. More than 3–5 failed electrodes signals impending failure. Permanent dysgeusia occurs in about 3%. Facial nerve injury is under 1%. Facial nerve stimulation is more common with cochlear otosclerosis, otic-capsule fractures, malformations or high stimulation levels; turn off the offending electrodes and revise if it persists. Children with CIs have about 30 times the meningitis rate of hearing children; S. pneumoniae causes about 62%. Risks are positioners (no longer used), malformations and CSF leak. Electrode migration shows as fluctuating thresholds, especially with malformed cochleae; skull growth does not cause it. At reimplantation, cut the old lead at the facial recess and leave it in the cochlea until the new receiver is fixed. Then swap arrays through the same fibrous tract so the tunnel does not collapse. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 20, p 387-389)

**Acute otitis media in a CI recipient**: never use watchful waiting. Within about 2 months of surgery, treat with parenteral antibiotics. After 2 months, use high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate, escalating to IV therapy at any sign of failure. Do tympanocentesis for treatment failure, and LP if meningitis is suspected. Tympanostomy tubes can coexist with CIs. For recurrent AOM, consider staged subtotal petrosectomy before implantation. Vaccination: the book cites PCV13 at least 2 weeks before surgery, then PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later. Current CDC adult schedules use PCV20 or PCV21 alone, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23, so follow the current CDC schedule. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 22, p 414-415); (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 20, p 382)

**Synchronous bilateral facial paralysis**: the main causes are Lyme disease, Möbius syndrome, NF2, brainstem lesions (cavernous hemangioma), bilateral temporal bone fractures, Guillain-Barré and HIV. Bilateral simultaneous palsy is rarely Bell palsy and needs a directed workup. Lyme palsy often comes with headache, fever, rash, arthralgia and fatigue. Treat it with antibiotics and eye care; adding steroids may worsen outcomes. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 21, p 394-395)

**Textbook acute-palsy algorithm**: Bell palsy (15–30/100,000) should be fully evolved by 72 hours. Give prednisone within 48–72 hours (about 60 mg for 5 days, then a 5-day taper), with or without an antiviral, plus eye care. Consider ENoG within about 12 days for complete paralysis; decompression is debated for under 10% residual response with no voluntary EMG units. Temporal bone fracture: immediate-onset palsy → consider exploration; delayed onset → serial ENoG, with decompression if below 10%. Iatrogenic palsy with unknown continuity: explore unless ENoG proves continuity. Repair tension-free; graft with great auricular (avoid if neck metastasis is possible), sural (longest) or medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve (branching pattern suits multiple distal branches). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 21, p 395-396)

**Textbook regimen and prognosis**: only about 60% regain normal facial function, worse than Bell palsy. Give high-dose steroid (about 1 mg/kg/day for 14 days) when there is facial palsy or SNHL, plus valacyclovir 1 g every 8 hours for 7 days. Decompression is not advised, because degeneration is diffuse rather than confined to the labyrinthine segment and geniculate ganglion. Use gabapentin for postherpetic neuralgia. A Tzanck smear (multinucleated giant cells) or viral titers can support the diagnosis; check for herpetic keratitis. Other cranial nerves (V, IX–XII) can be involved. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 22, p 403-404)

**Gracilis and nerve-transfer specifics**: consider nerve transfer when there is no recovery by about 6 months with viable muscle, ideally within 18 months of denervation. Masseteric transfer is the most used (strong, nearby, low morbidity, but no spontaneous smile). Hypoglossal transfer has fallen out of favor (tongue atrophy, synkinesis); a split XII reduces this. Cross-face grafting can give spontaneity but carries few axons. One-stage gracilis driven by the masseteric nerve suits patients over about 40 or with no usable contralateral VII: movement at 4–6 months, about 92% success. Two-stage gracilis: cross-face sural graft first, following the advancing Tinel sign, then the muscle at 6–9 months; about 80% success, less excursion but a spontaneous smile. Dual innervation combines both. Temporalis transfer (including orthodromic) is second line. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 21, p 397-399)

**Chemodenervation targets and PT types**: botulinum toxin to the contralateral frontalis evens out a paralyzed brow. To the affected orbicularis oculi it treats ocular synkinesis (avoid causing lagophthalmos). The lacrimal gland treats gustatory tearing (Bogorad, crocodile tears). Mentalis injection smooths chin dimpling. Multiple platysmal band injections free oral commissure excursion. The contralateral depressor labii inferioris balances the lower lip (resection makes it permanent). Facial PT uses facilitation (for weakness without synkinesis) and movement control (aggressive stretching, neuromuscular retraining with biofeedback, relaxation) for synkinesis. Terms: flaccid paralysis, post-paralysis facial palsy (hypertonicity plus synkinesis) and mixed. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 21, p 399-400)

**Static eye and face procedures**: platinum lid weights are preferred over gold (thinner, less capsule). Sew the weight to the tarsus centered between the midpupillary line and medial limbus; a platinum chain conforms to the tarsus. Palpebral springs blink more naturally but nearly all need revision. Tarsorrhaphy is for failed loading/lower-lid repair or corneal anesthesia or ulcer. Treat the lower lid with a lateral tarsal strip (canthotomy, cantholysis, suspension to orbital rim periosteum) or a fascia lata sling. Fascia lata 'three-ribbon' static suspension to temporalis fascia can treat external valve collapse, the nasolabial fold and the commissure. Office brow lifts (suture or bioabsorbable fixation) correct brow ptosis. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 21, p 396-397)

**Bullous and granular myringitis**: *Bullous myringitis* follows URIs, mostly in winter. Serous or bloody bullae on the TM and medial canal cause severe pain for 3–4 days. It comes with middle-ear effusion in 30–40%, and a usually reversible SNHL or mixed loss occurs in up to 60% (check bone conduction). Mycoplasma is unproven; pneumococcus, H. influenzae and Moraxella are found. Treat with analgesics, lancing the bullae and drops, and treat any AOM. *Granular (chronic) myringitis* is painless, foul otorrhea with granulation replacing TM epithelium (often posterosuperior) and a normal middle ear (CT if unsure). Late canal blunting can follow. Organisms are S. aureus, Pseudomonas and Proteus. Dilute-vinegar irrigation and surgical removal work best; recurrence is common. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 22, p 406-407)

**Labyrinthine fistula numbers and matrix decision**: a fistula is found in about 7–10% of cholesteatomas, the lateral semicircular canal in about 90%. Only about 60% have vertigo, the fistula test is positive in only 30–50% (specific but insensitive), and preoperative CT shows only about 60%. SNHL is present in 60–70%. Assume a fistula in every case. For large fistulas, cochlear fistulas or fistulas open to the membranous labyrinth (about 50% hearing-loss risk), leave matrix on the fistula and convert to canal wall down. Small fistulas can be cleared and sealed with bone wax/pâté and fascia, keeping the canal wall up. If the endosteum tears, stop and leave the matrix in place. Facial nerve and tegmen dehiscence often coexist. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 22, p 423-424)

**Facial palsy from chronic otitis**: dehiscence of the tympanic segment (up to about 30% congenitally) or erosion lets exotoxins and inflammation injure the nerve. Palsy from AOM starts abruptly, is usually incomplete and recovers with antibiotics plus myringotomy or a tube. Palsy from COM progresses slowly and often persists. Treat it with tympanomastoidectomy, clearing matrix and granulation off the epineurium and decompressing proximal and distal to the involved segment. Open the sheath only if cholesteatoma has invaded it. HB I–II recovery is reported in 52–83%. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 22, p 422-423)

**Routes and organism-specific risk in suppurative labyrinthitis**: meningitic labyrinthitis reaches the scala tympani through the cochlear aqueduct or along the IAC. Otogenic labyrinthitis now mostly comes from cholesteatoma through a fistula or a congenital defect. Deafness after bacterial meningitis averages about 10% (2–20%): about 20% with S. pneumoniae, 12% with H. influenzae and 5% with N. meningitidis. Steroids improve hearing outcomes in pneumococcal and Hib meningitis. Serous labyrinthitis shows basal-turn outer hair cell loss and often hydrops, and usually recovers. Follow SNHL with serial CT/MRI, and implant early if ossification begins in a bilaterally deaf child. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 22, p 430-432)

**Glandular odontogenic cyst**: A cyst of middle-aged adults, about 80% in the anterior mandible, that may be uni- or multilocular. Its lining contains mucous cells and microcysts, so a small incisional biopsy can be misread as central mucoepidermoid carcinoma. It can behave aggressively, with some series reporting recurrence above 30%, so treat with enucleation and curettage and consider en bloc resection. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 39, p 725)

**Traumatic (simple) bone cyst and lateral periodontal cyst**: The traumatic bone cyst is a pseudocyst with no epithelial lining, seen mostly at ages 10-20 in the mandible. It scallops between tooth roots, aspiration returns nothing or a little blood, and surgical exploration alone usually starts healing. The lateral periodontal cyst is an incidental, usually <1 cm unilocular lucency beside the roots of vital mandibular premolar/canine teeth in adults aged 40-70. It is treated by enucleation with the tooth kept. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 39, p 725-727)

**Central giant cell granuloma: rule out hyperparathyroidism**: A multilocular lucency of patients under 30, usually in the mandible, that may cross the midline anteriorly. Histology (multinucleated giant cells) is identical to the brown tumor, so check calcium and PTH in every case. Treatment is usually aggressive curettage. Medical options include intralesional steroids, calcitonin, and interferon. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 39, p 733)

**Cherubism**: An autosomal dominant giant-cell lesion that starts at ages 2-5. It causes painless bilateral cheek fullness from multilocular lucencies of the posterior mandible, sometimes the maxilla too. It enlarges during childhood and usually stabilizes or regresses after puberty. Management is observation, with surgical contouring only for symptoms or deformity. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 39, p 733-734)

**Aspirate before biopsying a jaw lucency**: Needle-aspirate a radiolucent jaw lesion before an open biopsy to exclude an arteriovenous malformation, which can bleed massively. Typical aspirates: straw-colored fluid in a dentigerous cyst, cheesy keratin in an OKC, blood in an aneurysmal bone cyst, nothing in a traumatic bone cyst, and a dry tap in a solid tumor. Test pulp vitality with cold or electric testing, because only the periapical cyst needs a nonvital tooth. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 39, p 722-727)

**Nerve-sparing details and complications**: Start with a level II-III neck dissection for exposure. Keep the hypoglossal-vagus connections intact, because separating them can impair both nerves. Dissect in the periadventitial plane; a routine subadventitial plane weakens the artery. Cranial nerve deficits (mostly X, XII, sympathetic chain) occur in up to about 55% and rise with size over 3 cm; about two-thirds recover within 6 months. Bilateral resection risks baroreflex failure (loss of Hering nerve input from CN IX). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 40, p 739)

**Embolization and radiation specifics**: If preoperative embolization is used, avoid ethanol because of nerve injury risk. After radiation, most tumors (about 80%) stay radiographically stable rather than shrinking. Radiation-induced malignancy is about 1% at 10 years. Observed tumors grow about 1 mm per year and are followed with annual CT or MRI. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 40, p 739)

**Vagal paraganglioma versus schwannoma**: Vagal paragangliomas usually arise from the nodose ganglion. They push the carotids anteromedially without splaying them and separate the IJV from the carotid; sympathetic tumors usually do not. Malignancy is higher than for carotid body tumors (about 16%). Resection almost always causes vagal paralysis, so it is reserved for aggressive or skull-base tumors or a nerve that is already paralyzed. If a vagal paraganglioma is found unexpectedly during planned carotid body surgery, it is reasonable to stop and choose observation or radiation. Schwannomas, by contrast, can often be enucleated with the nerve preserved. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 40, p 739-741)

topic: Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Low- vs high-risk features (NCCN-style)**: High-risk features include: H-zone location (central face, eyelids, nose, lips, chin, preauricular/postauricular skin, temple, ear) or a lesion of 10 mm or more on the cheek, forehead, scalp, or neck; poorly defined borders; recurrence; prior radiation; immunosuppression; rapid growth; neurologic symptoms; perineural or lymphovascular invasion; poor differentiation; depth of 2 mm or more or Clark level IV-V; and acantholytic, adenosquamous, desmoplastic, or metaplastic subtypes. Low-risk invasive tumors can be excised with 4-6 mm margins. High-risk tumors need Mohs surgery or complete margin assessment, and SLNB can be considered for clinically N0 high-risk disease. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 42, p 761-762)

topic: Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Adjuvant radiation and chemoradiation triggers**: Consider adjuvant RT for: a single node without ENE (selectively); two or more positive nodes; any node over 3 cm; ENE; incompletely excised nodes; an unresectable positive margin; or extensive or large-nerve perineural invasion. Consider concurrent systemic therapy (cisplatin, carboplatin, or cetuximab) for ENE, gross residual nodal disease, or an unresectable positive margin, though its benefit is unproven. Radiation is contraindicated in genetic skin-cancer syndromes and connective tissue disease. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 42, p 762)

topic: Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Nodal basin by primary site**: For temple, high cheek, and forehead primaries with nodal disease, do a parotidectomy plus neck dissection of levels I-IV.
