For posterior scalp and neck primaries, do a posterolateral neck dissection that extends to the posterior midline and removes level V, suboccipital, and retroauricular nodes. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 42, p 762)

topic: Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Chemoprevention in high-risk patients**: Oral nicotinamide may reduce new cSCC and actinic keratoses. Systemic retinoids (acitretin, isotretinoin) help selected high-risk patients, especially transplant recipients, and reducing immunosuppression (or switching to an mTOR inhibitor) is coordinated with the transplant team. Follow up every 3-12 months for 2 years, every 6-12 months for the next 3 years, then yearly. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 42, p 757, 763)

**Margins, SLNB yield, and adjuvant RT triggers**: Standard care is wide excision with 1-2 cm margins plus SLNB in the clinically N0 neck. About 33-40% of clinical stage I/II MCC already have occult nodal disease. Give adjuvant RT to the primary for narrow or positive margins, a tumor over 1 cm, immunosuppression, or LVI/PNI. Give it to the nodal basin for a positive SLNB, multiple nodes, or ENE. In-transit disease is N2 without nodes and N3 with nodes. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 42, p 763-764)

**Immunostain profile**: About 40% of MCC are hard to call on H&E, so immunostains are needed. MCC is CK20-positive in a paranuclear dot pattern and positive for neuroendocrine markers (synaptophysin, chromogranin). It is TTF-1-negative, which separates it from metastatic small cell lung cancer. CONFLICT NOTE: K.J. Lee lists CD117, S-100, and CD45 as positive markers; standard pathology teaches that MCC is S-100- and CD45-negative, which helps exclude melanoma and lymphoma. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 42, p 763)

topic: Basal Cell Carcinoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Low-risk BCC specifics**: Low-risk BCC (nodular or superficial, well defined, primary, <2 cm, outside the H-zone) can be excised with a 4 mm margin and postoperative margin check. C&E is fast and cheap but gives no margin histology and is unsuitable for hair-bearing scalp, because tumor tracks down follicles. Intralesional interferon works for superficial BCC but is rarely used (three injections a week for 3 weeks). Hedgehog inhibitor side effects are muscle cramps, dysgeusia, alopecia, weight loss, fatigue, and raised CK. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 42, p 759-760)

**Unresectability criteria at the skull base**: Disease is generally unresectable if it invades the brainstem, both internal carotid arteries, both cavernous sinuses, the spinal cord, or enough brain that resection would destroy quality of life. Optic chiasm invasion (resection means bilateral blindness) is a relative contraindication. Distant metastasis, major comorbidity, and chemo- or radio-responsive histology (such as lymphoma) also argue against surgery. Get tissue before any en bloc resection that sacrifices neurovascular structures. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 49, p 861)

**When endoscopic resection is not appropriate**: Expanded endonasal resection suits small midline tumors. Contraindications are orbital involvement, far-lateral maxillary sinus disease, dural involvement lateral to the orbit, brain parenchymal invasion, cavernous sinus or carotid involvement, and tumor lateral to the cavernous carotid or superolateral to the optic nerve. In selected cases, endoscopic 5-year survival (up to about 60%) is comparable to open craniofacial resection. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 49, p 864)

**Craniofacial resection details**: The pericranial flap is pedicled on the supraorbital and supratrochlear vessels and laid under the dural repair. Aim for about a 5 mm margin on involved dura or brain and 5-10 mm around tumor crossing the anterior fossa floor, confirmed with frozen sections. Exenteration is indicated for gross invasion of periorbital fat, extraocular muscles, or optic nerve. During exenteration, inject local anesthetic around the superior orbital fissure and optic foramen before division to blunt reflex cardiac arrhythmias. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 49, p 862)

**Fisch infratemporal fossa approaches A/B/C**: Type A targets the infralabyrinthine temporal bone and jugular foramen, with anterior facial nerve rerouting (glomus jugulare, temporal bone malignancy, cholesteatoma). Type B targets the petrous apex and clivus (chordoma, chondroma or chondrosarcoma, clival epidermoids, meningioma). Type C reaches the parasellar region, pterygopalatine fossa, and nasopharynx (salvage nasopharyngeal carcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma around the Eustachian tube, advanced JNA). All include blind-sac closure of the EAC and proximal carotid control in the neck. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 49, p 865-866)

**Middle fossa triangles**: The Glasscock (posterolateral) triangle lies between the foramen spinosum, the arcuate eminence/facial hiatus, the GSPN, and V3. The petrous carotid runs beneath the GSPN here. The Kawase (posteromedial) triangle is bounded by the GSPN, the petrous ridge, and the arcuate eminence. Drilling it (anterior petrosectomy) reaches the petroclival region and posterior fossa without crossing the cochlea, which sits at its posterolateral corner. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 49, p 857-858)

**Transcochlear approach**: The transcochlear approach reaches the skull base medial to the porus and anterior to the brainstem (petroclival lesions). Through a labyrinthectomy, the facial nerve is skeletonized from the stylomastoid foramen to the geniculate. The GSPN and chorda are cut, the nerve is rerouted posteriorly, and the cochlea is drilled out. The limits are the carotid anteriorly, the superior petrosal sinus above, the jugular bulb below, and the sigmoid sinus behind. It sacrifices hearing and almost always leaves at least temporary facial weakness. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 49, p 875)

**Avulsed arytenoid and stents**: A completely avulsed and displaced arytenoid is better removed than repositioned. Fix cartilage fractures with miniplates. Reserve stents for severe comminution, because they provoke granulation. Acute repair gives better results than delayed reconstruction. About half of patients with laryngeal fractures asphyxiate at the scene, and survivors may have a deceptively quiet interval before sudden obstruction. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 50, p 906-907)

**Laryngeal candidiasis**: Risk factors are inhaled (especially powder) corticosteroids, reflux, immunosuppression, and antibiotics. White plaques on red mucosa can mimic leukoplakia. Treat with a systemic antifungal (topical or swallowed nystatin is ineffective) and pause the inhaled steroid if possible. Biopsy plaques that persist after treatment to exclude carcinoma. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 50, p 901)

**Embryologic origin of the turbinates**: The maxilloturbinal becomes the inferior turbinate. The first ethmoturbinal becomes the middle turbinate, the second and third the superior turbinate, and the fourth and fifth the supreme turbinate. The nasoturbinal becomes the agger nasi. The inferior and middle turbinates and uncinate form around week 7 and the superior turbinate around week 8. The inferior turbinate is a separate bone, while the others are part of the ethmoid. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 51, p 932)

**Fourth-pouch tract course by side**: On the right, a fourth-arch tract runs low under the platysma, loops under the subclavian artery, passes deep to the carotid, lateral to XII and below the SLN, and opens into the lower piriform apex. On the left, the tract can be intrathoracic, looping around the aortic arch medial to the ligamentum arteriosum. This left-sided embryology explains why piriform sinus fistula thyroiditis is mostly left-sided. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 51, p 926)

**Work type II and the facial nerve**: Work II tracts run superficial to the facial nerve in about 57%, deep in about 30%, and between branches in about 13%. A deep course is more common in girls, young children, fistulas (vs sinuses), and tracts that do not open into the EAC. Plan a parotidectomy approach with nerve monitoring. Remember the shallow mastoid tip in young children leaves the nerve trunk superficial. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 53, p 1017)

topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
text: **Environmental risks and laterality**: Teratogens and exposures linked to clefting are retinoids, anticonvulsants, maternal smoking, alcohol, illicit drugs, organic solvents, nitrates, and lead. Low folate, B6, or B12 and amniotic bands also contribute, and risk rises with birth order. About 80% of clefts are unilateral, and two-thirds of unilateral cleft lips are left-sided. Monozygotic twin concordance is about 50-60% (dizygotic about 5%). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 52, p 942-943)

topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
text: **Palatoplasty outcomes and otologic burden**: After palatoplasty, oronasal fistula occurs in up to about 10% and VPI in up to about 25%. Chronic OME affects 95-100% of children with cleft palate, from a malpositioned tensor and levator, abnormal tube curvature, and lateral cartilage hypoplasia. Tubes are often placed at the time of lip repair, and middle ear disease usually improves after palate repair and with age. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 52, p 953)

**Wolfram syndrome vs WFS1 hearing loss**: CONFLICT NOTE: K.J. Lee calls 'Wolfram' the most common dominant low-frequency SNHL. More precisely, heterozygous dominant WFS1 mutations cause nonsyndromic low-frequency (upsloping) loss (DFNA6/14/38). Recessive WFS1 mutations cause Wolfram syndrome (DIDMOAD: diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy, deafness), a progressive neurodegenerative syndrome. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 53, p 971)

**Pilomatrixoma**: A common benign pediatric skin adnexal tumor from hair matrix cells, frequent on the face and neck and more common in girls. It is a firm, superficial, often bluish, sometimes faceted nodule tethered to skin. Ultrasound shows calcification. Treatment is complete excision with the overlying skin if needed, because it does not regress and recurs if incompletely removed. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 53, p 963)

**TEF repair outcomes**: About 85-90% are proximal esophageal atresia with distal TEF. The H-type (2-4% of primary TEF) needs a prone pull-back esophagram or bronchoscopy to find. Vocal fold paralysis follows about 11% of repairs (usually left) and about 50% of cervical H-type repairs. Most children compensate clinically within about 8 months, though only about a third recover nerve function. Recurrent fistula (about 20%) can be treated endoscopically by de-epithelialization, with 60-90% success over a mean of two sessions. Screen for VACTERL anomalies. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 53, p 1004-1005)

**Site pattern and sclerosant choice**: Microcystic lesions tend to lie above the mylohyoid (tongue, floor of mouth), and macrocystic lesions below it in the neck. Bleomycin causes less swelling but often needs more sessions, so it is favored near the aerodigestive tract. Doxycycline is more potent but swells more, so it suits the neck and limbs. Sirolimus treats residual or diffuse disease after sclerotherapy. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 53, p 1015-1016)

**Neonatal facial palsy**: Traumatic neonatal palsy is linked to first births, high birth weight, prolonged labor, and forceps or vacuum delivery, often with local bruising. About 90% recover spontaneously. Distinguish it from developmental palsy (Moebius, hemifacial microsomia, CHARGE), which lacks trauma signs, may be bilateral or segmental, and does not recover. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 53, p 1024)

**Airway ladder**: Escalate from side or prone positioning to a nasopharyngeal airway and a McGovern nipple, then tongue-lip adhesion (benefit debated), subperiosteal release of the floor-of-mouth muscles (about 84% effective in one series), mandibular distraction, and tracheostomy. Mandibular catch-up growth over 4-6 months often relieves mild obstruction. Screen for Stickler, which is associated with myopia, retinal detachment, and mixed hearing loss. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 53, p 990)

**Macroglossia causes**: True anterior macroglossia includes Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (11p15 imprinting; macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycemia, omphalocele, ear pits or creases, about 10% embryonal tumors such as Wilms and hepatoblastoma), treated with anterior wedge glossectomy. Other causes are mucopolysaccharidoses (Hurler, Hunter) and congenital hypothyroidism. Down syndrome causes relative macroglossia with a large tongue base. Lymphatic or venous malformations are also in the differential. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 53, p 989-990)

**Rhytidectomy complications by the numbers**: Hematoma is the most common complication (about 3-15%) and needs prompt evacuation. Skin necrosis is most common postauricularly and more frequent in smokers. The great auricular nerve is the most often injured nerve (about 7%). Temporal or marginal mandibular neurapraxia occurs in about 1%, and permanent motor injury in about 0.1%. Over-resecting subplatysmal fat without platysmaplasty produces a cobra-neck deformity. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 54, p 1036-1037)

**Why the deep-plane lift is safe medially**: Medially, the sub-SMAS dissection runs on the superficial surface of the zygomaticus major and minor. These muscles are innervated on their deep surfaces, so the facial nerve branches stay beneath the plane. SMAS imbrication improves the jowl, while the deep-plane lift mobilizes the malar fat pad and improves the nasolabial fold more. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 54, p 1036)

**Lower-lid laxity tests and red flags**: Lid retraction test: if the medial canthus moves 3 mm or more when the lid is pulled down, ectropion risk is high. Snap/distraction test: distraction over about 1 cm or slow recoil means laxity, so plan a canthopexy or canthoplasty. Do not remove fat in a negative-vector orbit. Festoons and malar bags respond poorly to blepharoplasty. In upper-lid surgery, leave at least 20 mm of skin between the lash line and the lower brow to avoid lagophthalmos. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 54, p 1033-1034)

**Choosing a revision by scar orientation**: Simple fusiform excision suits scars within about 0-30 degrees of the RSTLs. Z-plasty suits about 30-60 degrees. W-plasty or geometric broken-line closure suits about 60-90 degrees, with GBLC preferred for long scars. Dermabrasion or laser can be added about 6 weeks after revision. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 54, p 1051)

**Revision rates and timing**: About 5-10% of open and 10-15% of closed rhinoplasties need revision, and revision usually waits about 1 year for edema and scar to settle. Know the classic deformity-cause pairs: pollybeak (residual anterior septal angle, supratip dead-space scar, or loss of tip support); inverted-V (ULC detachment from the nasal bones or middle-vault collapse); open roof (no lateral osteotomies after hump removal); saddle (over-resected dorsum); alar retraction (over-resected lateral crura or vestibular skin). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 54, p 1040-1041)

topic: Reconstruction Selection After Head & Neck Ablation
text: **Trapezius flap system**: The lateral island trapezius flap rides the transverse cervical artery and vein, which must run under the anterior trapezius border clear of the brachial plexus. The lower island flap has the widest arc of the three, with dual supply from the transverse cervical and dorsal scapular arteries, but a prior neck dissection may have compromised the transverse cervical vessels. The superior trapezius flap runs on paraspinous intercostal perforators and holds its position well, but it leaves a poor cosmetic donor site. All three reach the lateral scalp, neck and cheek. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 55, p 1060)

topic: Reconstruction Selection After Head & Neck Ablation
text: **Jejunal free flap specifics**: Inset the jejunum isoperistaltically, as a tube for circumferential pharyngoesophageal defects or opened as a patch on its mesenteric arcade. An exteriorized monitoring segment can be brought out through the neck. Its reach is limited by how low an esophageal anastomosis can safely go without a thoracotomy (the thoracic inlet). Drawbacks: laparotomy with feeding jejunostomy, two neck enteric anastomoses with a high stricture rate, friable mesenteric vessels prone to intimal separation, dysphagia from uncoordinated peristalsis, and a poor (wet) tracheoesophageal voice. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 55, pp 1066-1067)

topic: Reconstruction Selection After Head & Neck Ablation
text: **Fibula and radial-forearm bone caveats**: A peroneal arteria magna (absent or diseased anterior tibial supply, leaving the foot dependent on the peroneal artery) precludes fibula harvest, so obtain CT angiography or MRA of the legs beforehand. A double-barreled fibula gains height for implants, but it shortens the pedicle and can compromise the skin perforators. Transient ankle stiffness is common. The osteocutaneous radial forearm carries only a monocortical radius segment of up to about 10 cm, which is too thin for osseointegrated implants. Plate the donor radius immediately to prevent a pathologic fracture. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 55, p 1065)

topic: Reconstruction Selection After Head & Neck Ablation
text: **Subscapular system anatomy**: The scapular and parascapular flaps arise from the circumflex scapular artery, a branch of the subscapular artery. The lateral scapular border gives a straight segment about 3 cm wide and up to 14 cm long. The scapular tip has its own supply from the angular branch of the thoracodorsal artery, so two separate bone segments can be raised on one pedicle. Separate bone and soft-tissue components give the most 3-dimensional insetting freedom of any composite flap, and latissimus, serratus and rib can join as a 'megaflap.' Downsides: decubitus positioning, thin bone (poor for implants), variable anatomy, and teres major division that weakens the shoulder. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 55, pp 1065-1066)

topic: Reconstruction Selection After Head & Neck Ablation
text: **Lateral arm free flap**: This fasciocutaneous flap runs on the posterior radial collateral vessels through the lateral intermuscular septum and is sensate via the posterior cutaneous nerves of the arm and forearm. It gives the best color match to facial skin of any free flap and can carry a 1 x 10 cm strip of humerus. The donor site closes primarily. Compared with the radial forearm, the pedicle is shorter and harder to dissect and the tissue is thicker. Expect lateral arm numbness and possible elbow pain. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 55, pp 1062-1063)

**Minimizing ischemia time**: Enteric, muscle and bone flaps are the most ischemia-sensitive. Fully dissect the flap in situ and prepare the recipient vessels before dividing the pedicle. Cooling the flap with iced saline during transfer lowers its metabolic demand. Postoperatively, keep the patient normotensive, euvolemic and normothermic to avoid peripheral vasoconstriction. Save the external jugular vein as a recipient vessel or vein graft, and leave stumps on any sacrificed vessels. Plan a saphenous vein graft when no recipient vessels are within reach. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 55, pp 1061-1062)

**Composite graft size limit**: Conchal skin-cartilage composite grafts rebuild alar rim and columellar defects. Like skin grafts, they depend completely on the recipient bed, so they are contraindicated in irradiated or infected beds. Grafts up to about 1.5 cm can be used, but those 1 cm or smaller survive most reliably. Epidermolysis or a superficial slough in the first week is common and does not mean the graft has failed. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 55, p 1058)

**Cross-facial nerve graft staging and babysitter**: Stage 1: transect contralateral buccal branches, coapt them to a sural graft tunneled across the upper lip, and tag the distal end. Axons need about 8-9 months to cross, which you track by an advancing Tinel sign. Stage 2: coapt the graft to the paralyzed-side branch, or to the nerve of a free gracilis. Because the face keeps denervating meanwhile, an ipsilateral 'babysitter' transfer (masseteric or partial XII) can be done at stage 1. It can be left in place for dual innervation, giving tone plus spontaneous smile. CFNG gives the most emotional, coordinated movement but is weaker (few axons, two coaptations). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 55, pp 1068-1069)

**Repair thresholds and timing**: Use an interposition graft when the gap between healthy nerve ends is 1 cm or more, because mobilizing the nerve further devascularizes it. Branch injuries medial to the pupillary line are usually not repaired, because midface arborization compensates. With an intact but paralyzed nerve, about 1 year of observation is the usual limit. After that, nerve tubules fibrose, and muscle atrophy becomes irreversible by about 2-3 years, leaving only muscle transfer. Repair traumatic or iatrogenic transections at the time of injury. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 55, p 1067)

**Microstomia and commissure rules**: Estlander flaps are for defects that include the commissure; Abbe flaps are for defects that spare it. For lower-lip defects of about one-third to one-half, bilateral advancement flaps through the mental crease work. One-half to two-thirds calls for Karapandzic flaps; beyond two-thirds, use Bernard-von Burow or Gillies fan flaps with or without an Abbe flap, or a free flap. Local lip and cheek flaps for defects over two-thirds commonly cause microstomia that may need stretching devices or commissuroplasty. Free-flap reconstruction avoids microstomia. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 55, pp 1071-1072)

**Choosing the CT plane**: Read facial CT in all three planes; 3-D reconstructions aid understanding but are less precise. Axial images best show vertically oriented structures (medial orbital walls, pterygoid plates). Coronal images best show horizontal structures (orbital floors, roof). Sagittal images, especially when angled along the orbital plane, best show the orbital floor's anteroposterior extent and the optic canal. A panoramic tomogram (orthopantomogram) remains a cheap screen for mandible fractures. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 56, pp 1076-1077)

**Le Fort II false-reduction trap**: A Le Fort II segment tends to rotate superiorly at the nasofrontal junction, which opens the bite anteriorly. MMF can look as if it corrects this by pulling the mandibular condyles forward and up out of their fossae. Confirm that the condyles are seated and the maxilla is truly reduced before plating, and disimpact first with Rowe forceps or a wire through the nasal root. Fix with 1.5-2.0 mm miniplates, 2-3 screws on each side of each fracture, and use microplates at the infraorbital rim to avoid palpable lower-lid hardware. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 56, p 1082)

**Posterior table algorithm and Draf III alternative**: A nondisplaced posterior-table fracture with a fully aerated, clear sinus needs no exploration. A displaced fracture or an opacified sinus means a CSF leak or brain herniation cannot be excluded, so explore it (osteoplastic flap, or trephination with endoscopy). With an intact posterior wall but injured outflow, options are a wide endoscopic Draf III (if follow-up is reliable) or obliteration after removing all mucosa. Cranialize a shattered posterior wall. Obliteration does not guarantee a 'safe sinus': meningitis and brain abscess have been reported, which is why Draf III is gaining favor. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 56, pp 1079-1080)

**Delayed septorhinoplasty timing**: If no septal hematoma is present and closed reduction is not done or fails, plan a formal septorhinoplasty. Most surgeons wait at least 6 months for bone healing before attempting osteotomies. During closed reduction of a shifted dorsum, lift (outfracture) the nasal bones before moving them laterally. Acute open reduction is controversial because osteotomies in freshly fractured bone can create unplanned fracture lines. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 56, p 1084)

**Most commonly missed facial fracture**: NOE is the facial fracture most often missed. Telecanthus can be minimal at first and worsen into a deformity that is much harder to fix late, so look for loss of dorsal height and an evolving epicanthal fold. For type 2 and 3 injuries, pull the canthal tendon posteriorly, medially and superiorly, against its natural drift (anterior, lateral, inferior). Bone-graft a deficient anterior medial orbit first, and drill a hole in the graft for the transnasal wire. Have a low threshold for silicone lacrimal stenting. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 56, pp 1083, 1087; Ch 57, p 1098)

**Dutton indications and timing**: Classic indications for floor repair: persistent diplopia with positive forced ductions and CT entrapment that has not improved after 1-2 weeks; early enophthalmos of 3 mm or more (other sources use 2 mm); significant globe ptosis; a floor defect over 50%; and associated rim or facial fractures. Emergent indications are an oculocardiac reflex and globe herniation into the maxillary sinus. Diplopia that interferes with work (pilots, athletes) is a relative indication. Usually wait 7-10 days for edema to settle and repair within 2 weeks; repairs after 6 weeks are much harder because of fibrosis. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 57, pp 1091-1092)

**Blow-in and orbital roof fractures**: A blow-in fracture drives a rim fragment into the orbit, causing exophthalmos rather than enophthalmos. Fragment position can threaten vision, so it is a repair indication. Orbital roof fractures are 3-9% of adult facial fractures but 18-35% of pediatric ones, because a child's cranium is proportionally large. The impure (rim plus roof) blow-in is the most common type. Clues include a delayed, expanding upper-lid hematoma, forehead numbness, CSF rhinorrhea and proptosis. Observe asymptomatic displaced roof fractures for pulsatile proptosis (herniated brain), and observe an isolated CSF leak for about 1 week before dural repair. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 57, pp 1089, 1098-1099)

**Medial wall fracture types**: Medial wall fractures are typed I (isolated), II (medial wall plus floor, the most common), III (II plus rim/malar fracture) and IV (with complex midface or NOE fractures). Enophthalmos is more likely with types II-IV. Entrapment of the medial rectus is uncommon, but trapped fat or septum can cause horizontal dysmotility. Ethmoid artery injury can cause epistaxis or an orbital hematoma. Combined defects usually need a fixed implant, anchored behind the rim rather than to it. The inferior oblique can be disinserted from its origin for exposure and does not need reattachment. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 57, pp 1093-1094)

**Arch stabilization and ZMC fixation order**: For an isolated arch fracture, the Gillies approach (2-3 cm temporal hairline incision, deep to temporalis fascia, Dingman elevator) usually gives a stable reduction. An arch that stays unstable can be held with a spinal needle passed under it through the skin for about 10 days, or opened through a coronal approach. In ZMC repair, confirm reduction at every fracture site before fixing anything, because alignment at one site can hide malrotation at another. Fix superior to inferior and lateral to medial, starting at the frontozygomatic suture, with a miniplate at the zygomaticomaxillary buttress to resist masseter pull. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 57, pp 1096-1097)

**Associated ocular injuries and repair complications**: Before repair, screen for corneal abrasion, traumatic iritis (photophobia, brow ache), hyphema with pressure problems, lens dislocation (can cause angle-closure glaucoma), retinal detachment (painless vision loss, flashes, field cut) and commotio retinae. A rise in intraocular pressure on upgaze supports inferior rectus entrapment. Repair complications include lower-lid retraction, ectropion after subciliary and entropion after transconjunctival approaches, and hematic cyst around some implants. A Frost suture taped above the brow for 2-5 days helps prevent lid retraction. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 57, pp 1090, 1093; Ch 56, p 1087)

**Canalicular laceration repair**: Each canaliculus runs about 2 mm vertically, then about 8 mm horizontally. Repair a lacerated canaliculus over a silicone tube looped through both puncta, passed down the nasolacrimal duct and tied in the nose, and suture the laceration over it. Leave the stent for about 6 weeks to 3 months. Medial-canthal lacerations warrant routine probing for canalicular injury. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 58, p 1106)

**Trochlear injury**: The trochlea, the only cartilage in the orbit, sits at the superomedial orbit between roof and medial wall. A frontal sinus floor trephination or an external (Lynch) ethmoidectomy can displace or injure it. That causes superior oblique dysfunction with oblique or vertical diplopia, worse on downgaze. Trochleitis (local superomedial pain and tenderness without motility loss) responds to NSAIDs or a local steroid injection. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 58, pp 1102, 1106)

**Phases and thyroid status**: About 5-10% of patients with Graves orbitopathy are euthyroid and about 10% are hypothyroid, so normal thyroid labs do not exclude it. The active inflammatory phase lasts roughly 1.5-3 years before the cicatricial phase. Immunosuppression works only in the active phase, while elective surgery waits for inactivity. Upgaze is usually the first motility limitation. The older NO SPECS scheme grades only severity, so it has been replaced by VISA (more used in North America) and EUGOGO, which also score activity. Smoking and radioiodine worsen the eye disease, whereas methimazole, PTU and thyroidectomy appear neutral. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 58, pp 1110-1112)

**Skin test rules and MQT**: SPT contraindications: uncontrolled asthma, unstable cardiovascular disease, current beta-blocker use and pregnancy. Space sites at least 2 cm apart; sensitivity and specificity are roughly 80%. In dilutional intradermal testing, never accept a #1 endpoint, because reactions at that strength are likely irritant. Modified quantitative testing (SPT followed by a single intradermal test) estimates the starting dose with fewer supplies. It correlates well with full IDT but gives a conservative, slightly weaker starting dose. Desloratadine can suppress wheals for 10-14 days, longer than other second-generation antihistamines (about 7 days). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 59, pp 1129-1132)

**Nasal cytology phenotypes**: Nasal cytology (surface scraping, stained and read over at least 50 high-power fields) separates nonallergic rhinitis phenotypes. These are NARES (eosinophils), NARMA (mast cells), NARNE (neutrophils) and NARESMA (eosinophils plus mast cells). In allergic rhinitis the infiltrate is eosinophils > mast cells > basophils. The test is rarely used and nonspecific, but these acronyms are tested. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 59, pp 1134-1135)

**Thommen postulates and pollen seasons**: A pollen causes clinical allergy only if it is windborne, light enough to travel far, made in large amounts, widely distributed and intrinsically allergenic (Thommen's postulates). Insect-pollinated flowers rarely qualify. Typical US seasons: trees February-May (birch, oak, maple, cedar), grasses April-August (timothy, Bermuda, Johnson), weeds July to first frost (ragweed, sage, lamb's quarter). Local pollen patterns matter for testing and immunotherapy choices. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 59, p 1126)

**Perennial allergen specifics**: The two US dust mite species, Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus and D. farinae, have major allergens Der p 1 and Der f 1. They thrive at 70-80°F and 35-70% relative humidity, and the feces are the main allergen. Cat allergen Fel d 1 is in pelt, saliva and urine and is potent and persistent. Dog allergen (Can f 1) is generally weaker, and 'hypoallergenic' breeds still shed allergen. Only about 4% of patients actually remove the pet; washing it at least twice weekly lowers allergen load. Acaricides are the most effective single mite measure, and bedding should be washed in water above 140°F. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 59, pp 1127, 1136)

**Steroid routes and decongestant choice**: Depot IM corticosteroid injections are discouraged because a long-acting dose cannot be withdrawn if adrenal suppression, psychiatric, musculoskeletal or cataract effects occur. Intraturbinate steroid injection helps but is not recommended routinely, because rare transient vision loss has been reported (more with large-particle preparations). Budesonide carries the most favorable pregnancy data of the intranasal steroids (historically category B). Start intranasal steroids about 2 weeks before pollen season. Oral phenylephrine is no better than placebo, so pseudoephedrine is the systemic option, and topical decongestants should be limited to 3 days or less. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 59, pp 1138-1140)

**SCIT escalation and maintenance mechanics**: Escalate as fast as tolerated, up to twice weekly; 0.05 mL weekly steps are very safe and 0.10 mL steps are usually tolerated. A 3-4 cm local reaction suggests maintenance is reached, and larger local reactions herald systemic ones. After 6-12 months at maintenance with good control, intervals can stretch from weekly to every 4-6 weeks. Cluster dosing (2-3 injections 30 minutes apart per visit, twice weekly) reaches maintenance in about 4 weeks without more systemic reactions. A sudden reaction should prompt a check for co-seasonal exposure, respiratory infection, poorly controlled asthma, or a vial/patient/dose error. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 59, pp 1143-1145)

**AAOA SLIT drop preparation**: The AAOA task-force scheme builds a 10-mL maintenance vial in 50% glycerin, which preserves the antigen and tastes sweet. The daily dose is 0.3 mL (about 33 days per vial), delivering roughly 30 times the monthly SCIT antigen dose. An escalation vial (0.5 mL of maintenance plus 2 mL glycerin) is used first, 1 drop on day 1 rising to 7 drops by day 7. The patient then escalates on the maintenance vial over days 8-14. If reactions occur, drop back to the last tolerated dose for 3 months. Continue 3-5 years; SLIT can be stopped without tapering. In the US, only grass, short ragweed and dust-mite tablets are FDA-approved. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 59, pp 1146-1148)

**Epinephrine route (book vs current)**: Older allergy texts, including this chapter's SCIT reaction protocol, give epinephrine 0.3 mL subcutaneously, along with lying the patient flat, oxygen, IV fluids, a proximal tourniquet, IV diphenhydramine and a steroid. Current guidelines instead give 1 mg/mL epinephrine intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh, 0.01 mg/kg up to 0.5 mg in adults, repeated every 5-15 minutes as needed. Intramuscular dosing reaches peak levels faster and is the board answer. Late reactions can follow apparent recovery, so observe the patient. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 59, p 1146)

**Food allergy vs intolerance and testing**: Food intolerance is nonimmune (lactose intolerance, vasoactive amines, additives such as sulfites, tartrazine and glutamate). Toxic reactions to contaminants affect anyone exposed. IgE-mediated allergy most often involves peanut, tree nuts, milk (casein), egg white (albumin) and wheat. Food-specific IgG reflects dietary exposure and does not diagnose allergy. The double-blind placebo-controlled food challenge is the reference standard, but it carries anaphylaxis risk in true IgE allergy and suffers from placebo effects. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 59, pp 1148-1150)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Topical cocaine dosing**: Cocaine is an ester anesthetic (metabolized by plasma cholinesterase; amides are cleared hepatically) and the only local anesthetic that is also a strong vasoconstrictor. It works by blocking norepinephrine and epinephrine reuptake. The usual maximum topical dose is about 200-300 mg (often quoted as about 3 mg/kg). Four mL of 4% solution contains 160 mg, and roughly 40% is absorbed from pledgets. Toxicity includes CNS excitation, hypertension, tachyarrhythmia and coronary vasospasm. Be cautious in patients with cholinesterase deficiency or on MAO inhibitors. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 60, p 1174)

topic: External Branch of the Superior Laryngeal Nerve Injury
text: **Gutman sign**: Normally, lateral compression of the thyroid cartilage raises vocal pitch and anterior pressure lowers it. With superior laryngeal nerve (cricothyroid) paralysis the response reverses, which is the Gutman sign. It is a bedside clue to add to stroboscopy (posterior glottic rotation toward the weak side) and laryngeal EMG. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 60, p 1197)

**Release maneuvers and length gained**: Typical length gained: blunt anterior mobilization of the larynx and trachea, about 3 cm; partial incision of annular ligaments on opposite sides above and below the anastomosis, about 1.5 cm; suprahyoid laryngeal release, about 5 cm. Infrahyoid (thyrohyoid) release gains length but causes more dysphagia and aspiration, so the suprahyoid release is preferred. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 60, p 1197)

**'Rule of 10s' is outdated**: Older review texts, including this one, still teach the rule of 10s (10% bilateral, 10% familial, 10% malignant). Current genetics shows that about one-third or more of head and neck paragangliomas are hereditary (mostly SDHx), and familial cases are often multicentric. Boards now expect genetic counseling and SDH testing for every patient. Treat a '10% familial' answer as historical. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 60, p 1201)

**Teflon granuloma recognition and imaging**: an expansile granuloma can appear years after a Teflon injection that gave a good voice, sometimes after later intubation trauma. It looks like a smooth submucosal bulge of the false fold, ventricle, true fold or subglottis, and stroboscopy shows a stiff, nonvibrating fold. Contrast CT shows a brightly enhancing, fairly well-circumscribed paraglottic mass and separates superficial granulomas (endoscopic removal) from extensive ones (open lateral laryngotomy). (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 50, p 441)

**Open Teflon granuloma removal and the empty paraglottic space**: a parasagittal laryngotomy 5-7 mm off midline is the only approach that usually removes a granuloma completely. It suits cases where the vocal ligament and free-edge mucosa are spared; ligament involvement favors endoscopic treatment. The defect is filled with a posteriorly based pedicled fat flap plus arytenoid adduction and, if no mucosal tear, a Silastic implant, slightly overmedialized because the flap atrophies over months to years. The same flap treats the atrophic 'empty paraglottic space' caused by an oversized implant. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 50, p 442-446)

**Imaging a laryngocele**: get the CT during a Valsalva maneuver so the sac fills; air (black) means laryngocele and mucus (soft-tissue density) means saccular cyst. A combined lesion has a dumbbell shape, narrowing where it passes through the thyrohyoid membrane at the superior laryngeal neurovascular foramen. Biopsy is rarely needed, but examine the anterior ventricle and use ductal lavage or biopsy if malignancy is suspected. Have the patient Valsalva during the office exam to show the neck component. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 51, p 448-449)

**Presentation details**: most laryngoceles are asymptomatic incidental findings, usually in men in their 50s-60s; when symptomatic, hoarseness is most common, followed by cough or globus, and some patients have only altered resonance. A combined lesion gives an intermittent, soft, compressible mass at the superolateral thyroid cartilage, and the medial piriform wall may bulge. A laryngopyocele presents as a warm, painful, enlarging neck mass with possible stridor, dyspnea or odynophagia. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 51, p 448-449)

**Who gets surgery**: absolute indications are a symptomatic combined laryngocele (hoarseness or airway compromise) and suspected malignancy; cosmesis (for example a large lesion in a horn player) is relative, and asymptomatic incidental lesions are not excised. For bilateral combined laryngoceles, some surgeons stage the two sides and confirm sensation on the first side with FEES, because injuring both internal SLN branches causes dysphagia and aspiration. Elderly patients tolerate this sensory loss worst. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 51, p 449, 453)

**External (transthyroid) excision keys**: do microlaryngoscopy with 30/70-degree telescopes first to exclude a ventricular tumor, then distend the sac by deflating the cuff and giving positive pressure. Stay right on the capsule posteriorly at the thyrohyoid membrane, where the SLN runs next to it, and reach the internal part through an inferiorly based outer perichondrial flap and a triangle of thyroid ala (base at the upper border, apex halfway down). The saccule base sits in the anterior ventricle, about 3-5 mm behind the midline at mid-lamina height. Excise it with a cuff of ventricular mucosa and close with a figure-of-eight suture, because a retained base causes recurrence. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 51, p 450-453)

**Who does not need open repair, and who needs observation**: no exploration for a nondisplaced thyroid fracture, an isolated hyoid fracture, a thyroid fracture limited to the posterior third of the lamina, or a nondisplaced cricoid fracture that does not narrow the subglottis. Also defer it in unstable patients (sepsis, head injury) or with cervical spine injury. Observe in hospital for 12-24 hours for laryngeal hematoma, generalized edema, or a strangulation or attempted hanging injury, which can swell late. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 52, p 456)

**Fixation specifics**: place miniplates perpendicular to a vertical thyroid fracture with two screws on each side, one plate superiorly and one inferiorly, using the calcified inferior border for purchase. In young, poorly calcified cartilage use larger 'emergency' screws or absorbable plates; Prolene suture reduction is more likely to loosen and malunite, and titanium mesh can bridge comminution. Keep any nonabsorbable suture outside the lumen to prevent granulation and stenosis. On closure, resuspend the anterior fold ends to the commissure. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 52, p 458-461)

**Stents after fracture repair**: stent only when the repaired framework is unstable or endolaryngeal lacerations are extensive. Options in order of preference are the Montgomery laryngeal stent, Aboulker stent, rolled Silastic sheet, a glove finger packed with foam, or a T-tube (best for cricotracheal injury, with the upper limb trimmed to sit at or just below the folds, or the patient aspirates). Secure it with transcervical sutures tied over buttons. The authors leave stents about 2-4 weeks; the commentator limits them to 7-14 days and considers mitomycin unproven. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 52, p 457-461)

**SLAD-R technique**: the operation is bilateral. Through an inferiorly based thyroid cartilage window (keeping a posterior strut with the cricothyroid joint to protect the main RLN and PCA branch), the TA adductor branch is divided distal to the PCA branches and its distal stump is reinnervated with an ansa cervicalis branch (sternohyoid or sternothyroid) using 7-0/8-0 epineural sutures. The LCA branch is cut and a partial LCA myotomy of only 15-30% of the muscle is added. A full myotomy causes a posterior glottic chink, especially in men. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 53, p 464-467)

**SLAD-R candidacy and recovery**: the best candidates are young, respond well to botulinum toxin and have little tremor; contraindications are abductor or mixed SD, functional dysphonia or MTD, relative age over 65, and prominent tremor, which does not improve. The voice is breathy for 3-6 months (like a large bilateral TA toxin dose), and thin-liquid dysphagia is common in the first days. Strength improves by 9-12 months, and over 75% end with a normal voice. True recurrence appears within 12 months and responds to toxin, while persistent breathiness is treated with augmentation. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 53, p 464, 469-470)

**Why ansa-RLN helps and when it falls short**: adductor fibers make up about 75-80% of RLN axons, so nonselective reinnervation restores tone and bulk that favor a medial fold, with no implant to damp vibration, but it does not restore purposeful motion. Cutting the RLN also removes unfavorable synkinesis, which is itself an indication. Results are poorer over age 60 and with a wide gap from a high vagal lesion, because the paralyzed cricothyroid no longer adds tonic adduction. A contralateral ansa takes up to about 6 months rather than 3-4, and voice therapy is still needed in about half of patients. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 54, p 471-477)

**Ansa-RLN technique points**: find the ansa on the internal jugular vein with a nerve stimulator before paralysis, using the largest branch or branches (sternothyroid, sternohyoid), and find the RLN by rotating the larynx and spreading vertically just behind the cricothyroid joint, then follow it 3-4 cm to Berry ligament. Leave about 1 cm of overlap so swallowing excursion does not tension the repair. Recut the ends with a scalpel on a tongue blade and coapt with about 4 epineural 8-0 nylon sutures, with an optional vein cuff; anastomose more distally after thyroidectomy injury. Add injection laryngoplasty to bridge the roughly 4 months until benefit appears. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 54, p 472-475)

**Hypopharyngeal pharyngoplasty for high vagal paralysis**: a static adjunct, usually done with medialization and arytenoid adduction, that removes a posterior block of thyroid cartilage (about 1.5 x 1 cm in men), excises the paralyzed piriform mucosa like a diverticulum (stapler flush with the muscular process), and advances the inferior constrictor-perichondrial flap about 1.5-2 cm forward on the ala. The narrower funnel lets the innervated side generate more bolus pressure, but the cricopharyngeus is not treated, so a myotomy may be added. Best candidates are under 65; contraindications include Chiari malformation, brainstem stroke and diffuse dysmotility. A Valsalva leak test under saline helps prevent pharyngocutaneous fistula. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 55, p 479-485)

**Rehabilitating a unilateral high vagal or bulbar deficit**: in a reasonably fit patient, surgical rehabilitation can combine medialization laryngoplasty, arytenoid adduction, cricopharyngeal myectomy, hypopharyngeal pharyngoplasty and, in selected cases, great auricular-to-SLN neurorrhaphy in one sitting. The palate is treated later by injection, a superiorly based flap, or unilateral palatal adhesion. Get FEES and a modified barium swallow first, and use esophageal manometry to exclude a major motility disorder. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 55, p 480-481)

**Gray minithyrotomy access**: it reaches the subepithelial plane of the membranous fold without an epithelial incision, through a 2-3 cm neck incision with microlaryngoscopic video guidance. A fine needle through the midline thyroid cartilage localizes the glottis, then a 1-3 mm drill tunnel is made about 3-5 mm off midline, angled along the fold's long axis rather than perpendicular to the lamina. Tympanoplasty instruments release the adhesion and create a pocket confined to the scar. It does not treat epithelium and gives little medialization. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 56, p 487-490)

**Adult laryngotracheal reconstruction with costal cartilage**: indications are failed endoscopic treatment, cartilage collapse or malacia, and stenosis longer than 2-3 cm; relative contraindications include immunosuppression, steroid dependence, significant lung or heart disease, untreated OSA, renal failure, active GPA and poorly controlled diabetes (follow HbA1c). Harvest the 7th or 8th rib (a thicker diaphragm lowers pneumothorax risk) and carve a beveled boat or hexagon with perichondrium facing the lumen; a septal composite graft can cover defects of about 2 cm. Keep the tracheotomy at least 2 rings below the graft to lower infection and restenosis risk. The Montgomery stent comes out at 3-4 weeks, and a single-stage repair needs at least 24 hours of ICU intubation. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 57, p 497-510)

**Staged and lining options for adult stenosis**: in an open-trough laryngotracheoplasty, excise the scar, line the trough with a buccal mucosal graft, and later prefabricate a skin flap over buried polypropylene mesh with a T-tube for 3-4 weeks. That flap is then rotated to close the anterior wall, and decannulation is assessed at 3-6 months. Alternatives are a split-thickness skin graft wrapped skin-side-in around a T-tube limb, or a strap muscle (sternohyoid myocartilaginous) flap, useful in diabetics with long-segment stenosis. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 57, p 503-508)

**Cricotracheal resection selection**: the best candidates have isolated short-segment grade III-IV subglottic stenosis at least 5 mm below the folds, with success over 90%. Operate only on mature scar; rapidly recurring stenosis (under 6 months), active autoimmune inflammation, glottic involvement, long segments and prior low tracheal resection are relative contraindications, and removing the cricoid arch adds about 2 cm to the defect. Cut the lateral cricoid at 45 degrees to spare the cricothyroid joints (RLN entry), thin the posterior plate with a diamond burr, and place internal Grillo detensioning sutures (thyroid to cricoid to trachea). If unsure between LTR and CTR, start with an anterior cricoid split carried into the stoma, which allows either. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 58, p 511-517)

**After cricotracheal resection**: a two-stage repair uses a suprastomal stent or a T-tube, which must be at least 8 mm and is generally avoided under age 4; if a leak is likely, a low temporary tracheotomy at least 3 rings below the anastomosis diverts airflow for 3-4 days. Dehiscence is an emergency: secure the airway by intubating over a rod telescope and revise. Treat early granulation by removal plus ciprofloxacin-dexamethasone drops and early restenosis by balloon dilation; unilateral fold paralysis often recovers. Routine laryngeal release is avoided because it worsens dysphagia. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 58, p 512-517)

**Tracheal resection planning**: CT can underestimate the resection length, so combine it with bronchoscopic identification of normal rings above and below. Post-tracheotomy stenosis usually spares the membranous wall, so a 6.0-7.0 tube often passes despite dyspnea. Up to about 5 cm can be resected without release maneuvers; uncontrolled LPR, GPA or infection, multilevel disease and glottic involvement are contraindications. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 59, p 519-520)

**Slide tracheoplasty beyond infants**: it is now a third option alongside grafting and resection, for subglottic, multilevel, short- or long-segment stenosis, A-frame deformity, TEF and revision cases; prior low tracheal surgery, TEF or esophageal atresia repair, prior slide or resection, and laryngotracheoesophageal cleft repair are relative contraindications. Cardiopulmonary bypass is used for complete rings or distal-third disease, while cervical cases are done without it, and circumferential dissection is avoided in older children and adults. A figure-of-8 deformity is usually asymptomatic, though some need a stent for 4-8 weeks. Success is 80-90%, and fold paralysis occurs in about 1-2%. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 60, p 525-530)

**Awake posterior pharyngeal wall augmentation in adults**: for partial or unilateral VPI (after stroke, cancer resection or radiation) when open palatal surgery is not appropriate; complete or bilateral palatal weakness is a contraindication. With a transnasal scope, map the gap dynamically, then inject submucosally at the level of Passavant ridge (transnasally, or perorally with a bent needle) as superficially as possible, through as few sites as possible because each adds extrusion risk, slightly overinjecting. Trial a temporary hyaluronic acid or CMC gel first, then calcium hydroxylapatite (about 12 months, repeatable). Aspirate before injecting laterally to avoid the carotid. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 63, p 549-552)

**UES balloon dilation protocol**: the UES is a 3-5 cm high-pressure zone shaped like a kidney bean, so side-by-side double balloons stretch it more completely. A typical 'series of three' for a CP bar is spaced about 1 month apart: one 18-20 mm balloon, then two 13-15 mm, then two 15-18 mm (about 30 mm total); a CP web often needs only one 20 mm dilation. Position the balloon with its upper end above the arytenoids but below the epiglottic tip, and hold each inflation 1 minute. Blanching and drag on withdrawal mean adequate stretch; stop if mucosa tears or bleeds, and be cautious after radiation. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 64, p 553-557)

**Selecting patients for dilation**: an obstructing bar with intact hyolaryngeal elevation does best, while weak pharyngeal squeeze or poor elevation predicts less benefit and more reflux risk; CP webs likely explain much undiagnosed solid-food dysphagia. Dilation can be definitive or a trial that predicts response to myotomy. Awake transnasal dilation under moderate sedation (for example midazolam about 0.03 mg/kg with fentanyl about 0.5 mcg/kg) gives a better UES view and avoids general anesthesia. Complications are mucosal tear, bleeding, perforation and, rarely, pneumomediastinum. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 64, p 553-558)

**Epidemiology and exam clues**: Zenker diverticulum is rare (prevalence about 0.01-0.11%, incidence about 2 per 100,000 per year) and peaks in the 70s-80s. Besides dysphagia and regurgitation, look for cervical borborygmi (Boyce sign), crepitus and malnutrition. Pain is unusual and should raise concern for malignancy. Symptoms can escalate quickly even when the pouch has not grown. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 65, p 559-560)

**Size classifications and preop checks**: Morton grades pouches as under 2 cm, 2-4 cm or over 4 cm; van Overbeek counts vertebral bodies spanned (1, 1-3, over 3); Lahey stages by shape. Evaluate the entire esophagus, because achalasia, a large hiatal hernia or a distal stricture must be treated first or the patient may worsen, and high-resolution manometry may need fluoroscopic catheter placement. Do flexible laryngoscopy or FEES before surgery to document fold motion, since an unknown contralateral paralysis plus an RLN injury can obstruct the airway. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 65, p 561-562)

**Endoscopic diverticulostomy pearls**: plan the airway with anesthesia (rapid sequence induction for a large food-filled pouch) and inspect the postcricoid mucosa first, biopsying and stopping if a lesion is found. The Weerda distending diverticuloscope is the only one that fits the commercial endoscopic stapler; put the longer anvil jaw in the esophagus and the cartridge in the pouch, and divide residual distal CP muscle with scissors or laser. With the CO2 laser (about 5-12 W), cut to the pouch floor while keeping the periesophageal/buccopharyngeal fascia intact to prevent mediastinitis. Afterward watch for fever, tachycardia and chest or back pain. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 65, p 563-568)

**Choosing open Zenker surgery**: diverticulectomy (most common), diverticulopexy and inversion all require a cricopharyngeal myotomy, and a pouch under 1 cm usually needs only the myotomy. An open approach is favored for younger patients, pouches over 5-6 cm, failed endoscopic exposure and, more controversially, revision; some also favor it for pouches under 2 cm, whose party wall is too short. Approach from the left with a bougie (about 36-40 Fr) in the esophagus and the pouch packed, staple the neck without narrowing the lumen, and extend the myotomy 4-5 cm into the esophagus. Get a barium study on postoperative day 1; morbidity is about 10.5% and mortality about 0.6%. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 66, p 569-575)

**Superior laryngeal nerve block indications**: an office injection for refractory neurogenic cough (over 8 weeks, workup negative) or paralaryngeal pain, with about 80% response. The best candidates feel an irritative focus localized to one posterior thyrohyoid space, and palpation there triggers cough. Contraindications are an incomplete workup, local anesthetic or steroid allergy, and uncontrolled diabetes (steroid-induced hyperglycemia). (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 67, p 577-578)

**Irritable larynx and the internal SLN**: neurogenic cough is thought to follow post-viral damage to the internal SLN, which enters through the posterior thyrohyoid membrane. Its upper division supplies the inferior pharynx, epiglottis, vallecula and vestibule, and its lower division supplies the aryepiglottic and false folds. Cough and pain share the TRPV1 receptor, so blocking the nerve may interrupt a sensory feedback loop. Neurogenic cough is often part of irritable larynx syndrome, along with throat clearing, globus, MTD and paradoxical vocal fold motion. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 67, p 577-578)

**Thyroid angle and the anterior commissure**: the thyroid alae meet at about 90 degrees in adult men and about 120 degrees in women, which is why the male notch (Adam's apple) projects after puberty. The anterior commissure tendon attaches on the inner midline of the thyroid cartilage, below the notch. Its level varies, so before any anterior cartilage resection, localize it with a needle passed under endoscopic view. Staying at or above the epiglottic petiole level is safe. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 62, p 541-544)

**Clothesline injury and laryngotracheal separation**: classically a motorcycle or snowmobile rider at dusk or dawn strikes a rope or wire; the neck may look nearly normal while edema builds over hours, with only soft tissue holding the airway open. Intubation can complete the separation, so tracheotomy is the safest airway, and bilateral RLN injury is common. Airway takes precedence over voice, and later cordotomy or arytenoidectomy may be needed to decannulate. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 52, p 455-456)

**Gray minithyrotomy grafting and recovery**: implant fat strips (8-15 mm long, about 1-2 mL per fold), and do not undercorrect, since too little fat is the usual cause of failure; fascia, perichondrium and acellular dermis have also been used. Pinhole epithelial perforations are acceptable, but a large tear means stopping and returning after healing. Expect about a week of voice rest and roughly 1 month of phonatory recovery. Late deterioration is blamed on poor fat-graft survival. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 56, p 489-492)

**Tracheal resection technique**: dissect directly on the cartilage without seeking the RLNs, and free no more than 1-2 cm of normal trachea beyond the cuts to preserve blood supply. Close the membranous wall first, keep all knots outside the lumen, and leak-test under saline. If the innominate artery is exposed, interpose a sternohyoid flap. This chapter keeps the chin-to-chest stitch for 2 weeks, with voice rest for 3-5 days and a chest film to check for pneumothorax. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 59, p 520-524)

**SLN block technique and schedule**: mix 1 mL 0.5% bupivacaine with 1 mL triamcinolone 40 mg/mL just before use, and inject with a 27 g needle into the posterior thyrohyoid membrane just anterior to the superior cornu, aspirating first to avoid intravascular injection. Relief begins in 2-3 days; if there is none at 2 weeks, inject the other side, and stop if that also fails. Repeat responding blocks every 4-16 weeks. Drop the steroid if more than 3-4 blocks per year are needed, to limit adrenal suppression and skin atrophy. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch 67, p 579-581)
